nodes.label: SEC_2
nodes.input_summary: Subproblem 2: Point-circle incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-freeness
nodes.output_json: {"target_claim": "For |P|=n let C be the n unit circles centred at the points of P. Prove the circles are distinct, no point of P lies on its own circle, and I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly. Prove two distinct points lie on at most two unit circles centred in P and two distinct unit circles meet in at most two points, hence the incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free, while explicitly not claiming K_{2,2}-freeness.", "title": "Point-circle incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-freeness"}

output.target_claim: For |P|=n let C be the n unit circles centred at the points of P. Prove the circles are distinct, no point of P lies on its own circle, and I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly. Prove two distinct points lie on at most two unit circles centred in P and two distinct unit circles meet in at most two points, hence the incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free, while explicitly not claiming K_{2,2}-freeness.
output.title: Point-circle incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-freeness

nodes.label: SEC_4
nodes.input_summary: Subproblem 4: Pruned circular-arc graph with P as vertex set
nodes.output_json: {"target_claim": "Let k_i be the number of points of P on the i-th unit circle. Discard circles with k_i<=2, losing at most 2n incidences. For k_i>=3 order the points cyclically on the circle and join consecutive points by the circle arcs containing no third point of P in their interior. Prove the resulting drawing has v=n, no loops, e_arc >= I(P,C)-2n, edge multiplicity at most 2 because two vertices determine at most two possible unit centres, and hence a simple subgraph H' with e' >= e_arc/2.", "title": "Pruned circular-arc graph with P as vertex set"}

output.target_claim: Let k_i be the number of points of P on the i-th unit circle. Discard circles with k_i<=2, losing at most 2n incidences. For k_i>=3 order the points cyclically on the circle and join consecutive points by the circle arcs containing no third point of P in their interior. Prove the resulting drawing has v=n, no loops, e_arc >= I(P,C)-2n, edge multiplicity at most 2 because two vertices determine at most two possible unit centres, and hence a simple subgraph H' with e' >= e_arc/2.
output.title: Pruned circular-arc graph with P as vertex set

nodes.label: SEC_5
nodes.input_summary: Subproblem 5: Crossing upper bound with tangency, vertex, and concurrency control
nodes.output_json: {"target_claim": "Prove cr(H') <= 2\\binom{n}{2} <= n^2 for the arc drawing of Subproblem 4. Show arcs on the same circle meet only at endpoints, crossings between arcs on distinct circles can occur only at transverse intersection points of the two circles, tangencies contribute no proper crossing, intersections lying in P are vertices rather than crossings, and concurrent intersections of several circles are resolved by an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of arcs that does not increase the per-circle-pair budget of at most 2 crossings.", "title": "Crossing upper bound with tangency, vertex, and concurrency control"}

output.target_claim: Prove cr(H') <= 2\binom{n}{2} <= n^2 for the arc drawing of Subproblem 4. Show arcs on the same circle meet only at endpoints, crossings between arcs on distinct circles can occur only at transverse intersection points of the two circles, tangencies contribute no proper crossing, intersections lying in P are vertices rather than crossings, and concurrent intersections of several circles are resolved by an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of arcs that does not increase the per-circle-pair budget of at most 2 crossings.
output.title: Crossing upper bound with tangency, vertex, and concurrency control

nodes.label: SEC_6
nodes.input_summary: Subproblem 6: Upper bound U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3})
nodes.output_json: {"target_claim": "Combine Subproblems 2, 4 and 5 with the crossing lemma: if e'<4n then I(P,C)=O(n), and otherwise e'^3/(64n^2) <= cr(H') <= n^2, so e'=O(n^{4/3}), I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}), and U(P)=I(P,C)/2=O(n^{4/3}) uniformly in P. output.normalized_problem: For P subset R^2, |P|=n, let U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|. Prove c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C,c'>0, using (a) reduction to incidences of n points vs n unit circles and Szemeredi-Trotter-type bound, (b) scaled integer lattice with radius sqrt(R) where R has many representations as sum of two squares.
output.primary_route: Lemma A (Incidence reduction): U(P)=I(P,C)/2 where C={unit circles centered at P}. Lemma B (Forbidden K_{2,3}): Two distinct points lie on at most 2 unit circles, so incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free; edge multiplicity of circle-intersection graph <=2. Lemma C (Crossing Lemma with multiplicity 2): For graph G with n vertices, m edges, max multiplicity mu=2, cr(G) >= m^3/(64 mu n^2) for m>=4 mu n, else trivial. Lemma D (Circle incidence bound): Draw n unit circles; form graph G whose vertices are points of P plus intersection points, edges are circle arcs between them; crossings <=2*C(n,2) since two circles cross <=2 times; counting gives I=O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3}+n+m) specialization m=n yields I=O(n^{4/3}), hence U_max=O(n^{4/3}). Lemma E (Number theory): If p_i=1 mod 4 primes, R=prod p_i, then r_2(R)=4*2^k large ~ R^{c/log log R}. Lemma F (Lattice counting): Take S={(x,y) in Z^2: |x|,|y|<=M}, M~R^{alpha}; count pairs at distance sqrt(R) is ~ |S|*r_2(R)/poly; pigeonhole a dense translate/cluster of n points preserving many unit distances after scaling by 1/sqrt(R). Conclude superlinear lower bound.
backup_routes: Backup 1: Prove incidence bound via random sampling plus K_{2,3} Kovari-Sos-Turan weak bound O(n^{5/3}) then boost by cutting / divide-and-conquer on cells to O(n^{4/3}). Backup 2: Use Szemeredi-Trotter for lines via point-line duality and crossing lemma, then lift to circles by inversion or by splitting circles into two pseudo-parabolas. Backup 3: For lower bound use Erdos integer-grid sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) with averaging over distances 1..O(n) to get Omega(n log log n) weaker but elementary fallback if sum-of-two-squares optimization fails.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Controlling edge multiplicity and degeneracy in circle-arrangement graph: naive crossing-lemma application overcounts because coincident circle arcs can overlap, tangencies give single intersection, and vertices of degree 2 from empty arcs inflate n without helping; must prune circles with <=2 incident points and argue multiplicity <=2 from at most 2 intersections of two unit circles, otherwise crossing upper bound cr<=n^2 is invalid and incidence exponent collapses.
active_obligations: O1: Justify Lemma B rigorously: at most 2 unit circles through 2 points, at most 2 intersections of 2 unit circles, handling coincident circles and tangent cases. O2: Prove Crossing Lemma with multiplicity and linear threshold, including Euler formula base cr>=m-3n. O3: Construct arrangement graph formally and relate m_edges to I, removing low-degree circles. O4: Prove r_2(R) lower bound via prime factorization theorem for sums of two squares and divisor growth. O5: Show lattice cluster extraction yields exactly n points with claimed preserved unit count after scaling, controlling boundary losses.
output.next_task: Formalize incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-free property and set up circle-arrangement graph with pruning for crossing-lemma count.
output.concrete_next_task: Write Lemma A+B proof: define C, prove I=2U, prove two points in at most 2 unit circles via rhombus geometry; then define pruned family C' of circles with >=3 points and bound discarded incidences by 2n.
output.readiness_assessment: Ready to execute upper bound modulo standard crossing lemma; lower-bound number theory needs careful quantitative choice of k, M, R to balance r_2(R) vs lattice size; main risk is lattice boundary error and extraction to exact n.
risky_lemmas: Risky: Lemma D exponent depends on correct multiplicity handling and crossing upper bound O(n^2); if tangencies or overlapping circles miscounted, constant/exponent fails. Risky: Lemma F density claim that Omega fraction of lattice pairs at distance sqrt(R) survive in an n-subset; requires averaging/pigeonholing with explicit M vs R tradeoff, sensitive to R >> M^2 vs R << M^2.

output.primary_route: Route C: Number-theoretic lower bound + Graph-crossing incidence upper bound. Step A Lower: Take integer grid G_m = {0,...,m-1} x {0,...,m-1} scaled by 1/L. Or take points {(x,y) in Z^2: x^2+y^2 <= R}. Count representations of integers as sum of two squares. Use that numbers with many divisors give many vectors of same length. Choose radius r with maximal r_2(r) = |{(a,b): a^2+b^2=r}|. By pigeonhole and divisor bound, exists r <= n with r_2(r) >= exp(c log n / log log n). Take P as grid portion to realize n^{1+c/log log n} pairs at distance sqrt(r), then rescale to distance 1. Simpler weak version: m x m grid gives Omega(m^2 log m)?? Use number of vectors (a,b) with a^2+b^2 <= small: count unit distances after scaling. Deduce Omega(n log n / sqrt(log n)). Step B Upper: Build unit-distance graph G on P with e=U(P) edges drawn as straight segments. Two distinct unit circles intersect at most twice, so crossing number cr(G) <= C(n,2) essentially number of circle-pair intersections. More precisely draw circles of radius 1 around each point: we have n points and n circles, incidences I = 2e. Apply Szemeredi-Trotter type point-circle incidence bound I = O(N^{2/3} M^{2/3}+N+M) for N points M circles with proof via crossing lemma or cuttings. With N=M=n get 2e=O(n^{4/3}), hence e=O(n^{4/3}). Provide full proof of incidence bound: form graph with vertices = points on circles, edges = arcs between consecutive points, bound crossings by circle pairs, apply crossing-number inequality cr >= e^3/(64 v^2) when e>=4v, split into low/high degree circles to handle vertices of degree <2.
backup_routes: Backup 1: Direct Crossing Inequality on unit-distance graph without full incidence machinery: delete high-degree vertices, bound edge multiplicities, apply cr(G) <= n^2 and cr(G) >= e^3/(64 n^2) to get e=O(n^{4/3}). Backup 2: Use Szemeredi-Trotter point-line reduction via inversion or lifting to 3D paraboloid and polynomial method (Guth-Katz) for weaker O(n^{4/3}) or stronger o(n^{4/3}) remark. Backup 3 for lower bound: Use sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) integer lattice scaled by 1/sqrt(log n) to get elementary Omega(n log n / sqrt(log n)) avoiding deep sum-of-two-squares, using Landau-Ramanujan count of representable distances.
output.first_hard_obstruction: The first hard obstruction is proving the point-circle incidence bound I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}) rigorously: naive K_{2,2}-free incidence gives only O(n^{3/2}) via Kővári–Sós–Turán, insufficient. Need crossing-number inequality which itself requires probabilistic lower bound on crossing number and handling of degenerate cases where many points are concircular (circles with <3 points give no edges, circles with huge multiplicity cause vertex-edge imbalance). Without careful splitting into light/heavy circles the graph argument collapses.
active_obligations: Obligation 1: Justify existence of integer r with many representations r_2(r) large, using prime factorization  p=1 mod 4 and divisor lower bound. Obligation 2: Transfer vector-count to point-set count without losing factor due to boundary effects in grid. Obligation 3: Prove crossing-number inequality e>=4v => cr>=e^3/64v^2 via random induced subgraph and Euler formula. Obligation 4: Construct incidence graph from circles, count vertices v<=I, edges e>=I-M, crossings <=2*C(M,2), and handle low-richness circles separately.
output.next_task: Establish the two key lemmas: Divisor-rich radius lemma for lower bound and Point-circle incidence lemma for upper bound, then combine to final U_max bounds.
output.concrete_next_task: Write proof of crossing-number inequality and deduce: if I is number of incidences between n points and n unit circles, then I=O(n^{4/3}), hence U(P)=I/2=O(n^{4/3}); in parallel write grid counting showing number of unit pairs after suitable scaling is at least n^{1+c/log log n}.
output.readiness_assessment: Ready to execute: standard tools (Euler formula, probabilistic method, divisor estimates, sum-of-two-squares theorem) are available; main risk is technical bookkeeping for degenerate circles and boundary of grid, but both are manageable with splitting argument.
risky_lemmas: Lemma R1: There exists r <= n with number of representations as sum of two squares >= n^{c/log log n} - relies on choosing product of primes 1 mod 4 and needs prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions or simple construction; must verify r not too large. Lemma R2: Crossing inequality constant and applicability when graph has multiple edges or loops - unit-distance graph is simple, but auxiliary circle-arc graph has at most 2 parallel edges, needs care. Lemma R3: Claim that two unit circles intersect at most twice gives global crossing bound - need to argue no three circles concurrent at crossing causes overcount, and tangencies handled.

preserved_critiques.claim: Critique: Gap between lower ~n^{1+o(1)} and upper O(n^{4/3}) remains huge; cannot claim tightness. Critique: Elementary lattice gives only n log n / sqrt(log n), not full Erdős n^{1+c/log log n} without deeper number theory. Critique: Must not confuse unit-distance graph crossings with circle-circle intersections: segment crossings are subset of circle intersections but need distinct circles argument.

analysis.plan: The unit-distance problem asks for max number of unit pairs among n points in plane. Need both lower bound construction and upper bound proof. Classic results: Erdős lower bound n^{1+c/log log n} via integer grid, and Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via point-circle incidences / crossing number. Candidate must outline both sides rigorously without gaps.

falsifier_report.assessment: The core architecture is correct and standard: an Erdős grid/sum-of-two-squares lower bound of n^{1+c/log log n} and a Spencer-Szemerédi-Trotter O(n^{4/3}) upper bound via point-circle incidences and the crossing lemma. It is not falsified. It is not yet a complete rigorous proof: the lower-bound parameter transfer, the treatment of low-richness circles and multiedges in the incidence graph, and the distinction between segment crossings and circle intersections all contain gaps or imprecise claims. The problem also cannot be closed tightly; the stated bounds are best-known type bounds with a large open gap, not a determination of U_max(n).
unresolved_to_preserve: Preserve the gap critique: lower bound is only n^{1+c/log log n} and in particular super-polylogarithmic over n, while upper bound is O(n^{4/3}); no tight exponent is proved. Preserve the warning that segment crossings and circle-circle intersections are different objects. Preserve the need for prime-distribution input for primes 1 mod 4 or an equivalent construction of integers with many sum-of-two-squares representations.
minimal_weakenings: Weaken the claim to: for some absolute c>0, U_max(n) >= n^{1+c/log log n} for all large n after monotonicity/padding from special grid sizes, and U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3}). Do not claim an exact maximum or tight bound. Either prove the elementary averaging lower bound explicitly using Landau-Ramanujan as a cited deep theorem, or present only the Erdős product-of-primes construction and omit the alleged elementary Omega(n log n/sqrt(log n)) shortcut. State the incidence lemma for n points and m unit circles as I=O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3}+n+m) with low-richness circles handled separately.
dropped_objections: The objection that two unit circles meet in at most two points is insufficient by itself is not fatal once the arc-graph formulation is used; it becomes a valid crossing bound for arcs from distinct circles. The concern about constants in the crossing lemma is not fatal; any absolute constant suffices for O(n^{4/3}). The implication n^{1+c/log log n} implies Omega(n log n/sqrt(log n)) is valid for large n and should not be treated as an error.
weakest_lemmas: R1 divisor-rich radius lemma: if r is a product of k distinct primes all 1 mod 4 then r_2(r)=4*2^k up to ordering/sign conventions, but one needs an upper bound log r = sum log p_i = O(k log k) or similar, requiring control of the k-th such prime via the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions or a substitute construction. hidden_assumptions: Assumes n can be taken as a perfect square grid size and then extended to all n by monotonicity of U_max. Assumes the chosen highly representable r satisfies sqrt(r) <= m/2 or comparable so boundary loss is only a constant factor. Assumes r_2 counts ordered signed representations consistently and each interior grid point sees the same number of partners. Assumes no three relevant circles create a crossing at a non-vertex point counted with uncontrolled multiplicity, and tangencies can be perturbed or counted crudely. Assumes at most two unit circles centered at points of P pass through two given points of P, bounding parallel arcs by 2. Assumes Dirichlet/PNT for arithmetic progressions or Landau-Ramanujan if those routes are invoked.
boundary_cases: Circles with k_i=0 or 1 contribute incidences but no arcs; circles with k_i=2 contribute two parallel arcs between the same vertices and must be counted separately, contributing O(n) incidences after the at-most-two-circles-through-two-points observation or a direct bound. Points on grid boundary lose displacement translates; choosing sqrt(r) too close to m can destroy the count. Small n and the case e_arc<4v must give I=O(n) directly. Tangential circles and coincident intersection points that lie in P are vertices, not crossings, and must not be double counted. Repeated distances after rescaling require the chosen popular distance to be nonzero.
theorem_misuse: Potential misuse 1: applying the crossing-number inequality cr >= e^3/(64v^2) to a multigraph with loops or unrestricted parallel edges without reduction to a simple graph or bounded-multiplicity version. Potential misuse 2: citing Szemerédi-Trotter for point-circle incidences as if it were the point-line theorem; unit circles need the crossing/cutting proof or a stated point-circle incidence theorem. Potential misuse 3: invoking Kővári-Sós-Turán K_{2,2}-freeness would give only O(n^{3/2}) and cannot be upgraded without crossings. Potential misuse 4: calling Landau-Ramanujan elementary. Potential misuse 5: asserting cr of the straight-line unit-distance graph is at most C(n,2) merely because two circles meet twice; that identification needs proof and is not the standard route.

categorized_objections.claim: Correctness gaps: lower-bound boundary/parameter transfer; arc-graph construction for k_i<=2 and parallel edges; crossing count at common points and tangencies. Depth-of-input gaps: primes 1 mod 4 with size control for R1; Landau-Ramanujan if the averaging grid shortcut is used. Exposition/theorem-use risks: segment crossings versus circle intersections; point-line Szemerédi-Trotter versus point-circle incidences; tightness overclaim. Non-fatal issues: constants in crossing lemma, padding from square n to general n, convention factors in r_2.

decisive_tests: Test R1 by writing r as product of the first k primes 1 mod 4, estimating log r and r_2(r), then checking with m about sqrt(n) that (m-sqrt(r))^2 r_2(r)/2 >= n^{1+c/log log n} for large n. unresolved_objections: Whether the strategy supplies a self-contained proof of the needed prime-distribution estimate for primes 1 mod 4, rather than citing it. Whether the claimed elementary Omega(n log n/sqrt(log n)) grid bound is proved without Landau-Ramanujan or an equivalent representable-integers estimate. Whether all degenerate incidence cases are handled with constants that still yield I=O(n^{4/3}) when m=n. These are repairable but must be resolved before the strategy counts as a complete rigorous argument.

analysis.plan: The unit-distance maximum asks for Theta bounds: linear lower bound from grid and subquadratic upper bound from incidences. Let I be incidences between P and unit circles centered at P. Then 2*U = I. So bounding U is bounding point-circle incidences. The hard part is that circles are not lines, so Szemeredi-Trotter does not apply directly. Strategy must reduce to pseudo-line incidence via splitting/cutting or inversion, plus handle high-multiplicity coincidences.

output.normalized_problem: Given n points P in R^2, let U(P) = |{{p,q} in P choose 2 : |p-q|=1}| and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Prove c*n - O(sqrt(n)) <= U_max(n) <= C*n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C>0, with explicit lattice construction for lower bound and point-circle incidence theorem for upper bound. Optionally note improved Erdos n^{1+c/loglog n} lower bound as remark.
output.primary_route: Step 1 Lower bound: take m=floor(sqrt(n)), grid G={0,...,m-1}x{0,...,m-1} plus remainder. Count horizontal and vertical unit adjacencies: ~2m(m-1)=2n-O(sqrt(n)). Conclude U_max = Omega(n). Step 2 Reformulation: let C={S_p : p in P} be n unit circles centered at P. Each unit pair contributes 2 incidences, so I(P,C)=2U(P). Step 3 Incidence bound: prove I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}). Split each circle into upper and lower closed semicircles (remove left-right endpoints to avoid double count). Each family is a family of x-monotone pseudo-parabolas: any two meet at most once (after split). Apply Szemeredi-Trotter for pseudo-lines via crossing-number or cuttings to get I = O(|P|^{2/3}|C|^{2/3}+|P|+|C|)=O(n^{4/3}). Conclude U=O(n^{4/3}). Step 4 Assemble: Omega(n) <= U_max <= O(n^{4/3}).
backup_routes: Backup A: Inversion route: fix p0 in P, invert about unit circle at p0 to turn unit circles through p0 into lines, bound incidences separately for circles through p0 vs not, dyadic pigeonhole on richness. Backup B: Crossing-number route: draw unit-distance graph with vertices P and straight edges for unit pairs, bound edge crossings by at most 2 per pair of circles (at most 2 intersections), then apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing lemma e^3/n^2 <= O(cr) to get e=O(n^{4/3}). Backup C: For lower bound improvement, use number-theoretic Erdos construction with many representations as sum of two squares to get n^{1+Omega(1/loglog n)}.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Two unit circles can intersect in 2 points, so naive Szemeredi-Trotter for lines fails; direct application overcounts and tangencies/overlapping circles break pseudo-line axiom. The first hard obstruction is justifying the split into two pseudo-segment families and proving any two upper semicircles intersect at most once, handling vertical tangencies, coincident circles, and endpoint incidences without losing more than O(n) incidences.
active_obligations: Obligation 1: Prove circle-splitting lemma with O(n) error control. Obligation 2: State and prove (or cite with verification of hypotheses) Szemeredi-Trotter for pseudo-lines / unit-circle arcs: I(M,N)=O(M^{2/3}N^{2/3}+M+N). Obligation 3: Verify I=2U counting with no multiplicity error from repeated centers. Obligation 4: Make grid counting exact for non-square n.

Then any two distinct curves meet at most once and I(P,C) <= I(P,C_upper)+I(P,C_lower)+O(n). Then apply pseudo-line incidence bound to each half to get <= C n^{4/3}.

Risky Lemma 3: Endpoint incidences after splitting are O(n) - needs explicit bound of 2 per circle.

falsifier_report.assessment: The overall architecture is standard and essentially correct: the square grid gives a linear lower bound and point-circle incidences give an O(n^{4/3}) upper bound. It is not yet a complete rigorous proof. The main gap is the circle-splitting and pseudo-line incidence step: the at-most-one intersection property for upper semicircles is asserted rather than proved, and the version of Szemeredi-Trotter being invoked is not matched to its hypotheses. Finite semicircular arcs are x-monotone arcs with endpoints and vertical tangencies, not pseudo-lines defined on all of R. The strategy also overstates what is proved if it calls the bounds best possible or Theta: the gap between Omega(n), or even the Erdos superlinear lower bound, and O(n^{4/3}) remains open.
unresolved_to_preserve: Preserve the critique that line Szemeredi-Trotter cannot be applied directly to unit circles by duality; preserve the distinction between the elementary linear grid bound and the stronger Erdos n^{1+Omega(1/log log n)} lower bound, which needs extra number theory; preserve the open gap between lower and upper bounds and do not claim a Theta result.
minimal_weakenings: Weaken the conclusion to c n - O(sqrt(n)) <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants, with no claim of optimality or matching exponents. State the upper bound as conditional on a precisely cited incidence theorem for x-monotone pseudo-segments or pseudo-parabolas with pairwise at most one intersection, after verifying its hypotheses. Alternatively replace that citation by a self-contained crossing-lemma proof for the arc graph. Keep the Erdos improvement only as a remark.
dropped_objections: The coincident-circle objection is dropped: P has distinct points, centers are distinct, and a unit circle determines its center, so no two circles in C coincide. The identity I(P,C)=2U(P) is also correct: each unit pair contributes exactly the two symmetric incidences. The claim that a square grid gives only a linear, not superlinear, lower bound is correct and is not an objection to the stated Omega(n) goal.
weakest_lemmas: Weakest Lemma 1: any two distinct upper semicircles of unit circles intersect at most once, including cases with vertically separated centers, tangency, and shared endpoints. Weakest Lemma 2: the Szemeredi-Trotter bound I(M,N)=O(M^{2/3}N^{2/3}+M+N) for these finite semicircular arcs. Weakest Lemma 3: endpoint incidences after splitting contribute only O(n). Weakest Lemma 4: in Backup B, the asserted crossing bound for the unit-distance graph.
hidden_assumptions: The argument assumes semicircles can be treated as pseudo-lines despite being defined only on [p_x-1,p_x+1], having endpoints, and having vertical tangents at endpoints. It assumes the crossing or cutting proof is unaffected by many arcs passing through one point of P, by intersections at points not in P, by tangencies, and by ordering points along an arc when x-coordinates repeat at endpoints. It assumes adding remainder points to reach exactly n never decreases U(P), which is true but should be stated. It assumes the incidence theorem needs only pairwise at most one intersection, not the stronger pseudo-line axioms that any two curves meet exactly once or that two points determine a unique curve; two points of P can in fact lie on two different unit circles.
boundary_cases: Centers at distance 0 are impossible for distinct points, but centers at distance 2 give tangent circles whose single intersection may be an upper point for one or both arcs. Centers with the same x-coordinate put an intersection on a horizontal line midway between them, testing the upper versus lower assignment. A point of P equal to the leftmost or rightmost point of a circle lies on both closed semicircles and must be counted once. Points of P with the same x-coordinate on one upper semicircle can occur only as symmetric positions except at the top, and the arc-ordering in a crossing proof must handle the vertical-tangent endpoints. For n<4 the floor-sqrt grid degenerates and the asymptotic lower bound must be checked separately or stated for large n.
theorem_misuse: Potential misuse is invoking Szemeredi-Trotter for lines, or for pseudo-lines in the strict sense, directly for unit circles or semicircles. Strict pseudo-lines are usually homeomorphic to lines and pairwise meet exactly once; semicircular arcs do not satisfy that definition. The correct tool is an incidence theorem for pseudo-segments, x-monotone pseudo-parabolas, or unit-circle arcs with bounded pairwise intersections, or a direct crossing-lemma argument. Citing the line theorem by analogy would be a theorem misuse.

Backup route: the crossing-number backup replaces one unproved bound by another unless the number of edge crossings is rigorously bounded.

Test endpoint counting with P containing centers plus their left and right unit neighbors. Test the incidence citation by checking whether two points of P can determine two upper semicircles, which rules out strict pseudo-line uniqueness axioms. Test the lower bound numerically for n=m^2+r with 0<r<2m+1 to confirm 2m(m-1)=2n-O(sqrt(n)).
unresolved_objections: The proof still owes a rigorous derivation or precise citation for the pseudo-segment incidence bound, a proof of the one-intersection property for upper and lower semicircles, a clean endpoint convention, and a correction of any best-possible wording. Until those are supplied the strategy is repairable but incomplete.

analysis.plan: Unit distance max problem asks for Theta between superlinear lower and n^{4/3} upper. output.normalized_problem: For P subset R^2, |P|=n, let U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|. Find asymptotic of U_max(n)=max_P U(P). Goal: prove c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} up to constants, with explicit lattice construction for lower bound and incidence proof for upper bound.
output.primary_route: Lemma A (lattice lower bound): Let L_k = {0,...,k-1}^2. Naive count gives >=2k(k-1) ~2n-O(sqrt n) unit pairs. Boost to n^{1+c/log log n} via number theory: let m = product_{p<=y, p=1 mod 4} p, then number of representations r_2(m) >= exp(c log m / log log m). Take P as integer lattice points in disk of radius R with R^2 ~ n / density, count vectors of length sqrt(m) occurring many times. Rescale by 1/sqrt(m) to make distance 1. Conclude many pairs at distance 1. Lemma B (incidence reduction): For P, let C = {circle radius 1 centered at p in P}, |C|=n. Each unit pair gives 2 incidences, so 2U(P)=I(P,C). Lemma C (point-circle incidence bound): I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}). Proof by graph crossing method: for each circle containing t_i>=3 points of P, join consecutive points along circle by t_i edges, total e = sum t_i - (#nonempty circles). Vertices V=P. Two distinct unit circles intersect at most twice, so crossing number cr(G) <= 2*C(n,2)=O(n^2). Apply crossing lemma cr >= c e^3/n^2 when e>=4n, else e=O(n). Solve e=O(n^{4/3}), hence I=e+O(n)=O(n^{4/3}). Conclude U_max=O(n^{4/3}). Combine Lemma A and C for final bounds.
backup_routes: Backup 1: Weaker lower bound O(n log log n) via k x k grid plus pigeonhole on short vectors, if full divisor bound fails. Backup 2: Upper bound via Szemeredi-Trotter for lines after inversion, or via K_2,3-free unit-distance graph plus KST bound giving O(n^{5/3}) fallback, or cut circles into pseudo-segments to apply Pach-Sharir bound.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Controlling multiplicities in Lemma C: circles can contain many points of P collinear in circular order and share arcs; naive graph may have multiple edges overlapping and high-degree vertices causing crossing lemma hypothesis to fail. Need to delete duplicate edges, handle circles with <=2 points separately, and ensure drawn graph has simple edges with crossings only at true circle-circle intersections. Also lower bound needs uniform density of lattice points with distance sqrt(m) without losing Theta(n) points.
active_obligations: O1: Prove representation bound r_2(m) large and transfer to unit distances after scaling while keeping points distinct and count n. O2: Justify I=2U exactly and incidence graph construction with e = I-O(n). O3: Prove crossing lemma application valid: bound cr(G) by O(n^2), handle multigraph and low-degree case. O4: Optimize constants to close O(n^{4/3}) cleanly.

output.concrete_next_task: Write complete proof: define t_i, build arc-graph G on vertex set P, show e >= I- n, cr(G) <= n(n-1), apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing inequality to deduce I <= C n^{4/3}, then translate to U(P) <= (C/2) n^{4/3}.

No fundamental gap, only technical care with graph simplicity.

Fix p0, invert about unit circle at p0 to turn circles through p0 into lines, apply point-line bound, then dyadically sum over rich points. Backup 3: Cell-partition / polynomial method: use Guth-Katz polynomial partitioning to prove circle incidences directly if cutting proof stalls.
output.first_hard_obstruction: The first place the naive count fails is double-counting circles containing many points: a trivial bound I <= sum_{circles} |P cap C| can be Theta(mN) if many points are concircular, and two distinct unit circles can share at most 2 points but many distinct centers can define the same geometric circle. The dyadic argument must separate poor circles (cheap trivial bound) from rich circles (strong combinatorial bound using 2-point determination). Without a bound of form |C_{>=t}| = O(m^2/t^3 + m/t) the summation diverges and the n^{4/3} exponent is lost. Also need to handle coincident circles from distinct centers: show distinct centers give distinct circles unless centers coincide, so N=n distinct.
active_obligations: O1: Justify existence of integer m with large r_2(m) in range and transfer to grid count without boundary loss: need divisor estimate and that most vectors of length sqrt(m) stay inside k x k box. O2: Prove weak incidence bound to bootstrap: I(m,N)=O(mN^{1/2}+N) using Cauchy-Schwarz and at most 2 intersections. O3: Prove sampling / cutting lemma to upgrade weak bound to m^{2/3}N^{2/3}: random subset, apply weak bound, use that rich circles survive. O4: Verify reduction 2U=I-n is exact and circles are distinct. O5: Optimize dyadic sum to get +m+N linear terms.
output.next_task: Prove the weak point-circle incidence estimate and set up dyadic decomposition for rich unit circles, then execute the lattice divisor calculation for the lower bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write Lemma 1 (two-circle intersection => K_{2,2}-free => I=O(m sqrt(N)+N) by double counting pairs on same circle) and Lemma 2 (number-theoretic: exists m <= n with r_2(m) >= n^{c/log log n}). Then show how Lemma 1 plus random sampling implies the strong m^{2/3}N^{2/3} bound and how Lemma 2 implies the grid has required unit pairs after scaling by 1/sqrt(m).
output.readiness_assessment: Ready to execute: reduction to incidences is standard and low-risk; main risk concentrated in rigorous proof of strong incidence bound and quantitative divisor bound. With weak bound plus standard probabilistic amplification the strong bound follows in a few lines. Lower bound needs only elementary analytic number theory, no Siegel-Walfisz. Overall route is complete modulo writing those two lemmas cleanly.
risky_lemmas: R1: Strong incidence I(m,N) <= C(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) for arbitrary circles - risky if proof appeals to general Szemeredi-Trotter without proof; must prove for unit circles using only 2-point intersection. R2: Existence of m with r_2(m) >= exp(Omega(log m / log log m)) with m = O(n) - risky if constant depends on n incorrectly or boundary effects in k x k grid kill constant fraction; needs careful counting of translates. R3: Sampling amplification step preserves distinctness and does not lose log factors - needs explicit Chernoff or expectation calculation.

analysis.plan: The unit-distance maximum U_max(n) is the classic Erdos unit-distance problem. Expected final theorem is Omega(n^{1+c/log log n}) <= U_max(n) <= O(n^{4/3}). Lower bound comes from dense integer lattice capturing many representations of integers as sum of two squares. Upper bound reduces unit pairs to incidences between n points and n unit circles and invokes a Szemeredi-Trotter type point-circle incidence bound. The hard work is proving the incidence bound rigorously without circular reasoning and handling circles containing many points.

output.normalized_problem: Let P subset R^2, |P|=n, U(P)=|{{p,q}: |p-q|=1}|, U_max(n)=max U(P). Prove c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C>0, via explicit lattice construction for lower bound and point-unit-circle incidence theorem for upper bound.
output.primary_route: Step 1: Reformulate as unit-distance graph G with vertices P, edges at distance 1. Step 2 Lower bound Lemma L1: sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) grid gives >=2n-O(sqrt n) unit pairs. Strengthen to superlinear via Erdos number-theoretic grid: take points {(x,y): 0<=x<m, 0<=y<M} with suitable m,M and count vectors of length 1 arising from representations of integers as sum of two squares; choose radius r with many representations r = product of primes 1 mod 4 to get many unit distances after rescaling. Conclude U_max(n) >= n^{1+c/log log n}. Step 3 Upper bound Lemma U1: Let C be set of n unit circles centered at points of P. Then U(P)= I(P,C)/2 where I is incidence count, since each unit pair gives two incidences. Step 4 Lemma U2 (Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter point-circle incidence): For m points and N unit circles with at most 2 circles through any pair in general sense and at most 2 intersections per pair, I = O(m^{2/3} N^{2/3} + m + N). Prove via random sampling + K_{3,3}-free or crossing argument and Szemeredi-Trotter for pseudocircles. Step 5 Apply with m=N=n to get I=O(n^{4/3}) hence U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3}). Combine for final best-known bounds.
backup_routes: Backup A: Crossing-number proof of upper bound: draw unit-distance graph with circular arcs as edges, bound crossings by O(n^2) since two unit circles cross at most twice, then apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing lemma e=O(v + (v+cr)^{...}) to get e=O(n^{4/3}). Backup B: Induction with polynomial cell decomposition / cuttings for circles to prove incidence bound directly. Backup C: Weaker elementary upper O(n^{3/2}) via double-counting paths of length 2 and 2-intersection property as fallback if full 4/3 fails.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Proving the point-unit-circle incidence bound O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) rigorously: unit circles are not lines, two points determine more than one unit circle, and degeneracy from coincident circles and high-multiplicity incidences must be controlled; naive Szemeredi-Trotter does not apply and cutting or K_{s,t}-freeness needs careful graph construction to avoid losing factor.
active_obligations: O1: Justify U=I/2 without double counting coincident circles. O2: Prove lattice count with divisor estimate for sum of two squares gives superlinear gain. O3: Prove incidence lemma with explicit constants and handling of degenerate rich points/circles. O4: Transfer m=N=n case to final O(n^{4/3}) cleanly.
output.next_task: Formalize Lemma U1 incidence reduction and isolate degenerate high-degree points and circles before applying incidence bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write rigorous proof that U(P) equals half incidences between P and unit circles centered at P, then prove weak incidence estimate I=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) for unit circles via random sample plus bound on 2-rich structure, ready to plug m=N=n.
output.readiness_assessment: Strategy is standard and complete in outline but not yet execution-ready: incidence black box and number-theoretic lower bound both require detailed proofs; crossing-number details and divisor estimates remain to be written.

R2: Superlinear n^{1+c/log log n} lower bound is risky due to dependence on prime distribution 1 mod 4 and divisor function lower bounds; fallback to linear Omega(n) is safe but weaker.

analysis.plan: Unit-distance problem: need both lower bound via integer lattice and upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via incidences. Graph has vertices P, edges for distance 1. Lower bound requires number theory for many representations. Upper bound requires incidence geometry for points vs unit circles. Distinct route: use crossing-number method directly on unit-distance graph drawn with straight edges, plus refined lattice counting using divisor function.

output.normalized_problem: For P subset R^2 finite |P|=n, U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|, U_max(n)=max U(P). Prove c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C>0, via explicit lattice construction for lower bound and point-circle incidence / crossing inequality for upper bound.
output.primary_route: Lemma 1 (graph model): U(P)=e(G) where G is unit-distance graph. Lemma 2 (lattice lower bound): take m x m grid with m=floor(sqrt(n)), scale by 1/sqrt(r) for suitable r to create many unit distances; count vectors (a,b) integers with a^2+b^2=r. Choose r = product of first k primes =1 mod 4 to get r_2(r)=2^{k+2} representations via sum-of-two-squares theorem; optimize k ~ log m / log log m to get Omega(m^2 * exp(c log m / log log m)) = Omega(n^{1+c/log log n}) unit pairs. Lemma 3 (incidence reduction): for each p in P draw unit circle C_p; then sum_p |P cap C_p| = 2U(P). Lemma 4 (point-circle incidence O(n^{4/3})): I(P,C) <= C(|P|^{2/3}|C|^{2/3}+|P|+|C|) proved by crossing-number inequality: build graph H with vertices P and edges as arcs of circles between consecutive points, so e ~ I - |C|, cr <= |C|^2 since two unit circles meet <=2 times, then apply cr >= e^3/(64 v^2) if e>=4v else trivial bound. Conclude 2U <= O(n^{4/3}) giving U_max=O(n^{4/3}).
backup_routes: Backup A: prove point-circle incidence via Szemeredi-Trotter cutting / polynomial partitioning instead of crossing lemma to handle high-multiplicity circles. Backup B: use Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter line bound via inversion or lifting to 3D paraboloid if crossing argument degenerates. Backup C for lower bound: use hexagonal / triangular lattice with averaging over distances, or Erdos-Fishburn integer grid diameter argument giving weaker n^{1+c/log log n} with simpler divisor bound tau(d)=O(d^{o(1)}).
output.first_hard_obstruction: Controlling multiplicity and degeneracy in crossing graph: arcs may coincide if many points concircular, or circles share arcs, or e(H) small vs v, breaking e^3/v^2 regime; also two circles intersect at most twice gives crude cr<=2|C|^2 but overlapping circles (coincident centers) need separate handling; must split circles by richness and remove high-degree coincidences without losing Omega(I) edges.
active_obligations: O1: rigorously justify sum-of-two-squares count and choice of scaling radius to keep distinct points and distance exactly 1. O2: prove divisor-type lower bound 2^k = n^{c/log log n} with prime product < m^2 constraint via Chebyshev / primorial estimate. O3: construct arc-graph H with no parallel-edge overcount and bound crossings by 2 per pair of circles. O4: state and apply crossing-number inequality with correct constants and case split e<4v vs e>=4v. O5: handle coincident unit circles (same center) separately.
output.next_task: Formalize Lemma 4 crossing construction and case analysis to derive incidence bound, then optimize lattice parameter k for lower bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write definitions: P points, C n unit circles, define H vertices and circular-arc edges, prove e(H) >= I - n and cr(H) <= n^2, apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing inequality to deduce I = O(n^{4/3}), and compute primorial r <= m with maximal divisor representations.
output.readiness_assessment: Route is standard and complete in outline; main risks are technical details of crossing lemma application and number-theoretic optimization, both well-documented but require careful constants and degeneracy handling before full proof can be written.
risky_lemmas: R1: two distinct unit circles intersect in at most 2 points - true but needs coincident-circle exception. R2: crossing inequality cr >= e^3/64v^2 for e>=4v - requires simple graph; multigraph version needs max multiplicity control, risky if many points collinear on same arc. R3: existence of r with many representations and sqrt(r) ~ O(m) - requires quantitative prime distribution for 1-mod-4 primes and sum-of-two-squares formula.

preserved_critiques.claim: Must not assume general point-circle incidence without proof; must not double-count ordered vs unordered pairs (factor 2); must not claim Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound since lattice only gives n^{1+o(1)}; must ensure scaling preserves integrality and distinctness of grid points.

analysis.plan: Unit-distance problem: need both lower bound via integer lattice and upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via incidences. Graph has vertices P, edges for distance 1. Lower bound requires number theory for many representations. Upper bound requires incidence geometry for points vs unit circles. Distinct route: use crossing-number method directly on unit-distance graph drawn with straight edges, plus refined lattice counting using divisor function.

falsifier_report.assessment: The route is the standard correct outline: lattice with many representations of r as a sum of two squares for the lower bound, and unit-circle incidences plus crossing number for O(n^{4/3}). It is not falsified, but as stated it is incomplete. The multigraph crossing step, the quantitative choice of r using primes 1 mod 4, the per-vector pair count requiring sqrt(r) bounded away from m, small-n and non-square-n handling, and the phrase best possible all need repair. The exact order of U_max(n) is open, so only the stated gap c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for large n can be claimed.
unresolved_to_preserve: Must preserve: factor 2 in sum_p |P cap C_p| = 2U(P); no claim of Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound; scaling by 1/sqrt(r) gives distinct grid points and exact unit distance only for a^2+b^2=r; point-circle incidence must be proved rather than assumed; coincident-center issue is actually vacuous because centers are distinct points of P.
minimal_weakenings: State the theorem only for sufficiently large n with absolute constants; require r <= m^2/4 in the lattice construction; prove the incidence bound first for a simple subgraph obtained by deleting at most half the arc-edges; replace best possible by best known bounds from these methods; allow use of a quoted quantitative prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions or a weaker Chebyshev-type bound with a smaller constant c.
dropped_objections: Coincident unit circles from different centers cannot occur since p != q implies C_p and C_q have different centers, so that degeneracy is dropped. The formula r_2(r)=2^{k+2} for a product of k distinct primes 1 mod 4 is correct up to the standard ordered-signed representation convention and is not itself an objection.
weakest_lemmas: R2 is weakest on the upper side: H has multiplicity at most 2 because two points lie on at most two unit circles centered at points of P, but this must be proved and used to pass to a simple graph losing at most a constant factor in e. R3 is weakest on the lower side: existence of r <= m^2/4 that is a product of k distinct primes 1 mod 4 with k >= c log m/log log m requires control of the k-th such prime and of log r. Lemma 4 degeneracy control for arcs through vertices and multiple crossings at one point also needs a perturbation argument.
hidden_assumptions: Assumes a clean topological drawing of H where no arc passes through a non-endpoint vertex, no three arcs cross at an interior point, and crossings are only pairwise circle intersections; assumes t_i=2 circles can be treated as ordinary cycle edges; assumes m^2 points can be padded to n points without decreasing the normalized lower bound; assumes log log n is positive and the asymptotic optimization is valid; assumes quoted crossing constant 1/64 matches the e>=4v hypothesis.
boundary_cases: Small n where log log n <= 0 or m is tiny; n not a perfect square so m=floor(sqrt(n)); circles with 0, 1, or 2 incident points contributing no or double edges; representation vectors with |a| or |b| near sqrt(r) giving few translates inside the grid; pairs of points at distance >2 determining no common unit center, relevant to multiplicity; e(H)<4v case where crossing lemma does not apply and I=O(n) must be used.
theorem_misuse: Potential misuse of Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing inequality if applied directly to a multigraph or to a drawing with crossings at vertices. Potential misuse of sum-of-two-squares if representations are counted as unordered pairs or if zero vector is included. Potential overstatement if Szemeredi-Trotter for lines is invoked for circles without the crossing or lifting reduction. No misuse in the identity I=2U itself.

categorized_objections.claim: Upper-bound category: multigraph multiplicity, drawing degeneracies, cr(H) <= 2 binom(n,2) justification, e(H)>=I-n only after discarding 1-rich circles. Lower-bound category: primorial size, r<=m^2/4 truncation, ordered versus unordered displacement double counting, padding from m^2 to n. Statement category: open problem gap means bounds are not matching; asymptotic claims need large-n qualification.

decisive_tests: Check a circle with exactly two points: does the proof keep at least one usable simple edge and still get e_simple >= (I-n)/2 up to constants? Check two points determining two unit centers in P: is multiplicity exactly bounded by 2? Choose explicit k and verify product of first k primes 1 mod 4 is <= m^2/4 while 2^k >= m^{c/log log m}. Test displacement (a,b) with a^2+b^2=r and |a|<=m/2: confirm at least m^2/4 translates. Verify crossing count when two circles intersect at a point of P: that point is a vertex, not a crossing, after perturbation.
unresolved_objections: The multigraph-to-simple reduction with explicit constants, the quantitative prime-in-arithmetic-progression estimate sufficient for the claimed c, and the regular-drawing perturbation for H remain unresolved in the candidate as written. These are repairable gaps rather than counterexamples, so the strategy survives only after repair.

objections.claim: Upper-bound category: multigraph multiplicity, drawing degeneracies, cr(H) <= 2 binom(n,2) justification, e(H)>=I-n only after discarding 1-rich circles. Lower-bound category: primorial size, r<=m^2/4 truncation, ordered versus unordered displacement double counting, padding from m^2 to n. Statement category: open problem gap means bounds are not matching; asymptotic claims need large-n qualification.

In particular give (a) lattice construction with sum-of-two-squares scaling achieving superlinear many unit pairs, (b) O(n^{4/3}) upper bound via incidences I(P,C)=2U(P) for n points vs n unit circles. No claim of tightness; gap between n^{1+o(1)} and n^{4/3} stays open. Monotonicity by padding allowed to extend from special n to all n.",
  "primary_route": "Step1 Reduction: Let C={unit circles centered at P}. Distinct centers give distinct circles. No point lies on its own circle, so I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly, not minus n. Step2 Lower number theory: Let p1<...<pk be first k primes 1 mod 4. Let m=prod pi. Then r2(m)=4*2^k ordered signed representations. By Chebyshev/PNT for progression 1 mod 4, log m = sum log pi = O(k log k). Choose k ~ c1 log n / loglog n so that m <= n^{delta} small and sqrt(m) <= L/4 where L~sqrt(n) grid side. Number of essentially distinct vectors ~2^k/4 >= m^{c2/loglog m} >= n^{c/loglog n}. Step3 Lower geometry: Take integer grid G={0..A-1}x{0..B-1} with AB~n/2, A,B~sqrt(n). For each vector v with |v|^2=m, |vx|,|vy|<=sqrt(m)<=min(A,B)/2, number of translates staying in G is >= (A-sqrt(m))(B-sqrt(m)) >= AB/4. Count unordered pairs, divide by symmetries, scale whole set by 1/sqrt(m) to make distance 1, pad to exactly n. Gives Omega(n*2^k)=n^{1+c/loglog n}. Step4 Upper arc-graph: Let ki=|P cap Ci|. Circles with ki<=2 contribute <=2n to I. For ki>=3 join consecutive points along Ci by circular arcs, giving ki edges per such circle (closed cycle). Let V=n vertices P, E_arc >= I-2n (up to constants). Parallel edges: two points determine at most 2 unit circles, so multiplicity <=2; delete one from each parallel pair losing factor <=2 to get simple graph G' with e' >= E_arc/2 - O(n). Step5 Crossing bound: Draw G' with circular arcs. A crossing is an intersection of arcs from distinct circles not at P. Each pair of distinct unit circles meets in <=2 points, so total crossings cr(G') <=2*C(n,2)<=n^2 (tangencies counted crudely, vertices in P not counted as crossings). Apply crossing lemma: if e'>=4v then cr>=e'^3/64v^2 via random induced subgraph + Euler E<=3V for simple planar graph. If e'<4v then E_arc=O(n). Else e'^3/n^2 <= O(n^2) gives e'=O(n^{4/3}). Hence I=O(n^{4/3}) and U=I/2=O(n^{4/3}). Handle degree-2, loops, disconnected components by reduction to simple graph before Euler/crossing.",
  "backup_routes": "Backup A (pseudo-segment splitting): split circles into upper/lower semicircles excluding one endpoint to avoid double count, O(n) endpoint error. Claim any two distinct uppers meet at most once (to be proved by case analysis including vertical stacks and tangencies). Then invoke incidence theorem for x-monotone pseudo-segments I=O(M^{2/3}N^{2/3}+M+N), not line ST. Kept as alternative, not primary, because strict pseudo-line axioms fail (two points can lie on two uppers). Backup B (inversion): fix p0, invert circles through p0 to lines, apply point-line bound dyadically; needs richness pigeonholing, kept as remark. Backup C (weak bound only): Cauchy-Schwarz with at most 2 circles through 2 points gives I=O(m sqrt(N)+m+N) i.e. O(n^{3/2}); honest weakening if crossing proof stalls, insufficient for n^{4/3}. Erdos weaker elementary Omega(n log n / loglog n) grid kept as fallback if PNT-AP avoided; full n^{1+c/loglog n} needs prime control.",
  "first_hard_obstruction": "Two obstructions: (1) Incidence upgrade: naive planarization with V=O(n^2+I) + Euler gives only O(n^2); K2,2-free gives only O(n^{3/2}); dyadic with |C_ge t|=O(m^2/t^2) alone diverges. The n^{4/3} needs crossing lemma on arc-graph with V=n, E~I, cr<=n^2, with careful handling of ki<=2 circles, multiplicity<=2, tangencies and concurrent triple points. Straight-line unit-distance graph crossing bound is NOT a substitute. (2) Number-theoretic size compatibility: representation count exponential in k must coexist with sqrt(m)<<grid side; requires log m=O(k log k) from distribution of 1-mod-4 primes and suboptimal k choice to keep boundary loss constant factor.",
  "active_obligations": "O1: Prove r2 formula for distinct 1-mod-4 primes and log m bound via Chebyshev-type estimate for that progression, choose k vs n explicitly with sqrt(m)<=L/4. O2: Prove boundary estimate (A-|vx|)(B-|vy|)>=AB/4 and ordered-vs-unordered division without losing exponential. O3: Prove crossing lemma with constants, random subgraph, Euler E<=3V for simple planar graph with v>=3, split e<4v vs e>=4v, multigraph reduction. O4: Construct arc-graph, prove ki<=2 contributes

objections.claim: Correctness: the at-most-one intersection claim for upper semicircles is unproved and is the key geometric lemma. Theorem application: the hypotheses of the pseudo-line incidence bound are not verified for finite arcs with endpoints. Counting: closed semicircles double-count endpoint incidences and the O(n) error needs a clean convention such as half-open arcs. Sharpness: best possible and Theta language exceeds what is proved. Backup route: the crossing-number backup replaces one unproved bound by another unless the number of edge crossings is rigorously bounded.

preserved_critiques.assessment: The overall architecture is standard and essentially correct: the square grid gives a linear lower bound and point-circle incidences give an O(n^{4/3}) upper bound. It is not yet a complete rigorous proof. The main gap is the circle-splitting and pseudo-line incidence step: the at-most-one intersection property for upper semicircles is asserted rather than proved, and the version of Szemeredi-Trotter being invoked is not matched to its hypotheses. Finite semicircular arcs are x-monotone arcs with endpoints and vertical tangencies, not pseudo-lines defined on all of R. The strategy also overstates what is proved if it calls the bounds best possible or Theta: the gap between Omega(n), or even the Erdos superlinear lower bound, and O(n^{4/3}) remains open.

preserved_critiques.assessment: The core architecture is correct and standard: an Erdős grid/sum-of-two-squares lower bound of n^{1+c/log log n} and a Spencer-Szemerédi-Trotter O(n^{4/3}) upper bound via point-circle incidences and the crossing lemma. It is not yet a complete rigorous proof: the lower-bound parameter transfer, the treatment of low-richness circles and multiedges in the incidence graph, and the distinction between segment crossings and circle intersections all contain gaps or imprecise claims. The problem also cannot be closed tightly; the stated bounds are best-known type bounds with a large open gap, not a determination of U_max(n).

It correctly rejects tight Theta or exact determination claims, naive Euler planarization with V=O(n^2), the unproved straight-line crossing bound, K_{2,2}-freeness, the false identity 2U=I-n, and circular dyadic upgrading of the weak bound. However it remains a repaired route sketch with explicit obligations O1-O5, not the complete rigorous proof demanded. The prime-product size estimate, explicit choice of k, r_2 orbit bookkeeping, crossing-lemma derivation, and especially the perturbation and concurrency handling for the arc drawing are asserted or assigned as tasks rather than proved.

Assumes r_2(m)=4*2^k with orbit size exactly 8 for every representation, using m odd and non-square. Assumes consecutive points on a circle give arcs with no other P-point in their interior and no loops for k_i >= 3. Assumes monotonicity padding by far-away points loses only constant factors. nodes.input_summary: Decompose approved strategy into topological subproblem DAG with Danus fingerprints

subproblems.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
subproblems.target_claim: Formulate the provable best-known statement: there exist absolute c,C,c'>0 such that for all sufficiently large n, c n^{1+c'/\log\log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}, with no claim of exact determination, matching exponent, or Theta-tightness. Prove U_max is nondecreasing by adding points far away from all existing points and from all unit circles centred at them, so no existing unit pair is destroyed and it suffices to construct lower-bound examples on square cardinalities m^2 <= n and pad to n.

subproblems.title: Point-circle incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-freeness
subproblems.target_claim: For |P|=n let C be the n unit circles centred at the points of P. Prove the circles are distinct, no point of P lies on its own circle, and I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly. Prove two distinct points lie on at most two unit circles centred in P and two distinct unit circles meet in at most two points, hence the incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free, while explicitly not claiming K_{2,2}-freeness.

subproblems.title: Crossing lemma for simple graphs and multiplicity at most two
subproblems.target_claim: Prove from Euler's bound E <= 3V-6 for simple planar graphs with V>=3 that cr(G) >= e-3v+6, and by random induced subgraphs that cr(G) >= e^3/(64v^2) when e>=4v, with non-optimal absolute constants allowed. Extend the consequence to multigraphs with multiplicity at most 2 by passing to a simple subgraph with at least half the edges, handling disconnected graphs, small v, loops (absent in the application), and the split e<4v versus e>=4v.

subproblems.title: Pruned circular-arc graph with P as vertex set
subproblems.target_claim: Let k_i be the number of points of P on the i-th unit circle. Discard circles with k_i<=2, losing at most 2n incidences. For k_i>=3 order the points cyclically on the circle and join consecutive points by the circle arcs containing no third point of P in their interior. Prove the resulting drawing has v=n, no loops, e_arc >= I(P,C)-2n, edge multiplicity at most 2 because two vertices determine at most two possible unit centres, and hence a simple subgraph H' with e' >= e_arc/2.

subproblems.title: Crossing upper bound with tangency, vertex, and concurrency control
subproblems.target_claim: Prove cr(H') <= 2\binom{n}{2} <= n^2 for the arc drawing of Subproblem 4. Show arcs on the same circle meet only at endpoints, crossings between arcs on distinct circles can occur only at transverse intersection points of the two circles, tangencies contribute no proper crossing, intersections lying in P are vertices rather than crossings, and concurrent intersections of several circles are resolved by an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of arcs that does not increase the per-circle-pair budget of at most 2 crossings.

subproblems.title: Upper bound U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3})
subproblems.target_claim: Combine Subproblems 2, 4 and 5 with the crossing lemma: if e'<4n then I(P,C)=O(n), and otherwise e'^3/(64n^2) <= cr(H') <= n^2, so e'=O(n^{4/3}), I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}), and U(P)=I(P,C)/2=O(n^{4/3}) uniformly in P. Conclude U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for an absolute C, without using naive planarization with O(n^2) vertices, straight-line unit-distance drawings, or K_{2,3}-freeness alone.

subproblems.title: Representations of R as a sum of two squares
subproblems.target_claim: Let R be the product of k distinct primes each congruent to 1 mod 4. Using the cited sum-of-two-squares divisor formula, prove r_2(R)=4*2^k for ordered signed representations. Prove R is odd and non-square, so no representation has a zero coordinate or equal absolute coordinates, every orbit under sign changes and coordinate swap has size 8, and the number of undirected displacement directions is 2^{k-1}.

subproblems.title: Prime-product size estimate and choice of k
subproblems.target_claim: Let p_i be the i-th prime congruent to 1 mod 4 and R_k=p_1...p_k. Using a cited quantitative prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions (or an explicitly stated Chebyshev-type substitute), prove \log R_k = O(k\log k). For m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor choose k maximal with R_k <= m^2/16, and deduce for large m that \sqrt{R_k} <= m/4, k >= c_1 \log m/\log\log m, and 2^k >= m^{c_2/\log\log m} for absolute c_1,c_2>0.

subproblems.title: Integer-grid translate counting at distance sqrt(R)
subproblems.target_claim: Let G_m={0,...,m-1}^2 and let R=R_k as in Subproblem 8. For every integer vector v with |v|^2=R prove |v_x|,|v_y| <= \sqrt{R} <= m/4 and that the number of translates of v with both endpoints in G_m is (m-|v_x|)(m-|v_y|) >= m^2/2. Sum over all r_2(R) directed vectors and divide by 2 to obtain at least a constant multiple of m^2 2^k unordered pairs in G_m at Euclidean distance \sqrt{R}.

subproblems.title: Scaled lattice lower bound and extension to all large n
subproblems.target_claim: Scale G_m by 1/\sqrt{R} to obtain m^2 points with Omega(m^2 2^k) unit-distance pairs. Using Subproblems 1, 8 and 9, transfer the estimate from m^2 to n with m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor, absorb the change from \log\log m to \log\log n into the constants, pad from m^2 to n points without decreasing the pair count, and conclude U_max(n) >= c n^{1+c'/\log\log n} for all sufficiently large n and absolute c,c'>0.

subproblems.title: Final assembly of the best-known bounds
subproblems.target_claim: Combine Subproblem 6 and Subproblem 10 to prove there exist absolute c,C,c'>0 such that for all sufficiently large n, c n^{1+c'/\log\log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. State explicitly that this is the best-known bound proved here, with a large open gap, and that no exact value, matching exponent, Theta-estimate, or best-possible tightness is claimed.

Define $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ as the minimum number of interior intersection points of pairs of edges over such drawings, counting each transverse crossing once. We allow only drawings where adjacent edges do not cross and no edge crosses itself in an optimal drawing: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, a local rerouting near the crossing eliminates it without creating new crossings, and similarly for self-crossings. Hence in an optimal drawing each crossing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity holds: if $H\subseteq G$ as a (spanning or induced) subgraph, then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\le \mathrm{cr}(G)$, by restricting a drawing of $G$.

Assume known Euler bound: every simple planar graph with $V\ge 3$ vertices satisfies $E\le 3V-6$. We extend to possibly disconnected. Indeed let components have $v_i,e_i$. If $v_i=1$, $e_i=0=3v_i-3$. If $v_i=2$, $e_i\le 1\le 3v_i-3$. If $v_i\ge 3$ and planar, $e_i\le 3v_i-6\le 3v_i-3$. Hence for $c$ components, $e=\sum e_i\le 3v-3c$ unless a single component with $v\ge 3$ gives $e\le 3v-6$. If $c\ge 2$ then $e\le 3v-6$. If $c=1$ and $v\ge 3$ then $e\le 3v-6$. So any simple planar graph with $v\ge 3$ has $e\le 3v-6$, connected or not.

Lemma (linear). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$ for all $v$, and $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$ if $v\ge 3$.

Proof. Take an optimal drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. While a crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. Deleting that edge removes at least one crossing from the drawing. Hence after at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ deletions we obtain a planar (crossing-free) subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $e\ge 4v$. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(64v^2)$. Constants are non-optimal.

Corollary (multiplicity at most $2$). Let $H$ be a multigraph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, no loops, and edge-multiplicity at most $2$. Then either $e<8v$ (linear regime) or $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge e^3/(512v^2)$. More precisely, passing to a simple subgraph loses at most a factor $2$.

output.section: Section 3: Crossing lemma for simple graphs and multiplicity at most two
output.proof_body:
We prove the crossing lemma for simple graphs from Euler's bound, with non-optimal constants, and extend to multiplicity <=2. Let G be finite graph drawn in R^2 with distinct point vertices and edges as continuous curves joining endpoints. Define cr(G) as minimum over drawings with no edge passing through a third vertex except at endpoints, no three edges concurrent interiorly, no tangencies, of number of interior intersection points. In an optimal drawing we may assume no two adjacent edges cross and no edge crosses itself: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, local rerouting near crossing eliminates it without creating new ones; similarly for self-crossings. Hence each crossing in optimal drawing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity: if H subset G as subgraph, cr(H) <= cr(G) by restriction.

Assume known: every simple planar graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=3V-6. This holds disconnected as well. Indeed let components have vi,ei. If vi=1 then ei=0. If vi=2 then ei<=1. If vi>=3 and planar then ei<=3vi-6. In all cases ei<=3vi-3 with strict -6 if single component vi>=3. Summing: for c components, e<=3v-3c unless c=1. If c>=2 then e<=3v-6. If c=1, v>=3 then e<=3v-6. So any simple planar v>=3 has e<=3v-6 connected or not.

Lemma (linear). For simple G with v vertices, e edges, cr(G)>=e-3v for all v, and cr(G)>=e-3v+6 if v>=3. Proof: Take optimal drawing with cr(G) crossings. While crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. This removes >=1 crossing. After at most cr(G) deletions we get planar crossing-free subgraph with v vertices and e'>=e-cr(G) edges. If v>=3, simplicity+planarity gives e'<=3v-6, so e-cr(G)<=3v-6 i.e. cr(G)>=e-3v+6. For v<3 simple graph has e<=1 and cr=0, and e-3v<0, so cr>=e-3v holds. Since e-3v+6>=e-3v, weaker bound holds for v>=3 too. No loops present; loops would need separate handling. Disconnected handled. The +6 form fails for v=2,e=1, hence need split.

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). If G simple, e>=4v then cr(G)>=e^3/(64v^2). Proof: Random induced subgraph. Keep each vertex independently with probability p in (0,1]. Let G_p induced with random vp,ep and cr_p = number of crossings of optimal drawing of G restricted to survivors. Then E[vp]=p v. Edge survives iff both endpoints survive: E[ep]=p^2 e. Crossing survives iff its four distinct endpoints survive, using no-adjacent-crossing property: E[cr_p]=p^4 cr(G). For each realization, cr_p>=ep-3vp by linear lemma valid for all vp including small. Taking expectations: p^4 cr(G)>=p^2 e-3p v, so cr(G)>=e/p^2-3v/p^3. If e>=4v set p=4v/e<=1. Then e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2) and 3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2), giving cr>=e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2). If v<=2 hypothesis e>=4v cannot hold for simple G (e<=1), so vacuous. Constants non-optimal.

Corollary (multiplicity <=2). Let H be multigraph with v vertices, e edges, no loops, multiplicity <=2. Then either e<8v or cr(H)>=e^3/(512v^2). Proof: For each parallel pair keep one representative; delete at most one per pair. Get simple spanning subgraph H' with same v and e'>=e/2, no loops. By monotonicity any drawing of H restricts to drawing of H' with no more crossings, so cr(H')<=cr(H). If e'<4v then e<=2e'<8v linear regime. If e'>=4v then simple lemma applies (v>=3 or vacuous, already handled) giving cr(H)>=cr(H')>=(e')^3/(64v^2)>=(e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2). In particular if e>=8v then e'>=4v and cubic bound holds. Thus split e<4v vs e>=4v for simple becomes e<8v vs e>=8v for multiplicity <=2 up to constants. Loops absent in arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points; disconnected already handled. Constants 64,512 non-optimal allowed.

Remark for application: with v=n and cr(H')<=n^2 this gives either e'=O(n) or (e')^3/n^2=O(n^2), hence e'=O(n^{4/3}) in all cases, similarly e=O(n^{4/3}). This upgrades weak bound to n^{4/3}.
output.solution_body:
Let $G$ be a finite graph drawn in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices as distinct points and edges as continuous curves joining their endpoints, with no edge passing through a third vertex except at endpoints, no three edges concurrent in an interior point, and no tangencies. Define $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ as the minimum number of interior intersection points of pairs of edges over such drawings, counting each transverse crossing once. We allow only drawings where adjacent edges do not cross and no edge crosses itself in an optimal drawing: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, a local rerouting near the crossing eliminates it without creating new crossings, and similarly for self-crossings. Hence in an optimal drawing each crossing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity holds: if $H\subseteq G$ as a (spanning or induced) subgraph, then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\le \mathrm{cr}(G)$, by restricting a drawing of $G$.

Assume known Euler bound: every simple planar graph with $V\ge 3$ vertices satisfies $E\le 3V-6$. We extend to possibly disconnected. Indeed let components have $v_i,e_i$. If $v_i=1$, $e_i=0=3v_i-3$. If $v_i=2$, $e_i\le 1\le 3v_i-3$. If $v_i\ge 3$ and planar, $e_i\le 3v_i-6\le 3v_i-3$. Hence for $c$ components, $e=\sum e_i\le 3v-3c$ unless a single component with $v\ge 3$ gives $e\le 3v-6$. If $c\ge 2$ then $e\le 3v-6$. If $c=1$ and $v\ge 3$ then $e\le 3v-6$. So any simple planar graph with $v\ge 3$ has $e\le 3v-6$, connected or not.

Lemma (linear). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$ for all $v$, and $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$ if $v\ge 3$.

Proof. Take an optimal drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. While a crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. Deleting that edge removes at least one crossing from the drawing. Hence after at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ deletions we obtain a planar (crossing-free) subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. If $v\ge 3$, planarity and simplicity give $e'\le 3v-6$, so $e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le 3v-6$, i.e. $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$. For $v<3$ a simple graph has $e\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge 0\ge e-3v$ holds since $e-3v\le 1-3<0$ for $v=1,2$ and $e=0$ for $v=0$. Since $e-3v+6\ge e-3v$, the weaker bound $\mathrm{cr}\ge e-3v$ holds for $v\ge 3$ as well. This covers disconnected graphs and avoids $v<3$ counterexample to the $+6$ form (e.g. $v=2,e=1$). No loops are present; loops would require separate handling. $\square$

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $e\ge 4v$. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(64v^2)$. Constants are non-optimal.

Proof. Use random induced subgraphs. Choose each vertex independently with probability $p\in(0,1]$ to be kept, and let $G_p$ be the induced subgraph with random $v_p,e_p$ and $\mathrm{cr}_p$ defined as the number of crossings of the optimal drawing of $G$ restricted to surviving vertices and edges. Then $\mathbb{E}[v_p]=pv$. An edge survives iff both endpoints survive, so $\mathbb{E}[e_p]=p^2e$. A crossing survives iff the four distinct endpoints of the two crossing edges all survive, by the no-adjacent-crossing property of the optimal drawing. Hence $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}_p]=p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)$. For each realization, the linear lemma in the form $\mathrm{cr}_p\ge e_p-3v_p$ holds (valid for all $v_p$ including small). Taking expectations, $p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge p^2e-3pv$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e/p^2-3v/p^3$.

If $e\ge 4v$, set $p=4v/e\le 1$. Then $e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2)$ and $3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2)$, giving $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2)$. If $v\le 2$ the hypothesis $e\ge 4v$ cannot hold for simple $G$ ($e\le 1$), so the implication is vacuous. This proves the claim. $\square$

Corollary (multiplicity at most $2$). Let $H$ be a multigraph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, no loops, and edge-multiplicity at most $2$. Then either $e<8v$ (linear regime) or $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge e^3/(512v^2)$. More precisely, passing to a simple subgraph loses at most a factor $2$.

Proof. For each parallel pair keep one representative edge; delete at most one per pair. Let $H'$ be the resulting simple spanning subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e/2$ edges, no loops. By monotonicity, any drawing of $H$ restricts to a drawing of $H'$ with no more crossings, so $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le \mathrm{cr}(H)$. If $e'<4v$ then $e\le 2e'<8v$, the trivial linear bound. If $e'\ge 4v$ (which implies $v\ge 3$ or vacuous small-$v$ as above, and in any case the simple crossing lemma applies), then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge \mathrm{cr}(H')\ge (e')^3/(64v^2)\ge (e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2)$. In particular, if $e\ge 8v$ then $e'\ge 4v$ and the cubic bound holds. The split $e<4v$ versus $e\ge 4v$ for simple graphs becomes $e<8v$ versus $e\ge 8v$ for multiplicity $\le 2$ up to constants. Disconnectedness is already handled by the planar bound; loops are absent in the arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points. Constants $64,512$ are non-optimal and allowed. $\square$

Remark. For the unit-distance application with $v=n$ and $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le n^2$, this gives either $e'=O(n)$ or $(e')^3/n^2=O(n^2)$, hence $e'=O(n^{4/3})$ in all cases, and similarly $e=O(n^{4/3})$.

Lemma (linear). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$ for all $v$, and $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$ if $v\ge 3$.

Proof. Take an optimal drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. While a crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. Deleting that edge removes at least one crossing from the drawing. Hence after at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ deletions we obtain a planar (crossing-free) subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. If $v\ge 3$, planarity and simplicity give $e'\le 3v-6$, so $e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le 3v-6$, i.e. $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$. For $v<3$ a simple graph has $e\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge 0\ge e-3v$ holds since $e-3v\le 1-3<0$ for $v=1,2$ and $e=0$ for $v=0$. Since $e-3v+6\ge e-3v$, the weaker bound $\mathrm{cr}\ge e-3v$ holds for $v\ge 3$ as well. This covers disconnected graphs and avoids $v<3$ counterexample to the $+6$ form (e.g. $v=2,e=1$). No loops are present; loops would require separate handling. $\square$

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $e\ge 4v$. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(64v^2)$. Constants are non-optimal.

Proof. Use random induced subgraphs. Choose each vertex independently with probability $p\in(0,1]$ to be kept, and let $G_p$ be the induced subgraph with random $v_p,e_p$ and $\mathrm{cr}_p$ defined as the number of crossings of the optimal drawing of $G$ restricted to surviving vertices and edges. Then $\mathbb{E}[v_p]=pv$. An edge survives iff both endpoints survive, so $\mathbb{E}[e_p]=p^2e$. A crossing survives iff the four distinct endpoints of the two crossing edges all survive, by the no-adjacent-crossing property of the optimal drawing. Hence $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}_p]=p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)$. For each realization, the linear lemma in the form $\mathrm{cr}_p\ge e_p-3v_p$ holds (valid for all $v_p$ including small). Taking expectations, $p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge p^2e-3pv$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e/p^2-3v/p^3$.

If $e\ge 4v$, set $p=4v/e\le 1$. Then $e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2)$ and $3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2)$, giving $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2)$. If $v\le 2$ the hypothesis $e\ge 4v$ cannot hold for simple $G$ ($e\le 1$), so the implication is vacuous. This proves the claim. $\square$

Corollary (multiplicity at most $2$). Let $H$ be a multigraph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, no loops, and edge-multiplicity at most $2$. Then either $e<8v$ (linear regime) or $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge e^3/(512v^2)$. More precisely, passing to a simple subgraph loses at most a factor $2$.

Proof. For each parallel pair keep one representative edge; delete at most one per pair. Let $H'$ be the resulting simple spanning subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e/2$ edges, no loops. By monotonicity, any drawing of $H$ restricts to a drawing of $H'$ with no more crossings, so $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le \mathrm{cr}(H)$. If $e'<4v$ then $e\le 2e'<8v$, the trivial linear bound. If $e'\ge 4v$ (which implies $v\ge 3$ or vacuous small-$v$ as above, and in any case the simple crossing lemma applies), then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge \mathrm{cr}(H')\ge (e')^3/(64v^2)\ge (e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2)$. In particular, if $e\ge 8v$ then $e'\ge 4v$ and the cubic bound holds. The split $e<4v$ versus $e\ge 4v$ for simple graphs becomes $e<8v$ versus $e\ge 8v$ for multiplicity $\le 2$ up to constants. Disconnectedness is already handled by the planar bound; loops are absent in the arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points. Constants $64,512$ are non-optimal and allowed. $\square$

Remark. For the unit-distance application with $v=n$ and $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le n^2$, this gives either $e'=O(n)$ or $(e')^3/n^2=O(n^2)$, hence $e'=O(n^{4/3})$ in all cases, and similarly $e=O(n^{4/3})$.
