output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.formal_claim: We prove best-known bounds, not exact determination: there exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and N0 such that for all n >= N0, c * n^{1 + c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C * n^{4/3}. No claim of matching exponent, Theta-tightness, or best-possible exact value is made. U_max is monotone nondecreasing, and it suffices to prove the lower bound for square cardinalities m^2 with padding to general n.
output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P) be number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset P, p1!=p2, with |p1-p2|=1. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). The max exists since for fixed n the count is integer in [0, C(n,2)] and the condition is closed; U_max(n) <= n(n-1)/2 < infinity.

We do not determine U_max exactly. The exponent gap is open. We prove only the stated upper O(n^{4/3}) and lower Omega(n^{1+c'/loglog n}) for large n. In particular no Theta claim.

Monotonicity: U_max(n+1) >= U_max(n). Indeed let P_n achieve U_max(n). Let S = P_n union (union_{p in P_n} S^1(p,1)), where S^1(p,1) is unit circle centred at p. S is finite union of 1-dimensional circles plus finite set, hence not equal to R^2; its complement is non-empty. Pick q not in S. Then q distinct from P_n and |q-p| != 1 for all p in P_n. Let P_{n+1}=P_n union {q}. Every unit pair of P_n remains a unit pair of P_{n+1}, and any pair involving q contributes >=0. Hence U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n)=U_max(n). Taking max over (n+1)-sets, U_max(n+1) >= U(P_{n+1}) >= U_max(n).

Iterating, adding k points successively outside the finite union of unit circles of the current set preserves all old pairs. Thus any construction on m points yields for any n>=m a construction on n points with at least as many unit pairs.

Padding from squares: Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2 = m^2+2m+1, and n-m^2 <= 2m+1 <= 3 sqrt(n). If we construct Q_m with |Q_m|=m^2 and U(Q_m) >= f(m^2) for some nondecreasing f, then by padding n-m^2 far points as above we obtain P_n with |P_n|=n and U(P_n) >= U(Q_m) >= f(m^2). Hence U_max(n) >= f(m^2). Since m^2 = n - O(sqrt(n)) >= n/2 for large n (e.g. n>=16), and f is of form t^{1+c'/loglog t}, we have f(m^2) >= c_1 n^{1+c_1'/loglog n} after adjusting constants, using loglog(m^2)=loglog n + o(1). Explicit transfer is done in lower-bound section; monotonicity justifies reduction to m^2.

Henceforth assume n >= N0 large enough that loglog n >0 (e.g. n>e) and m>=4, and prove upper bound for all n and lower bound for m^2 then transfer. Adding points far away never destroys existing unit distances.

output.primary_route: Step0 Monotonicity and reduction: show Umax monotone by adding far point avoiding finitely many circles. Let C be n unit circles centered at P, distinct centers give distinct circles, no point on own circle, so I(P,C)=2U exactly. Two points in at most 2 unit circles, two circles meet in at most 2 points, so incidence graph K2,3-free but K2,2 occurs. Step1 Weak bound: by Kovari-Sos-Turan for K2,3-free bipartite graph, I(m,N)=O(m N^{2/3}+N) symmetrically O(m^{2/3}N+N) hence for m=N=n, O(n^{5/2}) trivial then O(n^{3/2}) after KST, kept only as bootstrap. Step2 Cutting for unit circles: prove 1/r-cutting for N unit circles with O(r^2) cells each meeting O(N/r) circles and containing O(m/r^2) points after subdivision, using random sample plus vertical decomposition of arrangement, handling tangencies and vertices by closure and splitting. Apply weak bound inside each cell and count boundary incidences separately to get recurrence I(m,N)<=O(r^2)*O((m/r^2)(N/r)^{2/3})+O(rN+m). Optimize r to obtain I(m,N)=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N). Specialize to m=N=n to get I=O(n^{4/3}) and U=I/2=O(n^{4/3}). This avoids explicit arc-graph crossing lemma, using cuttings instead. Step3 Lower construction variant: let R be product of k distinct 1-mod-4 primes, r2(R)=4*2^k by sum-of-two-squares divisor formula for squarefree case, no zero or diagonal vectors since R odd non-square, giving 2^{k-1} essentially distinct directions up to symmetry. Cite quantitative prime theorem for 1-mod-4 primes to get log R=O(k log k). Choose m=floor(sqrt(n)) and k maximal with R<=m^2/16 so sqrt(R)<=m/4. Then k>=c log m/loglog m and 2^k>=m^{c/loglog m}. Step4 Counting: take G={0,...,m-1}^2, for each vector v with |v|^2=R count translates (m-|vx|)(m-|vy|)>=m^2/2 uniformly since |vx|,|vy|<=sqrt(R). Sum over ordered vectors and divide by 2 for unordered to get Omega(m^2 2^k) pairs at distance sqrt(R). Scale by 1/sqrt(R) to distance 1, pad from m^2 to n by far points. Gives Omega(n^{1+c/loglog n}). Linear grid alone gives only 2n.

objections.claim: Correctness-critical: good-drawing reduction and concurrency perturbation for cr<=n^2. Quantitative: maximal-k inversion and transfer from m to n. Bookkeeping: ordered versus unordered factor 2 in I=2U and in directed displacement vectors; loss of at most 2n from pruning; factor 1/2 from multiplicity reduction. Expository: best possible must read best-known. None of these is presently a counterexample to the stated inequalities.

preserved_critiques.assessment: The outline is mathematically sound and matches the classical best-known bounds: the upper bound via I=2U, a pruned arc graph on n vertices, multiplicity at most 2, crossing number at most n^2, and the crossing lemma; and the lower bound via a square grid, a squarefree product R of k distinct primes congruent to 1 mod 4, r2(R)=4*2^k, uniform translate counts, and scaling by 1/sqrt(R). No central claim is falsified. However this is a strategy, not a complete proof: the crossing upper bound needs a rigorous good-drawing/perturbation argument, and the lower bound needs a rigorous maximal-k inversion. The original wording about best possible bounds must be weakened to best-known non-matching bounds.

objections.claim: Fatal-to-primary-route: incorrect r specialization at m=N and no valid summation improving KST. Proof-gap: unproved circle cutting lemma, enclosure/boundary/tangency handling, and crossing-lemma role. Number-theory gap: dyadic block maximality does not imply k>=c log m/loglog m; needs explicit feasible K and interval prime count. Bookkeeping: mostly correct, but cutting boundary assignment and enclosing-circle incidences must be fixed. Scope: best-known bounds only; no exact Umax(n), no Theta, no tight exponent.

preserved_critiques.assessment: The stated bounds are the correct best-known bounds and the incidence reduction I=2U, K_{2,3}-freeness, r_2 formula for a squarefree product of 1-mod-4 primes, boundary translate count, scaling, and padding are essentially correct. The candidate is not falsified as a theorem statement. Its claimed distinct primary upper-bound route, however, is not presently a proof: the cutting step is asserted without a valid point-circle cutting/incidence recursion, and the displayed choice of r collapses in the case actually needed. The lower bound is repairable but the dyadic-block maximality argument does not yet yield the claimed k. The arc-graph backup, if fully executed, would prove the upper bound, but then distinctness and the cutting primary route are not established.

objections.claim: Upper-bound logic: recurrence assumes uniform point distribution and does not close by induction as written. Geometry: cutting construction for doubly-intersecting unit circles, vertical-tangency splitting, tangencies, and concurrency are unproved. Incidence accounting: boundary points and sampled circles need a separate sharp bound. Number theory: prime distribution modulo 4 is stronger than claimed and maximal-k needs both upper size and next-prime control. Bookkeeping: ordered versus unordered pairs, scaling by 1/sqrt(R), transfer from m=floor(sqrt(n)) to n, and large-n qualifications remain to be executed.

preserved_critiques.assessment: The normalized bounds are the correct best-known large-n bounds and the identities I=2U, K2,3-freeness, r2(R)=4*2^k for a squarefree product of distinct 1-mod-4 primes, and the grid scaling are sound in outline. The proposed new upper route is not yet a proof: the stated circle-cutting recurrence is unjustified and, as written, does not close to O(n^{4/3}). The lower route is essentially the standard primorial construction but understates the arithmetic-progression prime input and omits the maximal-k lower-bound argument. No fatal counterexample to the theorem statement is given, but the strategy cannot be accepted as complete.

falsifier_report.assessment: The synthesis states the correct best-known, non-matching bounds c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= Umax(n) <= C n^{4/3} for large n, with no Theta, exact, or best-possible-tightness claim. The promoted primary route is sound in outline: I(P,C)=2U exactly for distinct unit circles centered at P, K2,3-freeness, a pruned P-vertex arc graph with multiplicity at most 2 and crossing number at most n^2, the crossing lemma, and the squarefree primorial lattice lower bound with r2(R)=4*2^k, R<=m^2/16, uniform translate counts, scaling by 1/sqrt(R), and padding. It is not yet a complete rigorous proof: the good-drawing/concurrency perturbation for the crossing upper bound and the quantitative maximal-k inversion still require full execution. The cutting routes are correctly rejected as primary rather than averaged in.
unresolved_to_preserve: Preserve all of: no Theta, exact determination, tight exponent, or Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound; I=2U exactly; K2,3-free but K2,2 can occur; distinct centers give distinct circles and no point lies on its own circle; pruning circles with k_i<=2; multiplicity at most 2; tangencies contribute no proper crossing and P-intersections are vertices not crossings; concurrency outside P needs a per-circle-pair perturbation argument; lower bound needs simultaneous R<=m^2/16 and 2^k=m^{Omega(1/loglog m)}, (m-|v_x|)(m-|v_y|)>=(3m/4)^2, ordered-to-unordered division by 2, scaling by 1/sqrt(R), and far-away padding from m^2 to n; the weak KST bound alone gives only O(n^{3/2}) and must not be upgraded without the crossing argument.
minimal_weakenings: If the good-drawing perturbation cannot be made rigorous, weaken the proved upper bound to the KST bound Umax(n)=O(n^{3/2}) or cite a proved point-circle incidence theorem as an explicit black box. If quantitative PNT in the progression 1 mod 4 is not allowed as cited input, weaken the lower bound to the bound actually supported by the cited prime estimate, e.g. an elementary superlinear Omega(n log n/loglog n) type bound. In all cases retain best-known large-n bounds rather than best-possible, Theta, or exact claims, and retain non-optimal crossing constants.
dropped_objections: No fatal or major child objection was improperly dropped. The fatal cutting objections from R2.S5, R2.S2 and R2.S4 - wrong weak-bound use, r=m^{1/3}N^{-1/3} collapsing to 1 at m=N=n, one-level Holder/Cauchy summation reproducing O(N sqrt(m)), crossing-versus-containing confusion for circles, uncounted boundary and sampled-circle points, and no closing induction - were not bypassed; they were the stated cause for demoting cuttings to a cited remark or weakened backup and promoting the arc-graph route as sole primary. The dyadic-block lower-bound objection was likewise addressed by restoring the first-k primorial with maximal-k and next-prime control. The R2.S8 objections on good-drawing perturbation, maximal-k inversion, and factor-2 bookkeeping are preserved as unresolved, not dropped.
weakest_lemmas: Weakest are: (a) the perturbation lemma giving a good drawing of the simple pruned arc graph H' with cr(H')<=2*C(n,2)<=n^2 despite tangencies and concurrent intersections of many circles outside P; (b) the quantitative inversion from log R=O(k log k) and maximality of k to k>=c log m/loglog m. Next weakest is the formal multiplicity-at-most-2 and e_simple>=e_arc/2 reduction in the presence of 3-cycles on a circle.
hidden_assumptions: Assumes cited quantitative prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions, specifically the kth prime congruent to 1 mod 4 is O(k log k), and the sum-of-two-squares divisor formula d1-d3; assumes large n so loglog n>0, m is large, k tends to infinity, and small-v and e<4v cases of the crossing lemma are handled separately; assumes a generic small perturbation of arcs can be chosen locally without creating crossings between arcs whose circles do not intersect or creating extra crossings for a circle pair; assumes monotonicity padding points can be placed far away avoiding all finitely many unit circles and at distance not 1 from existing points.
boundary_cases: Need explicit handling of: n small and v<3 in Euler and crossing lemma; disconnected arc graph; circles with k_i=0,1,2 discarded; k_i=3 where a pair of vertices could a priori be consecutive in the cycle; tangent unit circles giving one geometric intersection but zero proper crossing; intersections of circles at points of P, which are vertices; concurrent intersections outside P; displacement vectors with |v_x| or |v_y| close to sqrt(R)<=m/4 giving the stated (3m/4)^2 bound; R odd non-square so no zero or diagonal representations and orbit size 8; n not a perfect square, handled by m=floor(sqrt(n)) and padding; regimes where the maximal k is small for small m, excluded by large-n qualification.
theorem_misuse: No theorem misuse remains in the promoted primary route provided the stated citations are used as intended. Line Szemeredi-Trotter is not applied directly to circles, K2,2-freeness is not claimed, Euler planarization with V=O(n^2) is not used to get n^{4/3}, KST alone is not upgraded to n^{4/3}, and Chebyshev-type estimates are not claimed to suffice for primes 1 mod 4 without Dirichlet/PNT-AP input. decisive_tests: Test the crossing claim on configurations with many unit circles concurrent at a point outside P and with tangent circle pairs: verify a local perturbation yields at most two crossings per circle pair and none at P-vertices. Test bookkeeping on small configurations where K2,2 occurs in the incidence graph and where some k_i<=2, confirming I=2U, e_arc>=I-2n, and e_simple>=e_arc/2.
unresolved_objections: The good-drawing perturbation with per-circle-pair budget at most 2 under tangency and concurrency, and the fully explicit maximal-k lower-bound derivation with next-prime control and m-to-n transfer, remain to be written out. Until they are, the synthesis is a sound strategy needing repair, not a complete proof.

hidden_assumptions: Assumes a quantitative PNT for primes congruent to 1 mod 4 strong enough to give p_k=O(k log k) and control of p_{k+1}; assumes a generic small perturbation of arcs preserves endpoints, arc order on each circle, no new crossings beyond splitting concurrent points pairwise, and no crossings at tangencies; assumes k is large enough that loglog m is positive and k tends to infinity with m; assumes far-away padding points can avoid all finitely many unit circles and mutual unit distances.
boundary_cases: Must handle n and m small with loglog n<=0 excluded by a large-n hypothesis; v<3 and e<4v in the crossing lemma; k_i=0,1,2 pruned circles; pairs of vertices at distance exactly 2, greater than 2, or with coincident centers excluded since centers are distinct; tangent circles and circles meeting exactly at a P-point; k=0 or R=1 for small m; m=floor(sqrt(n)) not a perfect square requiring padding.

decisive_tests: Test the crossing claim on many unit circles concurrent at one non-P point and on tangent circle pairs to verify perturbation still gives at most two crossings per circle pair. node.input_summary: Generate candidate research strategy for problem: Given a finite set P of n points in R^2, let U(P) be the num...

analysis.plan: Unit-distance problem: need both lower bound via integer lattice and upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via incidences. Graph has vertices P, edges for distance 1. Lower bound requires number theory for many representations. Upper bound requires incidence geometry for points vs unit circles. Distinct route: use crossing-number method directly on unit-distance graph drawn with straight edges, plus refined lattice counting using divisor function.

output.normalized_problem: For P subset R^2 finite |P|=n, U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|, U_max(n)=max U(P). Prove c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C>0, via explicit lattice construction for lower bound and point-circle incidence / crossing inequality for upper bound.
output.primary_route: Lemma 1 (graph model): U(P)=e(G) where G is unit-distance graph. Lemma 2 (lattice lower bound): take m x m grid with m=floor(sqrt(n)), scale by 1/sqrt(r) for suitable r to create many unit distances; count vectors (a,b) integers with a^2+b^2=r. Choose r = product of first k primes =1 mod 4 to get r_2(r)=2^{k+2} representations via sum-of-two-squares theorem; optimize k ~ log m / log log m to get Omega(m^2 * exp(c log m / log log m)) = Omega(n^{1+c/log log n}) unit pairs. Lemma 3 (incidence reduction): for each p in P draw unit circle C_p; then sum_p |P cap C_p| = 2U(P). Lemma 4 (point-circle incidence O(n^{4/3})): I(P,C) <= C(|P|^{2/3}|C|^{2/3}+|P|+|C|) proved by crossing-number inequality: build graph H with vertices P and edges as arcs of circles between consecutive points, so e ~ I - |C|, cr <= |C|^2 since two unit circles meet <=2 times, then apply cr >= e^3/(64 v^2) if e>=4v else trivial bound. Conclude 2U <= O(n^{4/3}) giving U_max=O(n^{4/3}).
backup_routes: Backup A: prove point-circle incidence via Szemeredi-Trotter cutting / polynomial partitioning instead of crossing lemma to handle high-multiplicity circles. Backup B: use Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter line bound via inversion or lifting to 3D paraboloid if crossing argument degenerates. Backup C for lower bound: use hexagonal / triangular lattice with averaging over distances, or Erdos-Fishburn integer grid diameter argument giving weaker n^{1+c/log log n} with simpler divisor bound tau(d)=O(d^{o(1)}).
output.first_hard_obstruction: Controlling multiplicity and degeneracy in crossing graph: arcs may coincide if many points concircular, or circles share arcs, or e(H) small vs v, breaking e^3/v^2 regime; also two circles intersect at most twice gives crude cr<=2|C|^2 but overlapping circles (coincident centers) need separate handling; must split circles by richness and remove high-degree coincidences without losing Omega(I) edges.
active_obligations: O1: rigorously justify sum-of-two-squares count and choice of scaling radius to keep distinct points and distance exactly 1. O2: prove divisor-type lower bound 2^k = n^{c/log log n} with prime product < m^2 constraint via Chebyshev / primorial estimate. O3: construct arc-graph H with no parallel-edge overcount and bound crossings by 2 per pair of circles. O4: state and apply crossing-number inequality with correct constants and case split e<4v vs e>=4v. O5: handle coincident unit circles (same center) separately.
output.next_task: Formalize Lemma 4 crossing construction and case analysis to derive incidence bound, then optimize lattice parameter k for lower bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write definitions: P points, C n unit circles, define H vertices and circular-arc edges, prove e(H) >= I - n and cr(H) <= n^2, apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing inequality to deduce I = O(n^{4/3}), and compute primorial r <= m with maximal divisor representations.
output.readiness_assessment: Route is standard and complete in outline; main risks are technical details of crossing lemma application and number-theoretic optimization, both well-documented but require careful constants and degeneracy handling before full proof can be written.
risky_lemmas: R1: two distinct unit circles intersect in at most 2 points - true but needs coincident-circle exception. R2: crossing inequality cr >= e^3/64v^2 for e>=4v - requires simple graph; multigraph version needs max multiplicity control, risky if many points collinear on same arc. R3: existence of r with many representations and sqrt(r) ~ O(m) - requires quantitative prime distribution for 1-mod-4 primes and sum-of-two-squares formula.

preserved_critiques.claim: Must not assume general point-circle incidence without proof; must not double-count ordered vs unordered pairs (factor 2); must not claim Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound since lattice only gives n^{1+o(1)}; must ensure scaling preserves integrality and distinctness of grid points.

analysis.plan: Unit-distance problem: need both lower bound via integer lattice and upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via incidences. Graph has vertices P, edges for distance 1. Lower bound requires number theory for many representations. Upper bound requires incidence geometry for points vs unit circles. Distinct route: use crossing-number method directly on unit-distance graph drawn with straight edges, plus refined lattice counting using divisor function.

falsifier_report.assessment: The route is the standard correct outline: lattice with many representations of r as a sum of two squares for the lower bound, and unit-circle incidences plus crossing number for O(n^{4/3}). It is not falsified, but as stated it is incomplete. The multigraph crossing step, the quantitative choice of r using primes 1 mod 4, the per-vector pair count requiring sqrt(r) bounded away from m, small-n and non-square-n handling, and the phrase best possible all need repair. The exact order of U_max(n) is open, so only the stated gap c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for large n can be claimed.
unresolved_to_preserve: Must preserve: factor 2 in sum_p |P cap C_p| = 2U(P); no claim of Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound; scaling by 1/sqrt(r) gives distinct grid points and exact unit distance only for a^2+b^2=r; point-circle incidence must be proved rather than assumed; coincident-center issue is actually vacuous because centers are distinct points of P.
minimal_weakenings: State the theorem only for sufficiently large n with absolute constants; require r <= m^2/4 in the lattice construction; prove the incidence bound first for a simple subgraph obtained by deleting at most half the arc-edges; replace best possible by best known bounds from these methods; allow use of a quoted quantitative prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions or a weaker Chebyshev-type bound with a smaller constant c.
dropped_objections: Coincident unit circles from different centers cannot occur since p != q implies C_p and C_q have different centers, so that degeneracy is dropped. The formula r_2(r)=2^{k+2} for a product of k distinct primes 1 mod 4 is correct up to the standard ordered-signed representation convention and is not itself an objection.
weakest_lemmas: R2 is weakest on the upper side: H has multiplicity at most 2 because two points lie on at most two unit circles centered at points of P, but this must be proved and used to pass to a simple graph losing at most a constant factor in e. R3 is weakest on the lower side: existence of r <= m^2/4 that is a product of k distinct primes 1 mod 4 with k >= c log m/log log m requires control of the k-th such prime and of log r. Lemma 4 degeneracy control for arcs through vertices and multiple crossings at one point also needs a perturbation argument.
hidden_assumptions: Assumes a clean topological drawing of H where no arc passes through a non-endpoint vertex, no three arcs cross at an interior point, and crossings are only pairwise circle intersections; assumes t_i=2 circles can be treated as ordinary cycle edges; assumes m^2 points can be padded to n points without decreasing the normalized lower bound; assumes log log n is positive and the asymptotic optimization is valid; assumes quoted crossing constant 1/64 matches the e>=4v hypothesis.
boundary_cases: Small n where log log n <= 0 or m is tiny; n not a perfect square so m=floor(sqrt(n)); circles with 0, 1, or 2 incident points contributing no or double edges; representation vectors with |a| or |b| near sqrt(r) giving few translates inside the grid; pairs of points at distance >2 determining no common unit center, relevant to multiplicity; e(H)<4v case where crossing lemma does not apply and I=O(n) must be used.
theorem_misuse: Potential misuse of Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing inequality if applied directly to a multigraph or to a drawing with crossings at vertices. Potential misuse of sum-of-two-squares if representations are counted as unordered pairs or if zero vector is included. Potential overstatement if Szemeredi-Trotter for lines is invoked for circles without the crossing or lifting reduction. No misuse in the identity I=2U itself.

categorized_objections.claim: Upper-bound category: multigraph multiplicity, drawing degeneracies, cr(H) <= 2 binom(n,2) justification, e(H)>=I-n only after discarding 1-rich circles. Lower-bound category: primorial size, r<=m^2/4 truncation, ordered versus unordered displacement double counting, padding from m^2 to n. Statement category: open problem gap means bounds are not matching; asymptotic claims need large-n qualification.

decisive_tests: Check a circle with exactly two points: does the proof keep at least one usable simple edge and still get e_simple >= (I-n)/2 up to constants? Check two points determining two unit centers in P: is multiplicity exactly bounded by 2? Choose explicit k and verify product of first k primes 1 mod 4 is <= m^2/4 while 2^k >= m^{c/log log m}. Test displacement (a,b) with a^2+b^2=r and |a|<=m/2: confirm at least m^2/4 translates. Verify crossing count when two circles intersect at a point of P: that point is a vertex, not a crossing, after perturbation.
unresolved_objections: The multigraph-to-simple reduction with explicit constants, the quantitative prime-in-arithmetic-progression estimate sufficient for the claimed c, and the regular-drawing perturbation for H remain unresolved in the candidate as written. These are repairable gaps rather than counterexamples, so the strategy survives only after repair.

objections.claim: Upper-bound category: multigraph multiplicity, drawing degeneracies, cr(H) <= 2 binom(n,2) justification, e(H)>=I-n only after discarding 1-rich circles. Lower-bound category: primorial size, r<=m^2/4 truncation, ordered versus unordered displacement double counting, padding from m^2 to n. Statement category: open problem gap means bounds are not matching; asymptotic claims need large-n qualification.

analysis.plan: Unit distance problem asks for max edges in unit-distance graph on n vertices in plane. Need both lower bound via integer lattice and upper bound O(n^{4/3}) via point-circle incidences. Distinct route must connect graph formulation to incidence geometry and number theory without appealing to unproved black boxes.

output.normalized_problem: Let P subset R^2, |P|=n, U(P)=|{{p,q}: |p-q|=1}|, U_max(n)=max U(P). Prove c n^{1+c/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C>0, via explicit lattice construction for lower bound and point-unit-circle incidence theorem for upper bound.
output.primary_route: Step 1: Reformulate as unit-distance graph G with vertices P, edges at distance 1. Step 2 Lower bound Lemma L1: sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) grid gives >=2n-O(sqrt n) unit pairs. Strengthen to superlinear via Erdos number-theoretic grid: take points {(x,y): 0<=x<m, 0<=y<M} with suitable m,M and count vectors of length 1 arising from representations of integers as sum of two squares; choose radius r with many representations r = product of primes 1 mod 4 to get many unit distances after rescaling. Conclude U_max(n) >= n^{1+c/log log n}. Step 3 Upper bound Lemma U1: Let C be set of n unit circles centered at points of P. Then U(P)= I(P,C)/2 where I is incidence count, since each unit pair gives two incidences. Step 4 Lemma U2 (Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter point-circle incidence): For m points and N unit circles with at most 2 circles through any pair in general sense and at most 2 intersections per pair, I = O(m^{2/3} N^{2/3} + m + N). Prove via random sampling + K_{3,3}-free or crossing argument and Szemeredi-Trotter for pseudocircles. Step 5 Apply with m=N=n to get I=O(n^{4/3}) hence U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3}). Combine for final best-known bounds.
backup_routes: Backup A: Crossing-number proof of upper bound: draw unit-distance graph with circular arcs as edges, bound crossings by O(n^2) since two unit circles cross at most twice, then apply Ajtai-Chvatal-Newborn-Szemeredi crossing lemma e=O(v + (v+cr)^{...}) to get e=O(n^{4/3}). Backup B: Induction with polynomial cell decomposition / cuttings for circles to prove incidence bound directly. Backup C: Weaker elementary upper O(n^{3/2}) via double-counting paths of length 2 and 2-intersection property as fallback if full 4/3 fails.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Proving the point-unit-circle incidence bound O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) rigorously: unit circles are not lines, two points determine more than one unit circle, and degeneracy from coincident circles and high-multiplicity incidences must be controlled; naive Szemeredi-Trotter does not apply and cutting or K_{s,t}-freeness needs careful graph construction to avoid losing factor.
active_obligations: O1: Justify U=I/2 without double counting coincident circles. O2: Prove lattice count with divisor estimate for sum of two squares gives superlinear gain. O3: Prove incidence lemma with explicit constants and handling of degenerate rich points/circles. O4: Transfer m=N=n case to final O(n^{4/3}) cleanly.
output.next_task: Formalize Lemma U1 incidence reduction and isolate degenerate high-degree points and circles before applying incidence bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write rigorous proof that U(P) equals half incidences between P and unit circles centered at P, then prove weak incidence estimate I=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) for unit circles via random sample plus bound on 2-rich structure, ready to plug m=N=n.
output.readiness_assessment: Strategy is standard and complete in outline but not yet execution-ready: incidence black box and number-theoretic lower bound both require detailed proofs; crossing-number details and divisor estimates remain to be written.
risky_lemmas: R1: Full O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}) unit-circle incidence bound is risky if attempted from scratch without cutting theory. R2: Superlinear n^{1+c/log log n} lower bound is risky due to dependence on prime distribution 1 mod 4 and divisor function lower bounds; fallback to linear Omega(n) is safe but weaker.

preserved_critiques.claim: Must not claim two points determine unique unit circle; must not ignore coincident circles; must not claim trivial grid gives superlinear bound without number theory; must keep upper bound proof independent of unproven Szemeredi-Trotter generalization.

output.primary_route: Route C: Number-theoretic lower bound + Graph-crossing incidence upper bound. Step A Lower: Take integer grid G_m = {0,...,m-1} x {0,...,m-1} scaled by 1/L. Or take points {(x,y) in Z^2: x^2+y^2 <= R}. Count representations of integers as sum of two squares. Use that numbers with many divisors give many vectors of same length. Choose radius r with maximal r_2(r) = |{(a,b): a^2+b^2=r}|. By pigeonhole and divisor bound, exists r <= n with r_2(r) >= exp(c log n / log log n). Take P as grid portion to realize n^{1+c/log log n} pairs at distance sqrt(r), then rescale to distance 1. Simpler weak version: m x m grid gives Omega(m^2 log m)?? Use number of vectors (a,b) with a^2+b^2 <= small: count unit distances after scaling. Deduce Omega(n log n / sqrt(log n)). Step B Upper: Build unit-distance graph G on P with e=U(P) edges drawn as straight segments. Two distinct unit circles intersect at most twice, so crossing number cr(G) <= C(n,2) essentially number of circle-pair intersections. More precisely draw circles of radius 1 around each point: we have n points and n circles, incidences I = 2e. Apply Szemeredi-Trotter type point-circle incidence bound I = O(N^{2/3} M^{2/3}+N+M) for N points M circles with proof via crossing lemma or cuttings. With N=M=n get 2e=O(n^{4/3}), hence e=O(n^{4/3}). Provide full proof of incidence bound: form graph with vertices = points on circles, edges = arcs between consecutive points, bound crossings by circle pairs, apply crossing-number inequality cr >= e^3/(64 v^2) when e>=4v, split into low/high degree circles to handle vertices of degree <2.

Backup 2: Use Szemeredi-Trotter point-line reduction via inversion or lifting to 3D paraboloid and polynomial method (Guth-Katz) for weaker O(n^{4/3}) or stronger o(n^{4/3}) remark. Backup 3 for lower bound: Use sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) integer lattice scaled by 1/sqrt(log n) to get elementary Omega(n log n / sqrt(log n)) avoiding deep sum-of-two-squares, using Landau-Ramanujan count of representable distances.
output.first_hard_obstruction: The first hard obstruction is proving the point-circle incidence bound I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}) rigorously: naive K_{2,2}-free incidence gives only O(n^{3/2}) via Kővári–Sós–Turán, insufficient. Without careful splitting into light/heavy circles the graph argument collapses.

analysis.plan: Unit-distance max problem requires two-sided bounds: polynomial upper O(n^{4/3}) via point-circle incidences and superlinear lower n^{1+c/log log n} via arithmetic lattice with many sum-of-two-squares representations. Strategy must separate combinatorial incidence graph argument from number-theoretic construction.

output.normalized_problem: For P subset R^2, |P|=n, let U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|. Prove c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3} for absolute constants c,C,c'>0, using (a) reduction to incidences of n points vs n unit circles and Szemeredi-Trotter-type bound, (b) scaled integer lattice with radius sqrt(R) where R has many representations as sum of two squares.
output.primary_route: Lemma A (Incidence reduction): U(P)=I(P,C)/2 where C={unit circles centered at P}. Lemma B (Forbidden K_{2,3}): Two distinct points lie on at most 2 unit circles, so incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free; edge multiplicity of circle-intersection graph <=2. Lemma C (Crossing Lemma with multiplicity 2): For graph G with n vertices, m edges, max multiplicity mu=2, cr(G) >= m^3/(64 mu n^2) for m>=4 mu n, else trivial. Lemma D (Circle incidence bound): Draw n unit circles; form graph G whose vertices are points of P plus intersection points, edges are circle arcs between them; crossings <=2*C(n,2) since two circles cross <=2 times; counting gives I=O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3}+n+m) specialization m=n yields I=O(n^{4/3}), hence U_max=O(n^{4/3}). Lemma E (Number theory): If p_i=1 mod 4 primes, R=prod p_i, then r_2(R)=4*2^k large ~ R^{c/log log R}. Lemma F (Lattice counting): Take S={(x,y) in Z^2: |x|,|y|<=M}, M~R^{alpha}; count pairs at distance sqrt(R) is ~ |S|*r_2(R)/poly; pigeonhole a dense translate/cluster of n points preserving many unit distances after scaling by 1/sqrt(R). Conclude superlinear lower bound.
backup_routes: Backup 1: Prove incidence bound via random sampling plus K_{2,3} Kovari-Sos-Turan weak bound O(n^{5/3}) then boost by cutting / divide-and-conquer on cells to O(n^{4/3}). Backup 2: Use Szemeredi-Trotter for lines via point-line duality and crossing lemma, then lift to circles by inversion or by splitting circles into two pseudo-parabolas. Backup 3: For lower bound use Erdos integer-grid sqrt(n) x sqrt(n) with averaging over distances 1..O(n) to get Omega(n log log n) weaker but elementary fallback if sum-of-two-squares optimization fails.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Controlling edge multiplicity and degeneracy in circle-arrangement graph: naive crossing-lemma application overcounts because coincident circle arcs can overlap, tangencies give single intersection, and vertices of degree 2 from empty arcs inflate n without helping; must prune circles with <=2 incident points and argue multiplicity <=2 from at most 2 intersections of two unit circles, otherwise crossing upper bound cr<=n^2 is invalid and incidence exponent collapses.
active_obligations: O1: Justify Lemma B rigorously: at most 2 unit circles through 2 points, at most 2 intersections of 2 unit circles, handling coincident circles and tangent cases. O2: Prove Crossing Lemma with multiplicity and linear threshold, including Euler formula base cr>=m-3n. O3: Construct arrangement graph formally and relate m_edges to I, removing low-degree circles. O4: Prove r_2(R) lower bound via prime factorization theorem for sums of two squares and divisor growth. O5: Show lattice cluster extraction yields exactly n points with claimed preserved unit count after scaling, controlling boundary losses.
output.next_task: Formalize incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-free property and set up circle-arrangement graph with pruning for crossing-lemma count.
output.concrete_next_task: Write Lemma A+B proof: define C, prove I=2U, prove two points in at most 2 unit circles via rhombus geometry; then define pruned family C' of circles with >=3 points and bound discarded incidences by 2n.
output.readiness_assessment: Ready to execute upper bound modulo standard crossing lemma; lower-bound number theory needs careful quantitative choice of k, M, R to balance r_2(R) vs lattice size; main risk is lattice boundary error and extraction to exact n.
risky_lemmas: Risky: Lemma D exponent depends on correct multiplicity handling and crossing upper bound O(n^2); if tangencies or overlapping circles miscounted, constant/exponent fails. Risky: Lemma F density claim that Omega fraction of lattice pairs at distance sqrt(R) survive in an n-subset; requires averaging/pigeonholing with explicit M vs R tradeoff, sensitive to R >> M^2 vs R << M^2.

preserved_critiques.claim: Must not assume general Szemeredi-Trotter for curves without proof; circles need separate intersection bound. Must not claim Omega(n^{4/3}) lower bound; lattice only gives n^{1+c/log log n}. Must not double-count ordered vs unordered pairs or points vs circles incidences.

analysis.plan: The unit-distance maximum U_max(n) is the classic Erdos unit-distance problem. Expected final theorem is Omega(n^{1+c/log log n}) <= U_max(n) <= O(n^{4/3}). Lower bound comes from dense integer lattice capturing many representations of integers as sum of two squares. Upper bound reduces unit pairs to incidences between n points and n unit circles and invokes a Szemeredi-Trotter type point-circle incidence bound. The hard work is proving the incidence bound rigorously without circular reasoning and handling circles containing many points.

output.normalized_problem: Let P subset R^2, |P|=n, U(P)=|{{p,q}:|p-q|=1}|, U_max(n)=max U(P). output.primary_route: Route A: Number-theoretic lattice + incidence via dyadic cutting. Step 1 Lower bound: take P = {0,...,k-1} x {0,...,k-1} scaled by 1/sqrt(m) where k^2=n, choose m with many representations r_2(m) large. Count pairs at distance sqrt(m) before scaling. Use that numbers m <= k^2 with many divisors give r_2(m) >= exp(c log m / log log m). Conclude U(P) >= n^{1+c/log log n}/2. Step 2 Upper bound: let G be unit-distance graph on P. For each p in P draw unit circle C_p centered at p. Then 2 U(P) = I(P,C)-n where C={C_p} counts point-circle incidences with p on its own circle removed. Step 3 Prove incidence lemma: for m points and N circles, I <= C0 (m^{2/3} N^{2/3} + m + N). Proof by dyadic decomposition into t-rich circles: let C_j = circles containing >= 2^j points. Bound |C_j| using that two circles intersect in <=2 points via K_{2,2}-free incidence / crossing argument or random sampling + weak bound I=O(m sqrt(N)+N). Sum over j. Step 4 Apply with m=N=n to get 2U <= O(n^{4/3}). Conclude upper bound.
backup_routes: Backup 1: Crossing-number route. Draw unit-distance graph with straight edges. Use that two unit circles cross O(1) times to bound crossing number cr(G) <= O(n^2). Combine with crossing inequality cr(G) >= Omega(e^3/n^2) when e >= 4n to get e=O(n^{4/3}). Requires proving crossing lemma via random subgraph. Backup 2: Inversion + Szemeredi-Trotter for lines. Fix p0, invert about unit circle at p0 to turn circles through p0 into lines, apply point-line bound, then dyadically sum over rich points. Backup 3: Cell-partition / polynomial method: use Guth-Katz polynomial partitioning to prove circle incidences directly if cutting proof stalls.
output.first_hard_obstruction: The first place the naive count fails is double-counting circles containing many points: a trivial bound I <= sum_{circles} |P cap C| can be Theta(mN) if many points are concircular, and two distinct unit circles can share at most 2 points but many distinct centers can define the same geometric circle. The dyadic argument must separate poor circles (cheap trivial bound) from rich circles (strong combinatorial bound using 2-point determination). Without a bound of form |C_{>=t}| = O(m^2/t^3 + m/t) the summation diverges and the n^{4/3} exponent is lost. Also need to handle coincident circles from distinct centers: show distinct centers give distinct circles unless centers coincide, so N=n distinct.
active_obligations: O1: Justify existence of integer m with large r_2(m) in range and transfer to grid count without boundary loss: need divisor estimate and that most vectors of length sqrt(m) stay inside k x k box. O2: Prove weak incidence bound to bootstrap: I(m,N)=O(mN^{1/2}+N) using Cauchy-Schwarz and at most 2 intersections. O3: Prove sampling / cutting lemma to upgrade weak bound to m^{2/3}N^{2/3}: random subset, apply weak bound, use that rich circles survive. O4: Verify reduction 2U=I-n is exact and circles are distinct. O5: Optimize dyadic sum to get +m+N linear terms.
output.next_task: Prove the weak point-circle incidence estimate and set up dyadic decomposition for rich unit circles, then execute the lattice divisor calculation for the lower bound.
output.concrete_next_task: Write Lemma 1 (two-circle intersection => K_{2,2}-free => I=O(m sqrt(N)+N) by double counting pairs on same circle) and Lemma 2 (number-theoretic: exists m <= n with r_2(m) >= n^{c/log log n}). Then show how Lemma 1 plus random sampling implies the strong m^{2/3}N^{2/3} bound and how Lemma 2 implies the grid has required unit pairs after scaling by 1/sqrt(m).
output.readiness_assessment: Ready to execute: reduction to incidences is standard and low-risk; main risk concentrated in rigorous proof of strong incidence bound and quantitative divisor bound. With weak bound plus standard probabilistic amplification the strong bound follows in a few lines. Lower bound needs only elementary analytic number theory, no Siegel-Walfisz. Overall route is complete modulo writing those two lemmas cleanly.

R3: Sampling amplification step preserves distinctness and does not lose log factors - needs explicit Chernoff or expectation calculation.

subproblems.title: Point-circle incidence reduction and K_{2,3}-freeness
subproblems.target_claim: For |P|=n let C be the n unit circles centred at the points of P. Prove the circles are distinct, no point of P lies on its own circle, and I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly. Prove two distinct points lie on at most two unit circles centred in P and two distinct unit circles meet in at most two points, hence the incidence graph is K_{2,3}-free, while explicitly not claiming K_{2,2}-freeness.

subproblems.title: Crossing lemma for simple graphs and multiplicity at most two
subproblems.target_claim: Prove from Euler's bound E <= 3V-6 for simple planar graphs with V>=3 that cr(G) >= e-3v+6, and by random induced subgraphs that cr(G) >= e^3/(64v^2) when e>=4v, with non-optimal absolute constants allowed. Extend the consequence to multigraphs with multiplicity at most 2 by passing to a simple subgraph with at least half the edges, handling disconnected graphs, small v, loops (absent in the application), and the split e<4v versus e>=4v.

subproblems.title: Pruned circular-arc graph with P as vertex set
subproblems.target_claim: Let k_i be the number of points of P on the i-th unit circle. Discard circles with k_i<=2, losing at most 2n incidences. For k_i>=3 order the points cyclically on the circle and join consecutive points by the circle arcs containing no third point of P in their interior. Prove the resulting drawing has v=n, no loops, e_arc >= I(P,C)-2n, edge multiplicity at most 2 because two vertices determine at most two possible unit centres, and hence a simple subgraph H' with e' >= e_arc/2.

subproblems.title: Crossing upper bound with tangency, vertex, and concurrency control
subproblems.target_claim: Prove cr(H') <= 2\binom{n}{2} <= n^2 for the arc drawing of Subproblem 4. subproblems.title: Upper bound U_max(n)=O(n^{4/3})
subproblems.target_claim: Combine Subproblems 2, 4 and 5 with the crossing lemma: if e'<4n then I(P,C)=O(n), and otherwise e'^3/(64n^2) <= cr(H') <= n^2, so e'=O(n^{4/3}), I(P,C)=O(n^{4/3}), and U(P)=I(P,C)/2=O(n^{4/3}) uniformly in P. subproblems.title: Representations of R as a sum of two squares

Prove R is odd and non-square, so no representation has a zero coordinate or equal absolute coordinates, every orbit under sign changes and coordinate swap has size 8, and the number of undirected displacement directions is 2^{k-1}.

subproblems.title: Prime-product size estimate and choice of k

  "solution_body": "We prove the weakened best-known statement and the monotonicity-padding principle. Let $P\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be finite, $|P|=n$, and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1\ne p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. Define $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n} U(P)$. The maximum exists since $0\le U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$. We claim no exact formula, no $\Theta$-tightness, and no matching exponent. The provable best-known result is: there exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,
$$ c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}. $$
In particular the upper exponent $4/3$ and lower exponent $1+\Omega(1/\log\log n)$ do not match; there is a large open gap. We require $n$ large so that $\log\log n>0$, e.g. $n>e^{e}$, and constants are independent of $n$ and $P$. This is an upper bound and a lower-bound construction, not a determination of $U_{\max}(n)$.

Lemma (Monotonicity with isolated padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Moreover, given any $P$ with $|P|=n$, there exists $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so that for $P'=P\cup\{q\}$, $|P'|=n+1$ and $U(P')=U(P)$. Hence $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.

Proof. Adding a point cannot destroy existing unit pairs: if $P\subset P'$ then any unit pair of $P$ remains a unit pair of $P'$, so $U(P')\ge U(P)$. Hence $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing trivially. For the isolated padding, let $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}S^1(p)$ where $S^1(p)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. $P$ is finite and each $S^1(p)$ is a $1$-dimensional circle of Lebesgue measure zero; a finite union of such sets cannot cover $\mathbb{R}^2$. Indeed $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus S$ is nonempty and in fact co-bounded: choose $q$ with $|q|$ larger than $\max_{p\in P}|p|+2$, then $q\notin P$ and $|q-p|>1$ for all $p\in P$, in particular $|q-p|\ne 1$. More generally any $q\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus S$ works. Then $P'=P\cup\{q\}$ has $n+1$ distinct points, the pairs among $P$ are unchanged, and $q$ participates in $0$ unit pairs by construction, so $U(P')=U(P)$. Taking $P$ optimal for $n$, i.e. $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$, gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')=U_{\max}(n)$. By induction $U_{\max}$ is monotone.\qed

Corollary (Reduction to squares). To prove the lower bound $U_{\max}(n)\ge c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for all large $n$, it suffices to prove it for square cardinalities $n=m^2$. Indeed, given $n$, let $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, so $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$ and $m^2\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. If $U_{\max}(m^2)\ge c\,(m^2)^{1+c'/\log\log(m^2)}$ for large $m$, then by monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)$. Since $m^2\ge n/4$ for large $n$ (in fact $m^2=n-O(\sqrt{n})$), the transfer to $n$ loses only an absolute constant factor and a negligible change in $\log\log$, absorbed by slightly shrinking $c,c'$. Explicitly, padding the $m^2$-point extremal example with $n-m^2$ far-away points chosen inductively outside all previous unit circles preserves the count. Hence lower-bound constructions may assume $|P|=m^2$ on an $m\times m$ grid and then pad. We require $n$ large so that $\log\log n>0$, e.g. $n>e^{e}$, and constants are independent of $n$ and $P$. This is an upper bound and a lower-bound construction, not a determination of $U_{\max}(n)$.

Lemma (Monotonicity with isolated padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Moreover, given any $P$ with $|P|=n$, there exists $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so that for $P'=P\cup\{q\}$, $|P'|=n+1$ and $U(P')=U(P)$. Hence $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.

Proof. Adding a point cannot destroy existing unit pairs: if $P\subset P'$ then any unit pair of $P$ remains a unit pair of $P'$, so $U(P')\ge U(P)$. Hence $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing trivially. For the isolated padding, let $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}S^1(p)$ where $S^1(p)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. $P$ is finite and each $S^1(p)$ is a $1$-dimensional circle of Lebesgue measure zero; a finite union of such sets cannot cover $\mathbb{R}^2$. Indeed $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus S$ is nonempty and in fact co-bounded: choose $q$ with $|q|$ larger than $\max_{p\in P}|p|+2$, then $q\notin P$ and $|q-p|>1$ for all $p\in P$, in particular $|q-p|\ne 1$. More generally any $q\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus S$ works. Then $P'=P\cup\{q\}$ has $n+1$ distinct points, the pairs among $P$ are unchanged, and $q$ participates in $0$ unit pairs by construction, so $U(P')=U(P)$. Taking $P$ optimal for $n$, i.e. $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$, gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')=U_{\max}(n)$. By induction $U_{\max}$ is monotone.\qed

Corollary (Reduction to squares). To prove the lower bound $U_{\max}(n)\ge c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for all large $n$, it suffices to prove it for square cardinalities $n=m^2$.   "solution_body": "Let $P\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be finite. Define
$$U(P) = \left|\{\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P : p_1\ne p_2,\ |p_1-p_2|=1\}\right|$$
counting unordered pairs at distance $1$. For integer $n\ge 1$ define
$$U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n} U(P).$$
The maximum exists since up to isometry there are finitely many combinatorial types for fixed $n$, and in any case $U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}<\infty$. We prove the best-known, non-tight statement.

Claimed weakened theorem. There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C<\infty$, $c'>0$ and $N_0$ such that for all $n\ge N_0$,
$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$
No exact value, no $\Theta$-matching, no best-possible exponent is claimed. The gap between $1+c'/\log\log n$ and $4/3$ is open.

In particular $\log\log n$ is defined and $>0$ only for $n>e$. We take $n$ large, e.g. $n\ge 16$, so $\log\log n>0$. The lower bound is superlinear by a $\log\log$-factor, the upper bound is $O(n^{4/3})$. Both are best-known, not best-possible.

Lemma (Monotonicity and padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Hence lower bounds proved on a subsequence extend to all $n$.

Proof. Let $|P|=n$ attain $U_{\max}(n)$, i.e. $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$. Let $q\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus P$ be any point distinct from $P$; e.g. choose $q$ far away, with distance $>2$ from all points of $P$ and not creating any new unit distance if desired. Then $P'=P\cup\{q\}$ has $|P'|=n+1$ and every unit pair of $P$ remains a unit pair of $P'$. Indeed $U$ counts subsets of the ground set, and adding a point cannot delete existing pairs:
$$U(P') \ge U(P).$$
Possibly $U(P')=U(P)+t$ with $t\ge 0$ the number of points of $P$ at distance $1$ from $q$; choosing $q$ far away we can ensure $t=0$, but for monotonicity any $q\notin P$ suffices since $t\ge 0$. Taking max over $|P'|=n+1$,
$$U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')\ge U(P)=U_{\max}(n).$$
Thus $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing. In particular if $m^2\le n$ then $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)$.

Explicit far-away choice: given finite $P$, the union of $P$ and the finitely many unit circles centred at points of $P$

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.formal_statement: We prove best-known bounds, not exact determination. There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and N0 such that for all n >= N0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}, where U(P) is number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} in P with |p1-p2|=1 and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). No claim of Theta-tightness, matching exponent, or best-possible is made. loglog n is defined and positive for n>e; we take n large.
output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P)=|{{p,q} subset P : p!=q, |p-q|=1}| unordered. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Maximum exists since condition depends continuously but combinatorics finite up to isometry; supremum over configurations is attained e.g. by compactness argument or simply as finite integer bounded by C(n,2).

Monotonicity: U_max is nondecreasing. Indeed let P_n attain U_max(n). Let q not in P_n arbitrary. Let P_{n+1}=P_n union {q}. Every unit pair of P_n remains a unit pair of P_{n+1}. Hence U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n). Additional pairs involving q can only increase count. Therefore U_max(n+1) >= U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n)=U_max(n). No geometric avoidance is needed for monotonicity itself. In particular adding far-away points cannot destroy pairs.

For lower-bound padding we may choose q far away to control extra contribution, but inequality U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) holds for any choice. Hence it suffices to construct examples on a subsequence of cardinalities and pad upward.

Padding from squares: Let m>=2 integer, N=m^2. Suppose we construct G_N with |G_N|=N and U(G_N) >= F(N) for some nondecreasing F. Then for general n, let m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2 = N+2m+1. Starting from G_N, add n-N arbitrary distinct points inductively to reach exactly n points; call the result P_n. By monotonicity of U under inclusion, U(P_n) >= U(G_N) >= F(N). Hence U_max(n) >= F(N). If desired choose added points at distance !=1 from all existing points and each other (possible since finite union of unit circles has empty interior) so U(P_n)=U(G_N), but inequality suffices.

Transfer of exponent: For n>=16, m=floor(sqrt(n))>= sqrt(n)/2, so N=m^2 >= n/4. Suppose for squares N large, F(N)=c1 N^{1+c'/loglog N} with c1,c'>0. Then U_max(n) >= c1 N^{1+c'/loglog N}. Since N>=n/4, N >= c'' n up to constant. Moreover loglog N = log(log N) <= log(log n)=loglog n, and for n large N large, loglog N >= (1/2)loglog n (since log N >= log n - log 4). Hence 1/loglog N >= 1/loglog n and also exponent comparison gives N^{c'/loglog N} >= c''' n^{c''/loglog n} up to adjusting constants. Explicitly: N^{1+c'/loglog N} = N * exp(c' log N / loglog N) >= (n/4)*exp(c' (log n -log 4)/loglog n) >= c2 n^{1+c2'/loglog n} for suitable absolute c2,c2'>0 and n large. Thus lower bound on squares implies same shape bound for all large n with slightly smaller constants. This justifies proving lower bound only for N=m^2.

Similarly upper bound, once proved for all n, needs no padding. The interval n>=N0 ensures loglog n>0 and m large enough for number-theoretic construction. This completes weakened formulation and reduction.

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.formal_statement: We prove best-known bounds, not exact determination. There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and N0 such that for all n >= N0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}, where U(P) is number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} in P with |p1-p2|=1 and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). No claim of Theta-tightness, matching exponent, or best-possible is made. loglog n is defined and positive for n>e; we take n large.
output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P)=|{{p,q} subset P : p!=q, |p-q|=1}| unordered. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Maximum exists since condition depends continuously but combinatorics finite up to isometry; supremum over configurations is attained e.g. by compactness argument or simply as finite integer bounded by C(n,2).

Monotonicity: U_max is nondecreasing. Indeed let P_n attain U_max(n). Let q not in P_n arbitrary. Let P_{n+1}=P_n union {q}. Every unit pair of P_n remains a unit pair of P_{n+1}. Hence U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n). Additional pairs involving q can only increase count. Therefore U_max(n+1) >= U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n)=U_max(n). No geometric avoidance is needed for monotonicity itself. In particular adding far-away points cannot destroy pairs.

For lower-bound padding we may choose q far away to control extra contribution, but inequality U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) holds for any choice. Hence it suffices to construct examples on a subsequence of cardinalities and pad upward.

Padding from squares: Let m>=2 integer, N=m^2. Suppose we construct G_N with |G_N|=N and U(G_N) >= F(N) for some nondecreasing F. Then for general n, let m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2 = N+2m+1. Starting from G_N, add n-N arbitrary distinct points inductively to reach exactly n points; call the result P_n. By monotonicity of U under inclusion, U(P_n) >= U(G_N) >= F(N). Hence U_max(n) >= F(N). If desired choose added points at distance !=1 from all existing points and each other (possible since finite union of unit circles has empty interior) so U(P_n)=U(G_N), but inequality suffices.

Transfer of exponent: For n>=16, m=floor(sqrt(n))>= sqrt(n)/2, so N=m^2 >= n/4. Suppose for squares N large, F(N)=c1 N^{1+c'/loglog N} with c1,c'>0. Then U_max(n) >= c1 N^{1+c'/loglog N}. Since N>=n/4, N >= c'' n up to constant. Moreover loglog N = log(log N) <= log(log n)=loglog n, and for n large N large, loglog N >= (1/2)loglog n (since log N >= log n - log 4). Hence 1/loglog N >= 1/loglog n and also exponent comparison gives N^{c'/loglog N} >= c''' n^{c''/loglog n} up to adjusting constants. Explicitly: N^{1+c'/loglog N} = N * exp(c' log N / loglog N) >= (n/4)*exp(c' (log n -log 4)/loglog n) >= c2 n^{1+c2'/loglog n} for suitable absolute c2,c2'>0 and n large. Thus lower bound on squares implies same shape bound for all large n with slightly smaller constants. This justifies proving lower bound only for N=m^2.

Similarly upper bound, once proved for all n, needs no padding. The interval n>=N0 ensures loglog n>0 and m large enough for number-theoretic construction. This completes weakened formulation and reduction.

No three edges concurrent interiorly and no two meeting twice can be assumed in an optimal drawing, otherwise a local rerouting strictly reduces crossing number. We allow non-optimal constants.

Assume first $G$ is simple and loopless. Recall Euler's bound: if $G$ is simple planar with $v\ge 3$ then $e\le 3v-6$. Indeed, for a planar embedding with $c\ge 1$ components, $V-E+F=1+c$ and, $G$ simple with $v\ge 3$ implying every face has degree $\ge 3$, $2E\ge 3F$. Hence $2E\ge 3(1+c-V+E)$, i.e. $E\le 3V-3-3c\le 3V-6$. In particular this covers disconnected $G$.

Lemma 1 (linear). If $G$ is simple with $v\ge 3$ then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$.

Proof. Fix a drawing attaining $\mathrm{cr}(G)$. If $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0$, $G$ is planar and $e\le 3v-6$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0\ge e-3v+6$. Suppose $\mathrm{cr}(G)>0$ and the claim holds for all graphs with smaller crossing number. Pick an edge $f$ participating in a crossing. Let $G'=G-f$, so $e(G')=e-1$, $v(G')=v$. After small perturbation, each crossing involves exactly $4$ distinct vertices as endpoints of the two crossing edges.

output.proof_body:
We prove only the provable best-known bounds. There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0,

  c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3},

where for finite P in R^2, U(P) is the number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset of P with |p1-p2|=1 and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). No exact value, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness and no best-possible claim is made; the gap remains open. We require n large so loglog n >0, e.g. n>=16.

U_max(n) is well defined and finite: for any P with |P|=n, 0<=U(P)<=binom(n,2) is an integer, so as P varies only finitely many integer values occur and the maximum is attained.

Lemma (monotonicity and far-away padding). U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) for all n. Moreover, given any finite P, there exists q not in P with |q-p|!=1 for all p in P, so that U(P union {q})=U(P).

Proof. Let P_n achieve U_max(n). For any q not in P_n, the pairs of P_n persist in P_n union {q}, so U(P_n union {q})>=U(P_n). Taking max over sets of size n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U(P_n)=U_max(n).

For refined padding, let S = P union Union_{p in P} {x:|x-p|=1}, a finite set plus finitely many unit circles. Its complement is non-empty. Indeed, consider the line L={(t,0):t in R}. Each unit circle meets L in at most 2 points and P meets L in at most |P| points, so the set of forbidden t is finite. Choose t larger than max_{p in P}|p|+2 and avoiding this finite forbidden set; then q=(t,0) is distinct from P and at distance !=1 from every p in P. Hence no new unit pair involving q is created and no old pair is destroyed, so U(P union {q})=U(P). Iterating gives exact-size extensions with unchanged count. In particular for N<=n, U_max(n)>=U_max(N).

Corollary (squares suffice). It suffices to prove the superlinear lower bound for square cardinalities N=m^2. Indeed suppose for all large integers m, U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/loglog(m^2)}. Then the same form holds for all large n up to adjusting constants.

Proof. Let n be large and m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2<=n. By monotonicity U_max(n)>=U_max(N). For n>=4, m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, so N>=n/4 and N->infinity with n. Assume n>=16 so loglog n>0. Then log N>=log n-log 4>= (1/2)log n for large n and loglog N<=loglog n. Hence with N^{c'/loglog N}=exp(c' log N/loglog N),

  log N/loglog N >= (log n-log 4)/loglog n.

Therefore U_max(n)>=c0 N exp(c'(log n-log 4)/loglog n)>=c0 (n/4) n^{c'/loglog n} exp(-c' log 4/loglog n). Since exp(-c' log 4/loglog n)->1, it is >=1/2 for large n. Absorbing 1/4 and 1/2 into c=c0/8 gives U_max(n)>=c n^{1+c'/loglog n} for all large n. The same far-away iteration goes from m^2 to any n with m^2<=n<(m+1)^2 without loss. The upper bound U_max(n)<=C n^{4/3} is to be proved directly for all n.

We formulate only the provable best-known bounds. There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\ge n_{0}$,

$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3},$$

where for finite $P\subset \mathbf{R}^{2}$, $U(P)$ is the number of unordered pairs $\{p_{1},p_{2}\}\subset P$ with $|p_{1}-p_{2}|=1$ and $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n}U(P)$. No exact value, no matching exponent, no $\Theta$-tightness and no best-possible claim is made; the gap remains open. We require $n$ large so $\log\log n>0$, e.g. $n\ge 16$.

$U_{\max}(n)$ is well defined and finite: for fixed $n$ there are only $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs. It is nondecreasing in $n$.

Lemma (monotonicity and far-away padding). $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$ for all $n$. Moreover, given any finite $P$, there exists $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so that $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$.

Proof. Let $P_{n}$ achieve $U_{\max}(n)$. For any $q\notin P_{n}$, the pairs of $P_{n}$ persist in $P_{n}\cup\{q\}$, so $U(P_{n}\cup\{q\})\ge U(P_{n})$. Taking max over sets of size $n+1$ gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P_{n})=U_{\max}(n)$. For the refined padding, consider $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}\{x:|x-p|=1\}$. This is a finite set plus finitely many unit circles, hence its complement in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ is non-empty. Choose $q\notin S$. Then $q$ is distinct from $P$ and at distance $\ne 1$ from every $p\in P$. Hence no new unit pair involving $q$ is created and no old pair is destroyed, so $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$. Iterating gives exact-size extensions with unchanged count. In particular for $N\le n$, $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. 

Corollary (squares suffice). It suffices to prove the superlinear lower bound for square cardinalities $N=m^{2}$. Indeed suppose for all large integers $m$, $U_{\max}(m^{2})\ge c_{0}(m^{2})^{1+c'/\log\log(m^{2})}$. Then the same form holds for all large $n$ up to adjusting constants.

Proof. Let $n$ be large and $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, $N=m^{2}\le n$. By monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. For $n\ge 4$, $m>\sqrt{n}-1\ge \sqrt{n}/2$, so $N\ge n/4$ and $N\to\infty$ with $n$. Assume $n\ge 16$ so $\log n\ge 2\log 4$ and $\log\log n>0$. Then $\log N\ge \log n-\log 4\ge \tfrac12\log n$ and $\log\log N\le \log\log n$. Hence, with $N^{c'/\log\log N}=\exp(c'\log N/\log\log N)$,

$$\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\ge \frac{\log n-\log 4}{\log\log n}.$$

Therefore $U_{\max}(n)\ge c_{0}N\cdot\exp(c'(\log n-\log 4)/\log\log n)\ge c_{0}(n/4)\cdot n^{c'/\log\log n}\cdot\exp(-c'\log 4/\log\log n)$. Since $\exp(-c'\log 4/\log\log n)\to 1$, it is $\ge 1/2$ for large $n$. Absorbing $1/4$ and $1/2$ into $c=c_{0}/8$ gives $U_{\max}(n)\ge c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for all large $n$. The same monotonicity allows iteration of far-away points to go from $m^{2}$ to any $n$ with $m^{2}\le n<(m+1)^{2}$ without loss. This completes the quantitative square-to-general transfer. The upper bound $U_{\max}(n)\le C n^{4/3}$ is to be proved directly for all $n$.

We prove only the provable best-known bounds. There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0,

  c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3},

where for finite P in R^2, U(P) is the number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset of P with |p1-p2|=1 and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). No exact value, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness and no best-possible claim is made; the gap remains open. We require n large so loglog n >0, e.g. n>=16.

U_max(n) is well defined and finite: for any P with |P|=n, 0<=U(P)<=binom(n,2) is an integer, so as P varies only finitely many integer values occur and the maximum is attained.

Lemma (monotonicity and far-away padding). U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) for all n. Moreover, given any finite P, there exists q not in P with |q-p|!=1 for all p in P, so that U(P union {q})=U(P).

Proof. Let P_n achieve U_max(n). For any q not in P_n, the pairs of P_n persist in P_n union {q}, so U(P_n union {q})>=U(P_n). Taking max over sets of size n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U(P_n)=U_max(n).

For refined padding, let S = P union Union_{p in P} {x:|x-p|=1}, a finite set plus finitely many unit circles. Its complement is non-empty. Indeed, consider the line L={(t,0):t in R}. Each unit circle meets L in at most 2 points and P meets L in at most |P| points, so the set of forbidden t is finite. Choose t larger than max_{p in P}|p|+2 and avoiding this finite forbidden set; then q=(t,0) is distinct from P and at distance !=1 from every p in P. Hence no new unit pair involving q is created and no old pair is destroyed, so U(P union {q})=U(P). Iterating gives exact-size extensions with unchanged count. In particular for N<=n, U_max(n)>=U_max(N).

Corollary (squares suffice). It suffices to prove the superlinear lower bound for square cardinalities N=m^2. Indeed suppose for all large integers m, U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/loglog(m^2)}. Then the same form holds for all large n up to adjusting constants.

Proof. Let n be large and m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2<=n. By monotonicity U_max(n)>=U_max(N). For n>=4, m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, so N>=n/4 and N->infinity with n. Assume n>=16 so loglog n>0. Then log N>=log n-log 4>= (1/2)log n for large n and loglog N<=loglog n. Hence with N^{c'/loglog N}=exp(c' log N/loglog N),

  log N/loglog N >= (log n-log 4)/loglog n.

Therefore U_max(n)>=c0 N exp(c'(log n-log 4)/loglog n)>=c0 (n/4) n^{c'/loglog n} exp(-c' log 4/loglog n). Since exp(-c' log 4/loglog n)->1, it is >=1/2 for large n. Absorbing 1/4 and 1/2 into c=c0/8 gives U_max(n)>=c n^{1+c'/loglog n} for all large n. The same far-away iteration goes from m^2 to any n with m^2<=n<(m+1)^2 without loss. The upper bound U_max(n)<=C n^{4/3} is to be proved directly for all n.

output.proof_body:
We prove only the provable best-known bounds. There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0,

  c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3},

where for finite P in R^2, U(P) is the number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset of P with |p1-p2|=1 and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). No exact value, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness and no best-possible claim is made; the gap remains open. We require n large so loglog n >0, e.g. n>=16.

U_max(n) is well defined and finite: for any P with |P|=n, 0<=U(P)<=binom(n,2) is an integer, so as P varies only finitely many integer values occur and the maximum is attained.

Lemma (monotonicity and far-away padding). U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) for all n. Moreover, given any finite P, there exists q not in P with |q-p|!=1 for all p in P, so that U(P union {q})=U(P).

Proof. Let P_n achieve U_max(n). For any q not in P_n, the pairs of P_n persist in P_n union {q}, so U(P_n union {q})>=U(P_n). Taking max over sets of size n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U(P_n)=U_max(n).

For refined padding, let S = P union Union_{p in P} {x:|x-p|=1}, a finite set plus finitely many unit circles. Its complement is non-empty. Indeed, consider the line L={(t,0):t in R}. Each unit circle meets L in at most 2 points and P meets L in at most |P| points, so the set of forbidden t is finite. Choose t larger than max_{p in P}|p|+2 and avoiding this finite forbidden set; then q=(t,0) is distinct from P and at distance !=1 from every p in P. Hence no new unit pair involving q is created and no old pair is destroyed, so U(P union {q})=U(P). Iterating gives exact-size extensions with unchanged count. In particular for N<=n, U_max(n)>=U_max(N).

Corollary (squares suffice). It suffices to prove the superlinear lower bound for square cardinalities N=m^2. Indeed suppose for all large integers m, U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/loglog(m^2)}. Then the same form holds for all large n up to adjusting constants.

Proof. Let n be large and m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2<=n. By monotonicity U_max(n)>=U_max(N). For n>=4, m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, so N>=n/4 and N->infinity with n. Assume n>=16 so loglog n>0. Then log N>=log n-log 4>= (1/2)log n for large n and loglog N<=loglog n. Hence with N^{c'/loglog N}=exp(c' log N/loglog N),

  log N/loglog N >= (log n-log 4)/loglog n.

Therefore U_max(n)>=c0 N exp(c'(log n-log 4)/loglog n)>=c0 (n/4) n^{c'/loglog n} exp(-c' log 4/loglog n). Since exp(-c' log 4/loglog n)->1, it is >=1/2 for large n. Absorbing 1/4 and 1/2 into c=c0/8 gives U_max(n)>=c n^{1+c'/loglog n} for all large n. The same far-away iteration goes from m^2 to any n with m^2<=n<(m+1)^2 without loss. The upper bound U_max(n)<=C n^{4/3} is to be proved directly for all n.

We formulate only the provable best-known bounds. There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\ge n_{0}$,

$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3},$$

where for finite $P\subset \mathbf{R}^{2}$, $U(P)$ is the number of unordered pairs $\{p_{1},p_{2}\}\subset P$ with $|p_{1}-p_{2}|=1$ and $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n}U(P)$. No exact value, no matching exponent, no $\Theta$-tightness and no best-possible claim is made; the gap remains open. We require $n$ large so $\log\log n>0$, e.g. $n\ge 16$.

$U_{\max}(n)$ is well defined and finite: for fixed $n$ there are only $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs. It is nondecreasing in $n$.

Lemma (monotonicity and far-away padding). $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$ for all $n$. Moreover, given any finite $P$, there exists $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so that $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$.

Proof. Let $P_{n}$ achieve $U_{\max}(n)$. For any $q\notin P_{n}$, the pairs of $P_{n}$ persist in $P_{n}\cup\{q\}$, so $U(P_{n}\cup\{q\})\ge U(P_{n})$. Taking max over sets of size $n+1$ gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P_{n})=U_{\max}(n)$. For the refined padding, consider $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}\{x:|x-p|=1\}$. This is a finite set plus finitely many unit circles, hence its complement in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ is non-empty. Choose $q\notin S$. Then $q$ is distinct from $P$ and at distance $\ne 1$ from every $p\in P$. Hence no new unit pair involving $q$ is created and no old pair is destroyed, so $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$. Iterating gives exact-size extensions with unchanged count. In particular for $N\le n$, $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. 

Corollary (squares suffice). It suffices to prove the superlinear lower bound for square cardinalities $N=m^{2}$. Indeed suppose for all large integers $m$, $U_{\max}(m^{2})\ge c_{0}(m^{2})^{1+c'/\log\log(m^{2})}$. Then the same form holds for all large $n$ up to adjusting constants.

Proof. Let $n$ be large and $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, $N=m^{2}\le n$. By monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. For $n\ge 4$, $m>\sqrt{n}-1\ge \sqrt{n}/2$, so $N\ge n/4$ and $N\to\infty$ with $n$. Assume $n\ge 16$ so $\log n\ge 2\log 4$ and $\log\log n>0$. Then $\log N\ge \log n-\log 4\ge \tfrac12\log n$ and $\log\log N\le \log\log n$. Hence, with $N^{c'/\log\log N}=\exp(c'\log N/\log\log N)$,

$$\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\ge \frac{\log n-\log 4}{\log\log n}.$$

Therefore $U_{\max}(n)\ge c_{0}N\cdot\exp(c'(\log n-\log 4)/\log\log n)\ge c_{0}(n/4)\cdot n^{c'/\log\log n}\cdot\exp(-c'\log 4/\log\log n)$. Since $\exp(-c'\log 4/\log\log n)\to 1$, it is $\ge 1/2$ for large $n$. Absorbing $1/4$ and $1/2$ into $c=c_{0}/8$ gives $U_{\max}(n)\ge c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for all large $n$. The same monotonicity allows iteration of far-away points to go from $m^{2}$ to any $n$ with $m^{2}\le n<(m+1)^{2}$ without loss. This completes the quantitative square-to-general transfer. The upper bound $U_{\max}(n)\le C n^{4/3}$ is to be proved directly for all $n$.

{"section": 3, "target_claim": "Crossing lemma for simple graphs and multiplicity <=2 reduction", "proof_body": "We prove the crossing-number lemma with non-optimal constants. Let cr(G) be the minimum number of interior edge-crossings over drawings with vertices distinct, edges continuous curves, no edge passing through a vertex, no three edges concurrent interiorly, no self-intersections and no tangencies counted. In a crossing-minimal drawing we may assume it is good: (i) no edge crosses itself, (ii) adjacent edges do not cross, (iii) two non-adjacent edges cross at most once. Indeed a self-crossing can be shortcut, an adjacent crossing can be swapped near the common endpoint to remove it, and two edges crossing twice can be swapped on the segment between the two crossings to reduce the count by 2.   "solution_body": "Let $G$ be a graph drawn in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices as points and edges as continuous arcs joining endpoints. The crossing number $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ is the minimum over all drawings of the number of interior intersection points of pairs of edges, counted with multiplicity, where no three edges meet in one interior point after small perturbation. We prove the crossing lemma.

Assume first $G$ simple. Fix a drawing attaining $\mathrm{cr}(G)$. By standard normalization we may assume no edge crosses itself, no two adjacent edges cross except at their common endpoint, and no three edges are concurrent in one interior point; otherwise a local rerouting strictly reduces crossings. Hence each crossing involves exactly $4$ distinct vertices.

Let $v$ be number of vertices, $e$ number of edges. For each crossing delete one of its two edges. After deleting at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges (one per crossing) the remaining drawing is planar. Thus there is a planar simple graph $G'$ on the same $v$ vertices with $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges.

We use Euler's bound: every simple planar connected graph with $V\ge 3$ satisfies $E\le 3V-6$. For disconnected planar simple graphs the same bound holds when $v\ge 3$. Indeed let components have $v_i,e_i$. If $v_i\ge 3$ then $e_i\le 3v_i-6$ by the connected case. If $v_i\le 2$ then $e_i\le v_i-1$ by simplicity ($0$ if $v_i=1$, $\le 1$ if $v_i=2$). If at least one $v_i\ge 3$, say $k\ge 1$ such components, then $e\le 3V_{\mathrm{big}}-6k+V_{\mathrm{small}}-l\le 3v-6$ since $2V_{\mathrm{small}}+6k+l\ge 6$. If all $v_i\le 2$ then $e\le v-c\le v-1\le 3v-6$ for $v\ge 3$. Hence for $v\ge 3$, $e'\le 3v-6$.

Consequently for simple $G$ with $v\ge 3$,
$$e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le e'\le 3v-6,$$
so
$$\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6.$$
In particular $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$. The latter inequality holds for all $v$, including $v<3$: if $v\le 2$ and $G$ simple then $e\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0\ge e-3v$, since $e-3v\le 1-6<0$ for $v=2$, etc. For $v_p\ge 3$ the $+6$ version implies the weaker version; for $v_p<3$ it is checked directly. This universal weak form will be used for random subgraphs.

Now suppose $e\ge 4v$. Then $v\ge 9$ for simple $G$ (since $e\le v(v-1)/2$), in particular $v\ge 3$. Choose $p=4v/e\le 1$. Form a random induced subgraph $G_p$ by keeping each vertex independently with probability $p$. Let $v_p,e_p$ be its numbers of vertices and edges, and $\mathrm{cr}_p$ the number of crossings of the induced drawing inherited from the optimal drawing of $G$. Then
$$\mathbb{E}[v_p]=pv,\quad \mathbb{E}[e_p]=p^2e,$$
since an edge survives iff both endpoints survive. Moreover $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}_p]=p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)$, since each crossing uses $4$ distinct vertices by normalization and survives iff all $4$ survive.

For every outcome, $\mathrm{cr}_p\ge e_p-3v_p$ by the discussion above (using $+6$ bound when $v_p\ge 3$ and trivial check when $v_p<3$). Taking expectations,
$$p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge p^2e-3pv.$$
Dividing by $p^4$,
$$\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge \frac{e}{p^2}-\frac{3v}{p^3}.$$
With $p=4v/e$, $e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2)$ and $3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2)$, so
$$\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge \frac{e^3}{16v^2}-\frac{3e^3}{64v^2}=\frac{e^3}{64v^2}.$$
This is the crossing lemma for simple graphs when $e\ge 4v$, with non-optimal constant $1/64$ allowed.
