node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.proof_body:
Let P\subset R^2 finite, |P|=n. Let U(P) be number of unordered pairs {p1,p2}\subset P, p1\neq p2, with |p1-p2|=1. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). The maximum exists: for fixed n, 0\le U(P)\le C(n,2), so the set of attained values is a non-empty finite subset of integers, hence has a max. We prove no exact formula. The provable best-known statement is: there exist absolute constants c,C,c'>0 and n0 such that for all n\ge n0 with loglog n>0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} \le U_max(n) \le C n^{4/3}. In particular no claim of exact determination, Theta-tightness, matching exponent, or best-possible is made; the gap remains open.

U_max is nondecreasing with exact preservation under far padding. Indeed fix P with |P|=n. Adding q\notin P cannot destroy pairs inside P, so U(P\cup{q})\ge U(P), whence U_max(n+1)\ge U_max(n). More strongly we can pad with no new pairs: \cup_{p\in P} closed B(p,2) is bounded, its complement is non-empty. Choose q with |q-p|>2 for all p\in P. Then |q-p|\neq 1 for all p, so no new unit pair involves q and U(P\cup{q})=U(P) exactly. Iterating, if we add k points successively each at distance >2 from all previous points, the witnessed count K is preserved exactly. Hence any configuration on m^2 points with K unit pairs extends to n>m^2 points with the same K pairs. Consequently U_max(n)\ge U_max(m^2) for n\ge m^2.

Hence it suffices to prove the upper bound for all large n and the lower bound for square cardinalities m^2\to\infty. Transfer to all n loses only constants. Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2\le n<(m+1)^2. For n\ge 4, m\ge sqrt(n)-1\ge sqrt(n)/2, i.e. m^2\ge n/4. Suppose for squares N=m^2 large we have U_max(N)\ge c0 N^{1+\delta_N} with \delta_N=c'/loglog N. Then by preservation U_max(n)\ge c0 N^{1+\delta_N}. Since N\le n, loglog N\le loglog n (for loglog>0), and log N= log(m^2)\ge log n-log 4. For n large, log n\ge 2 log 4 so log N\ge (1/2)log n. Hence N^{\delta_N}=exp(c' log N/loglog N)\ge exp((c'/2) log n/loglog n)=n^{c'/(2 loglog n)}. Since N\ge n/4, N^{1+\delta_N}\ge (n/4) n^{c'/(2 loglog n)}. Absorbing 1/4 into c and relabelling c'/2 as c', we get U_max(n)\ge c n^{1+c'/loglog n} for all sufficiently large n. This is the padding principle.

output.proof_body:
Let P\subset R^2 finite, |P|=n. Let U(P) be number of unordered pairs {p1,p2}\subset P, p1\neq p2, with |p1-p2|=1. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). The maximum exists: for fixed n, 0\le U(P)\le C(n,2), so the set of attained values is a non-empty finite subset of integers, hence has a max. We prove no exact formula. The provable best-known statement is: there exist absolute constants c,C,c'>0 and n0 such that for all n\ge n0 with loglog n>0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} \le U_max(n) \le C n^{4/3}. In particular no claim of exact determination, Theta-tightness, matching exponent, or best-possible is made; the gap remains open.

U_max is nondecreasing with exact preservation under far padding. Indeed fix P with |P|=n. Adding q\notin P cannot destroy pairs inside P, so U(P\cup{q})\ge U(P), whence U_max(n+1)\ge U_max(n). More strongly we can pad with no new pairs: \cup_{p\in P} closed B(p,2) is bounded, its complement is non-empty. Choose q with |q-p|>2 for all p\in P. Then |q-p|\neq 1 for all p, so no new unit pair involves q and U(P\cup{q})=U(P) exactly. Iterating, if we add k points successively each at distance >2 from all previous points, the witnessed count K is preserved exactly. Hence any configuration on m^2 points with K unit pairs extends to n>m^2 points with the same K pairs. Consequently U_max(n)\ge U_max(m^2) for n\ge m^2.

Hence it suffices to prove the upper bound for all large n and the lower bound for square cardinalities m^2\to\infty. Transfer to all n loses only constants. Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2\le n<(m+1)^2. For n\ge 4, m\ge sqrt(n)-1\ge sqrt(n)/2, i.e. m^2\ge n/4. Suppose for squares N=m^2 large we have U_max(N)\ge c0 N^{1+\delta_N} with \delta_N=c'/loglog N. Then by preservation U_max(n)\ge c0 N^{1+\delta_N}. Since N\le n, loglog N\le loglog n (for loglog>0), and log N= log(m^2)\ge log n-log 4. For n large, log n\ge 2 log 4 so log N\ge (1/2)log n. Hence N^{\delta_N}=exp(c' log N/loglog N)\ge exp((c'/2) log n/loglog n)=n^{c'/(2 loglog n)}. Since N\ge n/4, N^{1+\delta_N}\ge (n/4) n^{c'/(2 loglog n)}. Absorbing 1/4 into c and relabelling c'/2 as c', we get U_max(n)\ge c n^{1+c'/loglog n} for all sufficiently large n. This is the padding principle.

The maximum exists since up to isometry the distance-$1$ graph depends continuously on $P$ and the count is integer-valued; in any case $\sup$ is attained up to arbitrarily close perturbation and $U_{\max}(n)<\infty$ as $U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$.

Lemma (Monotonicity and far-away padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Indeed, given $P$ with $|P|=n$, there exists $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, whence $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$ and $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.

Proof. Let $P=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}$. Consider the finite set $P$ itself and the $n$ unit circles $S_{i}=\{x:|x-p_{i}|=1\}$. The union $P\cup\bigcup_{i}S_{i}$ is a finite union of points and $1$-dimensional circles, hence has Lebesgue measure zero and in particular does not cover $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. Pick any $q\in \mathbf{R}^{2}\setminus(P\cup\bigcup_{i}S_{i})$. Then $q\ne p_{i}$ and $|q-p_{i}|\ne 1$ for all $i$. Let $P'=P\cup\{q\}$, so $|P'|=n+1$. Unordered pairs of $P'$ are either both in $P$, whose distance-$1$ count is $U(P)$, or involve $q$, of which none has distance $1$ by construction. Hence $U(P')=U(P)$. Taking $P$ maximizing for $n$ gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')=U_{\max}(n)$. Iterating, adding $k$ such far points successively preserves all existing unit pairs and creates no new unit pairs involving the new points if each new point is chosen outside the finitely many forbidden points and circles determined by previous points. Thus padding does not decrease the count. $\square$

Corollary (Reduction to squares). To prove a lower bound of the stated shape it suffices to prove it for $n=m^{2}$ perfect squares, for all large $m$, and then pad to general $n$.

Indeed suppose for all large squares $N=m^{2}$ we have $U_{\max}(N)\ge c_{0}N^{1+c'/\log\log N}$ with absolute $c_{0},c'>0$. Let $n$ be general large and let $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, so $m^{2}\le n<(m+1)^{2}$. By monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^{2})$. For $n\ge 16$ say, $m\ge \sqrt{n}-1\ge \sqrt{n}/2$, so $m^{2}\ge n/4$. Moreover $\log\log(m^{2})\le \log\log n$

output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Define U(P)=|{{p1,p2} subset P : |p1-p2|=1}| unordered, p1!=p2, and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since 0<=U(P)<=binom{n}{2}, the max over n-sets exists as max of integers in bounded range. We prove no exact formula, no Theta-tightness, no matching exponent. Provable best-known statement: there exist absolute c,C,c'>0 and N0 such that for all n>=N0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. Upper and lower exponents do not match; large gap remains open. Upper is proved directly for all n; lower suffices on squares.

Lemma (Monotonicity with far-away padding). U_max is nondecreasing. More precisely adding a point cannot destroy pairs, and points far away create no new pair.

Proof. If P'=P cup {q}, q not in P, every unit pair of P persists in P'. Hence U(P')>=U(P)+|{p in P:|p-q|=1}|>=U(P). Taking P optimal for n gives U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n).

For equality-preserving padding, let S=P cup union_{p in P} C_p where C_p={x:|x-p|=1}. If q not in S then q distinct and |q-p|!=1 for all p, so U(P cup {q})=U(P). Such q exists arbitrarily far: S is finite set plus finite union of circles, of measure zero, so R^2\S nonempty. Explicitly, for M>2+max_{p in P}|p|, |(M,0)-p|>1 for all p, so (M,0) not in S. Iterate: given P_k, choose q_{k+1} outside P_k cup union_{p in P_k} C_p, far away, with U preserved. By induction any m^2-set pads to any n>m^2 with at least as many pairs, indeed with equality if desired. Hence U_max(N)>=U(P) for all N>=|P|. QED

Corollary (Reduction to squares). Suppose for large squares N=m^2>=N1 with loglog N>0, U_max(N)>=c0 N^{1+c0/loglog N}. Then same shape holds for all large n up to absolute constant.

Proof. Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2. Then N<=n<(m+1)^2 and U_max(n)>=U_max(N) by monotonicity. For n>=16, m>=3, sqrt(n)<m+1<=2m for m>=1, so m>sqrt(n)/2 and n/4<N<=n. Also log N>=log n-log 4 and loglog N<=loglog n (for loglog>0). Write exponent delta=c0/loglog N >= c0/loglog n. Then U_max(n)>=c0 N^{1+delta}. Since N>=n/4, N^{1+delta}=(n/4)^{1+delta} N^{delta}/(n/4)^{delta}? Direct: c0 N*N^{delta}>=c0 (n/4)*exp(c0 log N/loglog N). Now log N/loglog N >= (log n-log 4)/loglog n. Hence N^{c0/loglog N}>=n^{c0/loglog n} 4^{-c0/loglog n}. For n>=e^e, loglog n>=1 so 4^{-c0/loglog n}>=4^{-c0}. Thus U_max(n)>=c0 (n/4) n^{c0/loglog n} 4^{-c0}=c n^{1+c'/loglog n} with c'=c0, c=c0 4^{-1-c0}. Small loglog<=0 excluded by taking n large. QED

Therefore lower bound need only be built on m x m grid {0,...,m-1}^2 of size m^2, scaled to make popular distance 1, then padded far away to exactly n without loss of order apart from absolute factor. Upper O(n^{4/3}) is proved directly for all n via point-unit-circle incidences.

rollouts.solution_body:
We prove the weakened best-known statement and the monotonicity-padding principle. Let $P\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ finite, $|P|=n$, and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1\ne p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. Put $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n}U(P)$. The maximum exists since $U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$. We claim no exact formula, no $\Theta$-tightness and no matching exponent. The provable best-known form is: there exist absolute constants $c,C,c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,
$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$
In particular the upper and lower exponents do not match and a large gap remains open. It suffices to prove the upper bound for every $n$ and the lower bound for square cardinalities $N=m^2$, then transfer by monotonicity.

Lemma (monotonicity with far-away padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. More precisely, if $P$ is finite then there are points $q\notin P$ arbitrarily far away with $U(P\cup\{q\})\ge U(P)$, and indeed with equality if desired. Hence $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.

Proof. Let $|P|=n$ and let $P=\{p_1,\dots,p_n\}$. Any pair counted in $U(P)$ remains at distance $1$ after adding a new distinct point $q$; adding points cannot destroy existing pairs. Thus for any $q\notin P$, with $P'=P\cup\{q\}$,
$$U(P')\ge U(P),$$
since the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of $P$ persist. Taking $P$ optimal for $n$, i.e. $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$, and any $q\notin P$ gives a set of $n+1$ points with at least $U_{\max}(n)$ unit pairs, so $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.
For a controlled padding we choose $q$ far away creating no new unit pair. Let $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}C_p$ where $C_p=\{x:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. If $q\notin S$ then $|q-p|\ne 0,1$ for all $p\in P$, so $q$ is distinct and forms no unit pair with $P$, whence $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$. Such $q$ exists arbitrarily far: fix e.g. $p_0\in P$ and consider the ray $\{(M,0):M\in\mathbb{R},\,M\to+\infty\}$. For each fixed $p$, $|(M,0)-p|=1$ for at most two $M$, and $|(M,0)-p|=0$ for at most one $M$. Hence for all sufficiently large $M$, $(M,0)\notin S$. Explicitly choose $M>2+\max_{p\in P}|p|$; then $|(M,0)-p|>1$ for all $p$, in fact $\to\infty$. Thus far-away padding points exist. Iterating, from any $m^2$-set we obtain $n$-sets for any $n>m^2$ with at least as many unit pairs. In particular with zero new pairs if the $q$'s are chosen inductively outside all previous unit circles. This proves monotonicity. $\square$

Corollary (reduction to squares). Suppose for all sufficiently large integers $m$, with $N=m^2$,
$$U_{\max}(N)\ge c_0\, N^{1+c_0/\log\log N}$$
for some absolute $c_0>0$ (with $\log\log N>0$). Then there exist $c,c'>0$ and $n_1$ such that for all $n\ge n_1$,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n}.$$

Proof. Let $n$ be large and $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, $N=m^2$. Then $N\le n<(m+1)^2$ and by monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. Assume $m$ is large enough that the square bound applies and $\log\log N>0$. For $n\ge 16$, $m\ge 4$ and $\sqrt{n}<m+1\le 2m$, so $m>\sqrt{n}/2$ and
$$n/4 < N \le n.$$
Moreover $\log N\ge \log n-\log 4$ and $\log\log N\le \log\log n$. Hence, writing $N^{c_0/\log\log N}=\exp(c_0\log N/\log\log N)$,
$$\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\ge \frac{\log n-\log 4}{\log\log n}.$$
Thus
$$N^{c_0/\log\log N}\ge \exp\left(c_0\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}-c_0\frac{\log 4}{\log\log n}\right)=n^{c_0/\log\log n}\,4^{-c_0/\log\log n}.$$
For $n\ge e^{e}$ we have $\log\log n\ge 1$, so $4^{-c_0/\log\log n}\ge 4^{-c_0}$. Using $N\ge n/4$,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge c_0 N\cdot N^{c_0/\log\log N}\ge c_0\frac{n}{4}\,n^{c_0/\log\log n}\,4^{-c_0}.$$
Hence $c=c_0 4^{-1-c_0}$ and $c'=c_0$ work for all large $n$. The hypothesis $\log\log\le 0$ is excluded by taking $n$ large. This gives the quantitative transfer from $m^2$ to $n$ losing only an absolute constant factor. $\square$

Therefore the superlinear lower bound need only be constructed on the integer grid $\{0,\dots,m-1\}^2$ of size $m^2$, scaled to make the popular distance $1$, and then padded to arbitrary $n$ without loss of order. The upper bound $O(n^{4/3})$ is proved directly for all $n$ via point-unit-circle incidences and does not need padding.

output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Define U(P)=|{{p1,p2} subset P : |p1-p2|=1}| unordered, p1!=p2, and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since 0<=U(P)<=binom{n}{2}, the max over n-sets exists as max of integers in bounded range. We prove no exact formula, no Theta-tightness, no matching exponent. Provable best-known statement: there exist absolute c,C,c'>0 and N0 such that for all n>=N0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. Upper and lower exponents do not match; large gap remains open. Upper is proved directly for all n; lower suffices on squares.

Lemma (Monotonicity with far-away padding). U_max is nondecreasing. More precisely adding a point cannot destroy pairs, and points far away create no new pair.

Proof. If P'=P cup {q}, q not in P, every unit pair of P persists in P'. Hence U(P')>=U(P)+|{p in P:|p-q|=1}|>=U(P). Taking P optimal for n gives U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n).

For equality-preserving padding, let S=P cup union_{p in P} C_p where C_p={x:|x-p|=1}. If q not in S then q distinct and |q-p|!=1 for all p, so U(P cup {q})=U(P). Such q exists arbitrarily far: S is finite set plus finite union of circles, of measure zero, so R^2\S nonempty. Explicitly, for M>2+max_{p in P}|p|, |(M,0)-p|>1 for all p, so (M,0) not in S. Iterate: given P_k, choose q_{k+1} outside P_k cup union_{p in P_k} C_p, far away, with U preserved. By induction any m^2-set pads to any n>m^2 with at least as many pairs, indeed with equality if desired. Hence U_max(N)>=U(P) for all N>=|P|. QED

Corollary (Reduction to squares). Suppose for large squares N=m^2>=N1 with loglog N>0, U_max(N)>=c0 N^{1+c0/loglog N}. Then same shape holds for all large n up to absolute constant.

Proof. Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), N=m^2. Then N<=n<(m+1)^2 and U_max(n)>=U_max(N) by monotonicity. For n>=16, m>=3, sqrt(n)<m+1<=2m for m>=1, so m>sqrt(n)/2 and n/4<N<=n. Also log N>=log n-log 4 and loglog N<=loglog n (for loglog>0). Write exponent delta=c0/loglog N >= c0/loglog n. Then U_max(n)>=c0 N^{1+delta}. Since N>=n/4, N^{1+delta}=(n/4)^{1+delta} N^{delta}/(n/4)^{delta}? Direct: c0 N*N^{delta}>=c0 (n/4)*exp(c0 log N/loglog N). Now log N/loglog N >= (log n-log 4)/loglog n. Hence N^{c0/loglog N}>=n^{c0/loglog n} 4^{-c0/loglog n}. For n>=e^e, loglog n>=1 so 4^{-c0/loglog n}>=4^{-c0}. Thus U_max(n)>=c0 (n/4) n^{c0/loglog n} 4^{-c0}=c n^{1+c'/loglog n} with c'=c0, c=c0 4^{-1-c0}. Small loglog<=0 excluded by taking n large. QED

Therefore lower bound need only be built on m x m grid {0,...,m-1}^2 of size m^2, scaled to make popular distance 1, then padded far away to exactly n without loss of order apart from absolute factor. Upper O(n^{4/3}) is proved directly for all n via point-unit-circle incidences.

rollouts.solution_body:
We prove the weakened best-known statement and the monotonicity-padding principle. Let $P\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ finite, $|P|=n$, and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1\ne p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. Put $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n}U(P)$. The maximum exists since $U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$. We claim no exact formula, no $\Theta$-tightness and no matching exponent. The provable best-known form is: there exist absolute constants $c,C,c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,
$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$
In particular the upper and lower exponents do not match and a large gap remains open. It suffices to prove the upper bound for every $n$ and the lower bound for square cardinalities $N=m^2$, then transfer by monotonicity.

Lemma (monotonicity with far-away padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. More precisely, if $P$ is finite then there are points $q\notin P$ arbitrarily far away with $U(P\cup\{q\})\ge U(P)$, and indeed with equality if desired. Hence $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.

Proof. Let $|P|=n$ and let $P=\{p_1,\dots,p_n\}$. Any pair counted in $U(P)$ remains at distance $1$ after adding a new distinct point $q$; adding points cannot destroy existing pairs. Thus for any $q\notin P$, with $P'=P\cup\{q\}$,
$$U(P')\ge U(P),$$
since the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of $P$ persist. Taking $P$ optimal for $n$, i.e. $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$, and any $q\notin P$ gives a set of $n+1$ points with at least $U_{\max}(n)$ unit pairs, so $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$.
For a controlled padding we choose $q$ far away creating no new unit pair. Let $S=P\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}C_p$ where $C_p=\{x:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. If $q\notin S$ then $|q-p|\ne 0,1$ for all $p\in P$, so $q$ is distinct and forms no unit pair with $P$, whence $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$. Such $q$ exists arbitrarily far: fix e.g. $p_0\in P$ and consider the ray $\{(M,0):M\in\mathbb{R},\,M\to+\infty\}$. For each fixed $p$, $|(M,0)-p|=1$ for at most two $M$, and $|(M,0)-p|=0$ for at most one $M$. Hence for all sufficiently large $M$, $(M,0)\notin S$. Explicitly choose $M>2+\max_{p\in P}|p|$; then $|(M,0)-p|>1$ for all $p$, in fact $\to\infty$. Thus far-away padding points exist. Iterating, from any $m^2$-set we obtain $n$-sets for any $n>m^2$ with at least as many unit pairs. In particular with zero new pairs if the $q$'s are chosen inductively outside all previous unit circles. This proves monotonicity. $\square$

Corollary (reduction to squares). Suppose for all sufficiently large integers $m$, with $N=m^2$,
$$U_{\max}(N)\ge c_0\, N^{1+c_0/\log\log N}$$
for some absolute $c_0>0$ (with $\log\log N>0$). Then there exist $c,c'>0$ and $n_1$ such that for all $n\ge n_1$,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n}.$$

Proof. Let $n$ be large and $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, $N=m^2$. Then $N\le n<(m+1)^2$ and by monotonicity $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(N)$. Assume $m$ is large enough that the square bound applies and $\log\log N>0$. For $n\ge 16$, $m\ge 4$ and $\sqrt{n}<m+1\le 2m$, so $m>\sqrt{n}/2$ and
$$n/4 < N \le n.$$
Moreover $\log N\ge \log n-\log 4$ and $\log\log N\le \log\log n$. Hence, writing $N^{c_0/\log\log N}=\exp(c_0\log N/\log\log N)$,
$$\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\ge \frac{\log n-\log 4}{\log\log n}.$$
Thus
$$N^{c_0/\log\log N}\ge \exp\left(c_0\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}-c_0\frac{\log 4}{\log\log n}\right)=n^{c_0/\log\log n}\,4^{-c_0/\log\log n}.$$
For $n\ge e^{e}$ we have $\log\log n\ge 1$, so $4^{-c_0/\log\log n}\ge 4^{-c_0}$. Using $N\ge n/4$,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge c_0 N\cdot N^{c_0/\log\log N}\ge c_0\frac{n}{4}\,n^{c_0/\log\log n}\,4^{-c_0}.$$
Hence $c=c_0 4^{-1-c_0}$ and $c'=c_0$ work for all large $n$. The hypothesis $\log\log\le 0$ is excluded by taking $n$ large. This gives the quantitative transfer from $m^2$ to $n$ losing only an absolute constant factor. $\square$

output.proof_body:
We prove the crossing lemma for simple graphs from Euler's bound, with non-optimal constants, and extend to multiplicity <=2. Let G be finite graph drawn in R^2 with distinct point vertices and edges as continuous curves joining endpoints. Define cr(G) as minimum over drawings with no edge passing through a third vertex except at endpoints, no three edges concurrent interiorly, no tangencies, of number of interior intersection points. In an optimal drawing we may assume no two adjacent edges cross and no edge crosses itself: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, local rerouting near crossing eliminates it without creating new ones; similarly for self-crossings. Hence each crossing in optimal drawing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity: if H subset G as subgraph, cr(H) <= cr(G) by restriction.

Assume known: every simple planar graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=3V-6. This holds disconnected as well. Indeed let components have vi,ei. If vi=1 then ei=0. If vi=2 then ei<=1. If vi>=3 and planar then ei<=3vi-6. In all cases ei<=3vi-3 with strict -6 if single component vi>=3. Summing: for c components, e<=3v-3c unless c=1. If c>=2 then e<=3v-6. If c=1, v>=3 then e<=3v-6. So any simple planar v>=3 has e<=3v-6 connected or not.

Lemma (linear). For simple G with v vertices, e edges, cr(G)>=e-3v for all v, and cr(G)>=e-3v+6 if v>=3. Proof: Take optimal drawing with cr(G) crossings. While crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. This removes >=1 crossing. After at most cr(G) deletions we get planar crossing-free subgraph with v vertices and e'>=e-cr(G) edges. If v>=3, simplicity+planarity gives e'<=3v-6, so e-cr(G)<=3v-6 i.e. cr(G)>=e-3v+6. For v<3 simple graph has e<=1 and cr=0, and e-3v<0, so cr>=e-3v holds. Since e-3v+6>=e-3v, weaker bound holds for v>=3 too. No loops present; loops would need separate handling. Disconnected handled. The +6 form fails for v=2,e=1, hence need split.

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). If G simple, e>=4v then cr(G)>=e^3/(64v^2). Proof: Random induced subgraph. Keep each vertex independently with probability p in (0,1]. Let G_p induced with random vp,ep and cr_p = number of crossings of optimal drawing of G restricted to survivors. Then E[vp]=p v. Edge survives iff both endpoints survive: E[ep]=p^2 e. Crossing survives iff its four distinct endpoints survive, using no-adjacent-crossing property: E[cr_p]=p^4 cr(G). For each realization, cr_p>=ep-3vp by linear lemma valid for all vp including small. Taking expectations: p^4 cr(G)>=p^2 e-3p v, so cr(G)>=e/p^2-3v/p^3. If e>=4v set p=4v/e<=1. Then e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2) and 3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2), giving cr>=e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2). If v<=2 hypothesis e>=4v cannot hold for simple G (e<=1), so vacuous. Constants non-optimal.

Corollary (multiplicity <=2). Let H be multigraph with v vertices, e edges, no loops, multiplicity <=2. Then either e<8v or cr(H)>=e^3/(512v^2). Proof: For each parallel pair keep one representative; delete at most one per pair. Get simple spanning subgraph H' with same v and e'>=e/2, no loops. By monotonicity any drawing of H restricts to drawing of H' with no more crossings, so cr(H')<=cr(H). If e'<4v then e<=2e'<8v linear regime. If e'>=4v then simple lemma applies (v>=3 or vacuous, already handled) giving cr(H)>=cr(H')>=(e')^3/(64v^2)>=(e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2). In particular if e>=8v then e'>=4v and cubic bound holds. Thus split e<4v vs e>=4v for simple becomes e<8v vs e>=8v for multiplicity <=2 up to constants. Loops absent in arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points; disconnected already handled. Constants 64,512 non-optimal allowed.

Remark for application: with v=n and cr(H')<=n^2 this gives either e'=O(n) or (e')^3/n^2=O(n^2), hence e'=O(n^{4/3}) in all cases, similarly e=O(n^{4/3}). This upgrades weak bound to n^{4/3}.
output.solution_body:
Let $G$ be a finite graph drawn in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices as distinct points and edges as continuous curves joining their endpoints, with no edge passing through a third vertex except at endpoints, no three edges concurrent in an interior point, and no tangencies. Define $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ as the minimum number of interior intersection points of pairs of edges over such drawings, counting each transverse crossing once. We allow only drawings where adjacent edges do not cross and no edge crosses itself in an optimal drawing: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, a local rerouting near the crossing eliminates it without creating new crossings, and similarly for self-crossings. Hence in an optimal drawing each crossing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity holds: if $H\subseteq G$ as a (spanning or induced) subgraph, then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\le \mathrm{cr}(G)$, by restricting a drawing of $G$.

Assume known Euler bound: every simple planar graph with $V\ge 3$ vertices satisfies $E\le 3V-6$. We extend to possibly disconnected. Indeed let components have $v_i,e_i$. If $v_i=1$, $e_i=0=3v_i-3$. If $v_i=2$, $e_i\le 1\le 3v_i-3$. If $v_i\ge 3$ and planar, $e_i\le 3v_i-6\le 3v_i-3$. Hence for $c$ components, $e=\sum e_i\le 3v-3c$ unless a single component with $v\ge 3$ gives $e\le 3v-6$. If $c\ge 2$ then $e\le 3v-6$. If $c=1$ and $v\ge 3$ then $e\le 3v-6$. So any simple planar graph with $v\ge 3$ has $e\le 3v-6$, connected or not.

Lemma (linear). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$ for all $v$, and $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$ if $v\ge 3$.

Proof. Take an optimal drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. While a crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. Deleting that edge removes at least one crossing from the drawing. Hence after at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ deletions we obtain a planar (crossing-free) subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. If $v\ge 3$, planarity and simplicity give $e'\le 3v-6$, so $e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le 3v-6$, i.e. $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$. For $v<3$ a simple graph has $e\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge 0\ge e-3v$ holds since $e-3v\le 1-3<0$ for $v=1,2$ and $e=0$ for $v=0$. Since $e-3v+6\ge e-3v$, the weaker bound $\mathrm{cr}\ge e-3v$ holds for $v\ge 3$ as well. This covers disconnected graphs and avoids $v<3$ counterexample to the $+6$ form (e.g. $v=2,e=1$). No loops are present; loops would require separate handling. $\square$

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $e\ge 4v$. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(64v^2)$. Constants are non-optimal.

Proof. Use random induced subgraphs. Choose each vertex independently with probability $p\in(0,1]$ to be kept, and let $G_p$ be the induced subgraph with random $v_p,e_p$ and $\mathrm{cr}_p$ defined as the number of crossings of the optimal drawing of $G$ restricted to surviving vertices and edges. Then $\mathbb{E}[v_p]=pv$. An edge survives iff both endpoints survive, so $\mathbb{E}[e_p]=p^2e$. A crossing survives iff the four distinct endpoints of the two crossing edges all survive, by the no-adjacent-crossing property of the optimal drawing. Hence $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}_p]=p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)$. For each realization, the linear lemma in the form $\mathrm{cr}_p\ge e_p-3v_p$ holds (valid for all $v_p$ including small). Taking expectations, $p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge p^2e-3pv$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e/p^2-3v/p^3$.

If $e\ge 4v$, set $p=4v/e\le 1$. Then $e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2)$ and $3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2)$, giving $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2)$. If $v\le 2$ the hypothesis $e\ge 4v$ cannot hold for simple $G$ ($e\le 1$), so the implication is vacuous. This proves the claim. $\square$

Corollary (multiplicity at most $2$). Let $H$ be a multigraph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, no loops, and edge-multiplicity at most $2$. Then either $e<8v$ (linear regime) or $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge e^3/(512v^2)$. More precisely, passing to a simple subgraph loses at most a factor $2$.

Proof. For each parallel pair keep one representative edge; delete at most one per pair. Let $H'$ be the resulting simple spanning subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e/2$ edges, no loops. By monotonicity, any drawing of $H$ restricts to a drawing of $H'$ with no more crossings, so $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le \mathrm{cr}(H)$. If $e'<4v$ then $e\le 2e'<8v$, the trivial linear bound. If $e'\ge 4v$ (which implies $v\ge 3$ or vacuous small-$v$ as above, and in any case the simple crossing lemma applies), then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge \mathrm{cr}(H')\ge (e')^3/(64v^2)\ge (e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2)$. In particular, if $e\ge 8v$ then $e'\ge 4v$ and the cubic bound holds. The split $e<4v$ versus $e\ge 4v$ for simple graphs becomes $e<8v$ versus $e\ge 8v$ for multiplicity $\le 2$ up to constants. Disconnectedness is already handled by the planar bound; loops are absent in the arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points. Constants $64,512$ are non-optimal and allowed. $\square$

Remark. For the unit-distance application with $v=n$ and $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le n^2$, this gives either $e'=O(n)$ or $(e')^3/n^2=O(n^2)$, hence $e'=O(n^{4/3})$ in all cases, and similarly $e=O(n^{4/3})$.

objections.claim_attacked: An optimal drawing may be assumed good: adjacent edges do not cross, no self-crossings, and every crossing has four distinct endpoints, which is essential for E[cr_p]=p^4 cr(G).
objections.quote: We allow only drawings where adjacent edges do not cross and no edge crosses itself in an optimal drawing: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, a local rerouting near the crossing eliminates it without creating new crossings, and similarly for self-crossings.
objections.why: The one-sentence rerouting does not prove existence of an optimal good drawing. Edges may cross several times, rerouting one adjacent crossing can create other crossings or tangencies/concurrencies excluded by the drawing definition, and two edges crossing more than once is not excluded. The p^4 survival calculation fails if any counted crossing has only three distinct endpoints (survival p^3). This is standard and repairable by citing/proving the good-drawing lemma, including pairwise at-most-one crossing, but it is not proved as stated.
objections.cheap_test: Draw edges uv and uw crossing twice away from u; local swapping at one crossing need not remove the second and can change crossings with a fourth edge through the swapped region.

objections.claim_attacked: Applying the linear lemma to the random restricted drawing.
objections.quote: $\mathrm{cr}_p$ defined as the number of crossings of the optimal drawing of $G$ restricted to surviving vertices and edges.
objections.why: The linear lemma bounds cr(G_p), the minimum over drawings, not the crossing count cr_p of this particular restricted drawing. The needed inequality cr_p >= cr(G_p) >= e_p-3v_p is true but omitted. Without explicitly inserting cr(G_p), the expectation step formally applies the lemma to a non-optimal drawing.
objections.cheap_test: Take any non-optimal drawing of K4 with one crossing restricted from a larger graph: its drawing crossing count is an upper bound on cr(G_p), so the direction of the comparison must be stated.

objections.claim_attacked: Small-v vacuity in the simple crossing lemma, especially division by v^2 and p=4v/e.
objections.quote: If $v\le 2$ the hypothesis $e\ge 4v$ cannot hold for simple $G$ ($e\le 1$), so the implication is vacuous.
objections.why: For v=0, e=0 satisfies e>=4v (0>=0), p=0 is outside the stated p in (0,1], and e^3/(64v^2) is undefined. For v>0 with e>=4v the argument is fine, and the application has v=n large, so this is only a boundary repair: state v>=1 or v>=3 in the lemma.
objections.cheap_test: Substitute v=0,e=0 into e>=4v and into e^3/(64v^2).

objections.claim_attacked: Extension of cr and monotonicity from simple graphs to the multiplicity-at-most-2 multigraph H.
objections.quote: By monotonicity, any drawing of $H$ restricts to a drawing of $H'$ with no more crossings, so $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le \mathrm{cr}(H)$.
objections.why: cr was defined for a finite (simple) graph drawing; the corollary uses cr(H) for a multigraph with parallel edges sharing both endpoints without defining admissible drawings/crossings for parallel pairs or stating that an optimal H-drawing restricts to an admissible H'-drawing. The crossing number $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ is the minimum number of interior intersection points of distinct edges over all such drawings. Deleting edges cannot increase $\mathrm{cr}$: the restriction of a drawing of $G$ is a drawing of any subgraph with at most as many crossings. In an optimal drawing we may assume adjacent edges do not cross: if two edges sharing an endpoint cross, a local rerouting near the endpoint removes that crossing without creating new ones. Hence every crossing involves $4$ distinct vertices.

Assume first $G$ is simple, with $v$ vertices and $e$ edges. Recall Euler's bound: if $G'$ is simple planar with $v'\ge 3$ then $e'\le 3v'-6$. Indeed for connected $G'$, $v'-e'+f=2$ and each face has degree $\ge 3$ (no loops or $2$-cycles; a bridge is counted twice in the face walk, still giving length $\ge 3$), so $2e'\ge 3f$ and $2=v'-e'+f\le v'-e'/3$. For disconnected planar simple $G'$, let components have $v_i$ vertices and $e_i$ edges. If $v_i=1$, $e_i=0$; if $v_i=2$, $e_i\le 1$; if $v_i\ge 3$, $e_i\le 3v_i-6$ by the connected case. Summing, with $a$ large components, $b$ $2$-vertex components and $c$ isolated vertices, $e'\le 3\sum_{large}v_i-6a+b =3v-5b-3c-6a$. If $a\ge 1$ this is $\le 3v-6$; if $a=0$ then $e'\le v/2\le 3v-6$ for $v\ge 3$. Hence $e'\le 3v-6$ holds for any simple planar graph with $v\ge 3$.

Now let $G$ be simple with $v\ge 3$ and consider a drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. Delete one edge from each crossing pair. At most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges are deleted, leaving a planar (simple) subgraph $G'$ with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. If $G'$ still has $v\ge 3$, $e'\le 3v-6$, so $e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le 3v-6$, i.e.
$$ \mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6. $$
In particular $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$. For $v'<3$ we use the trivial bound: a simple graph has $e'\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}'=0\ge e'-3v'$. Combined with the above, for any induced subgraph $G'$ (any $v'$),
$$ \mathrm{cr}(G')\ge e'-3v' $$
with the convention $\mathrm{cr}\ge 0$. This avoids separate small-$v$ analysis later. For $v=1,2$ the bound $e-3v+6$ need not hold, but $e-3v$ does.

We upgrade to a cubic bound when $e$ is large. Suppose $G$ simple with $e\ge 4v$ (hence $v>0$). Choose $p=4v/e\le 1$ and form a random induced subgraph $G'$ by keeping each vertex independently with probability $p$. Let $v',e',c'$ be the numbers of vertices, edges, and crossings of $G'$ in the drawing inherited from an optimal drawing of $G$. Since $\mathrm{cr}(G')\le c'$, taking expectations and using $\mathrm{cr}(G')\ge e'-3v'$ pointwise,
$$ p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge \mathbb{E}[c']\ge \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}(G')]\ge \mathbb{E}[e'-3v']=p^2e-3pv. $$
Dividing by $p^4$, $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e/p^2-3v/p^3$. With $p=4v/e$,
$$ \frac{e}{p^2}=\frac{e^3}{16v^2},\quad \frac{3v}{p^3}=\frac{3e^3}{64v^2}, $$

$$ \mathrm{cr}(G)\ge \frac{e^3}{16v^2}-\frac{3e^3}{64v^2}=\frac{e^3}{64v^2}. $$

$$ \mathrm{cr}(G)\ge \mathrm{cr}(G_s)\ge \frac{e_s^3}{64v^2}\ge \frac{(e/2)^3}{64v^2}=\frac{e^3}{512v^2}. $$
Thus in all cases either $e=O(v)$ or $e^3=O(v^2\mathrm{cr}(G))$ with absolute constants. Disconnectedness is already covered since the Euler bound and expectation argument use no connectivity. output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.statement: We prove no exact formula. The provable best-known result is: there exist absolute constants c,C,c'>0 such that for all sufficiently large n, c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No matching exponent, no Theta, no best-possible tightness is claimed. U_max is well defined and nondecreasing, so lower bounds on square cardinalities imply bounds for all n by padding.
output.proof: Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P)=|{{p1,p2} subset P: |p1-p2|=1| unordered. Then 0<=U(P)<= binomial(n,2) integer. Hence the set of attained values for fixed n is a finite subset of integers, so U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P) exists and is finite; sup is attained. We claim only best-known upper and lower bounds with a large gap, not exact determination or Theta. In particular log log n requires n>e, and we work with n sufficiently large so log log n>0 and auxiliary number-theoretic estimates apply. Monotonicity under inclusion: if P subset Q then every unit pair of P is a unit pair of Q, so U(Q)>=U(P). Hence U_max is nondecreasing. Indeed let P* with |P*|=n and U(P*)=U_max(n). For any q not in P*, Q=P* union {q} has |Q|=n+1 and U(Q)>=U(P*). Taking max over |Q|=n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n). For padding we may choose q far away to preserve count exactly: let S=P* union union_{p in P*} S^1(p,1), finite union of points and unit circles, of Lebesgue measure zero. Its complement is non-empty and unbounded. Choosing q not in S gives dist(q,p)!=1 for all p in P* and q not in P*, so U(P* union {q})=U(P*). Iterating, any configuration on m^2 points can be extended to n>m^2 points with no loss of pairs (any extra pairs among padded points only increase U). Thus U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) for n>=m^2. It therefore suffices to construct lower-bound examples on square cardinalities N=m^2<=n and pad to n. Explicitly let m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2<=n<(m+1)^2. For n>=4, sqrt(n)>=2 so m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, hence m^2>=n/4. If we prove U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/log log(m^2)} for large m, then U_max(n)>=that. Since m^2>=n/4 and log log(m^2)=log log n+o(1), this transfers to >=c n^{1+c''/log log n} for large n after adjusting c,c''>0 absolute. Similarly upper bound proved for all n directly implies bound for squares. This padding principle allows us to assume N is a square grid size in the lattice construction.

node.label: SEC_1
node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.statement: We prove no exact formula. The provable best-known result is: there exist absolute constants c,C,c'>0 such that for all sufficiently large n, c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No matching exponent, no Theta, no best-possible tightness is claimed. U_max is well defined and nondecreasing, so lower bounds on square cardinalities imply bounds for all n by padding.
output.proof: Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P)=|{{p1,p2} subset P: |p1-p2|=1| unordered. Then 0<=U(P)<= binomial(n,2) integer. Hence the set of attained values for fixed n is a finite subset of integers, so U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P) exists and is finite; sup is attained. We claim only best-known upper and lower bounds with a large gap, not exact determination or Theta. In particular log log n requires n>e, and we work with n sufficiently large so log log n>0 and auxiliary number-theoretic estimates apply. Monotonicity under inclusion: if P subset Q then every unit pair of P is a unit pair of Q, so U(Q)>=U(P). Hence U_max is nondecreasing. Indeed let P* with |P*|=n and U(P*)=U_max(n). For any q not in P*, Q=P* union {q} has |Q|=n+1 and U(Q)>=U(P*). Taking max over |Q|=n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n). For padding we may choose q far away to preserve count exactly: let S=P* union union_{p in P*} S^1(p,1), finite union of points and unit circles, of Lebesgue measure zero. Its complement is non-empty and unbounded. Choosing q not in S gives dist(q,p)!=1 for all p in P* and q not in P*, so U(P* union {q})=U(P*). Iterating, any configuration on m^2 points can be extended to n>m^2 points with no loss of pairs (any extra pairs among padded points only increase U). Thus U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) for n>=m^2. It therefore suffices to construct lower-bound examples on square cardinalities N=m^2<=n and pad to n. Explicitly let m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2<=n<(m+1)^2. For n>=4, sqrt(n)>=2 so m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, hence m^2>=n/4. If we prove U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/log log(m^2)} for large m, then U_max(n)>=that. Since m^2>=n/4 and log log(m^2)=log log n+o(1), this transfers to >=c n^{1+c''/log log n} for large n after adjusting c,c''>0 absolute. Similarly upper bound proved for all n directly implies bound for squares. This padding principle allows us to assume N is a square grid size in the lattice construction.

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.statement: We prove no exact formula. The provable best-known result is: there exist absolute constants c,C,c'>0 such that for all sufficiently large n, c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No matching exponent, no Theta, no best-possible tightness is claimed. U_max is well defined and nondecreasing, so lower bounds on square cardinalities imply bounds for all n by padding.
output.proof: Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P)=|{{p1,p2} subset P: |p1-p2|=1| unordered. Then 0<=U(P)<= binomial(n,2) integer. Hence the set of attained values for fixed n is a finite subset of integers, so U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P) exists and is finite; sup is attained. We claim only best-known upper and lower bounds with a large gap, not exact determination or Theta. In particular log log n requires n>e, and we work with n sufficiently large so log log n>0 and auxiliary number-theoretic estimates apply. Monotonicity under inclusion: if P subset Q then every unit pair of P is a unit pair of Q, so U(Q)>=U(P). Hence U_max is nondecreasing. Indeed let P* with |P*|=n and U(P*)=U_max(n). For any q not in P*, Q=P* union {q} has |Q|=n+1 and U(Q)>=U(P*). Taking max over |Q|=n+1 gives U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n). For padding we may choose q far away to preserve count exactly: let S=P* union union_{p in P*} S^1(p,1), finite union of points and unit circles, of Lebesgue measure zero. Its complement is non-empty and unbounded. Choosing q not in S gives dist(q,p)!=1 for all p in P* and q not in P*, so U(P* union {q})=U(P*). Iterating, any configuration on m^2 points can be extended to n>m^2 points with no loss of pairs (any extra pairs among padded points only increase U). Thus U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) for n>=m^2. It therefore suffices to construct lower-bound examples on square cardinalities N=m^2<=n and pad to n. Explicitly let m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2<=n<(m+1)^2. For n>=4, sqrt(n)>=2 so m>sqrt(n)-1>=sqrt(n)/2, hence m^2>=n/4. If we prove U_max(m^2)>=c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/log log(m^2)} for large m, then U_max(n)>=that. Since m^2>=n/4 and log log(m^2)=log log n+o(1), this transfers to >=c n^{1+c''/log log n} for large n after adjusting c,c''>0 absolute. Similarly upper bound proved for all n directly implies bound for squares. This padding principle allows us to assume N is a square grid size in the lattice construction.

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.formal_statement: Let U(P) be number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} in finite P in R^2 with |p1-p2|=1, and U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). We prove best-known bounds: there exist absolute c,C,c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0, c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No exact determination, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness is claimed. U_max is nondecreasing, so lower bounds on square cardinalities imply bounds for all n by padding.
output.proof_body: U(P) is integer with 0 <= U(P) <= C(|P|,2). Hence for each n the maximum over |P|=n exists and is finite, 0 <= U_max(n) <= n(n-1)/2. We make no claim of exact value or Theta-tightness; the exponents 1+c'/loglog n below and 4/3 above do not match, and a large gap remains open. This is the best-known form. Monotonicity: If P subset Q then every unit pair of P is a unit pair of Q, so U(Q) >= U(P). In particular given P with |P|=n, pick q not in P; then Q=P union {q} has |Q|=n+1 and U(Q) >= U(P). Taking P optimal for n gives U_max(n+1) >= U_max(n). Hence U_max is nondecreasing. For a sharp padding we may choose q far away: let S = P union Union_{p in P} {x:|x-p|=1}, a finite union of points and circles, closed nowhere dense of measure zero. Choose q not in S and with |q| large. Then q creates no new unit pair with P, so U(P union {q})=U(P) exactly. Iterating gives exact extension. Consequently it suffices to construct lower-bound examples on square cardinalities. Indeed let m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2 and m^2 -> infinity with n. If for all large squares N=m^2 we have U_max(N) >= c0 N^{1+c'/loglog N}, then for general n >= n0, by monotonicity U_max(n) >= U_max(m^2) >= c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/loglog(m^2)}. Since m^2 > n/2 for large n (in fact m^2 = n-O(sqrt(n))), and loglog(m^2)=loglog n+o(1), this is >= c n^{1+c''/loglog n} after adjusting constants c,c''. Similarly upper bound proved for all n directly applies. Loglog is defined positive only for n>e; finitely many small n are absorbed by adjusting c,C and taking n0 large. Thus padding from m^2 to n loses only an absolute constant factor.

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.proof_body:
Define for finite P in R^2, U(P) = number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset of P with |p1-p2|=1. For integer n>=1 define U_max(n) = max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since U(P) is an integer in [0, C(n,2)], the maximum over configurations is attained; U_max(n) is well defined and finite, <= n(n-1)/2.

Provable best-known statement. We do NOT claim exact determination, matching exponent, Theta-tightness, or best-possible optimality. There is a large open gap. What is provable is: there exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n>=n0 with log log n>0,
  c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}.
In particular upper exponent 4/3 and lower exponent 1+Omega(1/log log n). No claim that 4/3 is sharp, that lower exponent is sharp, or that upper and lower meet up to constants.

Lemma (Monotonicity and padding). U_max is nondecreasing: U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) for all n. Hence lower-bound constructions on a subsequence imply bounds for all n by padding with far-away points without destroying existing unit pairs.

Proof. Let P with |P|=n attain U_max(n). Consider the finite set P and the n unit circles S(p,1) = {x:|x-p|=1} for p in P. The union F = P union (union_{p in P} S(p,1)) is a finite union of points and 1-dimensional circles, hence its complement in R^2 is nonempty (indeed co-infinite; e.g. take a point of norm larger than max_{p in P}|p|+2). Choose q not in F. Then q not in P so |P union {q}|=n+1, and for every p in P, |q-p| != 1 by q not in S(p,1). Hence no new unit pair involving q is created, and all old unit pairs in P are preserved:
  U(P union {q}) = U(P) = U_max(n).
Therefore U_max(n+1) = max_{|Q|=n+1} U(Q) >= U(P union {q}) = U_max(n). By induction, adding k points one by one far from all previous points and their unit circles preserves the count: for any m^2 <= n there is Q with |Q|=n and U(Q)>=U_max(m^2), so U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2).

Consequence for lower bounds. It suffices to construct, for arbitrarily large integers m, a set G of m^2 points with many pairs at a fixed distance, then scale to distance 1 and pad to general n. Explicitly, let m = floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2. For n>=16, sqrt(n)-1 >= sqrt(n)/2, so m^2 >= n/4. If we prove U_max(m^2) >= c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/log log(m^2)} for large m, then for general n, U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) gives the same shape up to adjustment of absolute constant c, using m^2 >= n/4 and comparability of log log(m^2) with log log n for large n. Small n with log log n <=0 are excluded by the n>=n0 qualification. Upper bounds need no padding. This reduces the lower-bound task to square cardinalities.

node.label: SEC_1
node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.proof_body:
Define for finite P in R^2, U(P) = number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset of P with |p1-p2|=1. For integer n>=1 define U_max(n) = max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since U(P) is an integer in [0, C(n,2)], the maximum over configurations is attained; U_max(n) is well defined and finite, <= n(n-1)/2.

Provable best-known statement. We do NOT claim exact determination, matching exponent, Theta-tightness, or best-possible optimality. There is a large open gap. What is provable is: there exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n>=n0 with log log n>0,
  c n^{1+c'/log log n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}.
In particular upper exponent 4/3 and lower exponent 1+Omega(1/log log n). No claim that 4/3 is sharp, that lower exponent is sharp, or that upper and lower meet up to constants.

Lemma (Monotonicity and padding). U_max is nondecreasing: U_max(n+1)>=U_max(n) for all n. Hence lower-bound constructions on a subsequence imply bounds for all n by padding with far-away points without destroying existing unit pairs.

Proof. Let P with |P|=n attain U_max(n). Consider the finite set P and the n unit circles S(p,1) = {x:|x-p|=1} for p in P. The union F = P union (union_{p in P} S(p,1)) is a finite union of points and 1-dimensional circles, hence its complement in R^2 is nonempty (indeed co-infinite; e.g. take a point of norm larger than max_{p in P}|p|+2). Choose q not in F. Then q not in P so |P union {q}|=n+1, and for every p in P, |q-p| != 1 by q not in S(p,1). Hence no new unit pair involving q is created, and all old unit pairs in P are preserved:
  U(P union {q}) = U(P) = U_max(n).
Therefore U_max(n+1) = max_{|Q|=n+1} U(Q) >= U(P union {q}) = U_max(n). By induction, adding k points one by one far from all previous points and their unit circles preserves the count: for any m^2 <= n there is Q with |Q|=n and U(Q)>=U_max(m^2), so U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2).

Consequence for lower bounds. It suffices to construct, for arbitrarily large integers m, a set G of m^2 points with many pairs at a fixed distance, then scale to distance 1 and pad to general n. Explicitly, let m = floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2. For n>=16, sqrt(n)-1 >= sqrt(n)/2, so m^2 >= n/4. If we prove U_max(m^2) >= c0 (m^2)^{1+c'/log log(m^2)} for large m, then for general n, U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) gives the same shape up to adjustment of absolute constant c, using m^2 >= n/4 and comparability of log log(m^2) with log log n for large n. Small n with log log n <=0 are excluded by the n>=n0 qualification. Upper bounds need no padding. This reduces the lower-bound task to square cardinalities.

node.label: SEC_1
node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.proof_body:
Let P subset R^2 be finite and let U(P) be the number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset P, p1 != p2, with |p1-p2|=1. For n>=1 define U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since U(P) is an integer in [0, C(n,2)], the set of attainable values is finite, so the maximum exists.

Theorem (best-known, not exact). There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No exact determination, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness and no best-possible claim is made. The gap remains open. We require n large so loglog n >0, e.g. n>=16.

Lemma (monotonicity and padding). U_max(n) is nondecreasing in n. Hence to lower bound U_max(n) it suffices to construct examples on square cardinalities m^2 <= n and pad to n.

Proof. Let |P|=n and q not in P, P'=P union {q}. Every unit pair of P remains a unit pair of P', since P subset P'. New pairs can only involve q, hence are >=0 in number. Thus U(P')>=U(P). Taking P extremal with U(P)=U_max(n) gives U_max(n+1)>=U(P')>=U(P)=U_max(n). So U_max is nondecreasing.

In particular if m^2 <= n then U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2). If a set G_m with |G_m|=m^2 has U(G_m)>=f(m^2), then U_max(n)>=f(m^2) for all n>=m^2. This is the padding principle.

For the lower bound we take m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2<=n<(m+1)^2 and m->infty as n->infty. For the inequality U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) any distinct padding points suffice, since extra pairs can only help the lower bound. If desired, padding can be done with no new unit distances: given finite P_j, the set union_{p in P_j}({p} union S^1(p)) where S^1(p) is the unit circle about p is a finite union of points and circles, whose complement in R^2 is nonempty. Choosing q_{j+1} in the complement preserves U exactly. This reduces the construction to squares and handles all large n, avoiding any claim about small n or loglog n <=0.

Let $P\subset \mathbf{R}^2$ be finite and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1
e p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. For $n\ge 1$ define $U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n} U(P)$. The maximum exists since there are finitely many pairs. We prove the best-known, not exact, bounds.

Theorem (weakened, best-known). There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$, $c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}$. No exact determination, no matching exponent, no $\Theta$-tightness and no best-possible claim is made. The gap remains open. We require $n$ large so $\log\log n>0$.

Lemma (monotonicity and padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Hence to lower bound $U_{\max}(n)$ it suffices to construct examples on square cardinalities $m^2\le n$ and pad to $n$.

Proof. Let $|P|=n$ and let $q
otin P$. Let $P'=P\cup\{q\}$. Every unit pair of $P$ remains a unit pair of $P'$. New pairs can only involve $q$, hence are $\ge 0$ in number. Thus $U(P')\ge U(P)$. Taking $P$ extremal with $U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$ gives $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')\ge U(P)=U_{\max}(n)$. So $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing.

In particular, if $m^2\le n$, then $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)$. If a set $G_m$ with $|G_m|=m^2$ has $U(G_m)\ge f(m^2)$, then $U_{\max}(n)\ge f(m^2)$ for all $n\ge m^2$. This is the padding principle.

For the lower bound we will take $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}floor$, so $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$ and $m	o\infty$ as $n	o\infty$. If desired, padding can be done with no new unit distances: given finite $P_j$, the set $ igcup_{p\in P_j}(\{p\}\cup S^1(p))$ where $S^1(p)$ is the unit circle about $p$ is a finite union of points and circles, whose complement in $\mathbf{R}^2$ is nonempty. Choosing $q_{j+1}$ in the complement and far away preserves $U$ exactly. For the inequality $U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)$ any distinct padding points suffice, since extra pairs can only help the lower bound. This reduces the construction to squares and handles all large $n$, avoiding any claim about small $n$ or $\log\log n\le 0$.

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.proof_body:
Let P subset R^2 be finite and let U(P) be the number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset P, p1 != p2, with |p1-p2|=1. For n>=1 define U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). Since U(P) is an integer in [0, C(n,2)], the set of attainable values is finite, so the maximum exists.

Theorem (best-known, not exact). There exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and n0 such that for all n >= n0, c n^{1+c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C n^{4/3}. No exact determination, no matching exponent, no Theta-tightness and no best-possible claim is made. The gap remains open. We require n large so loglog n >0, e.g. n>=16.

Lemma (monotonicity and padding). U_max(n) is nondecreasing in n. Hence to lower bound U_max(n) it suffices to construct examples on square cardinalities m^2 <= n and pad to n.

Proof. Let |P|=n and q not in P, P'=P union {q}. Every unit pair of P remains a unit pair of P', since P subset P'. New pairs can only involve q, hence are >=0 in number. Thus U(P')>=U(P). Taking P extremal with U(P)=U_max(n) gives U_max(n+1)>=U(P')>=U(P)=U_max(n). So U_max is nondecreasing.

In particular if m^2 <= n then U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2). If a set G_m with |G_m|=m^2 has U(G_m)>=f(m^2), then U_max(n)>=f(m^2) for all n>=m^2. This is the padding principle.

For the lower bound we take m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2<=n<(m+1)^2 and m->infty as n->infty. For the inequality U_max(n)>=U_max(m^2) any distinct padding points suffice, since extra pairs can only help the lower bound. If desired, padding can be done with no new unit distances: given finite P_j, the set union_{p in P_j}({p} union S^1(p)) where S^1(p) is the unit circle about p is a finite union of points and circles, whose complement in R^2 is nonempty. Choosing q_{j+1} in the complement preserves U exactly. This reduces the construction to squares and handles all large n, avoiding any claim about small n or loglog n <=0.

$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$

rollouts.solution_body:
Let $P\subset \mathbf{R}^2$ be finite and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1\ne p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. For $n\ge 1$ put
$$U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n} U(P).$$
Since $0\le U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$ is integer-valued, the maximum exists. We prove the best-known, non-tight statement. No exact formula, no $\Theta$-matching, no best-possible exponent is claimed; the gap remains open.

Claim: There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,
$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$
In particular $\log\log n$ is defined and $>0$ for $n\ge n_0$ (e.g. $n_0\ge 16$). The upper bound holds for all $n$ after adjusting $C$; the lower bound is asymptotic.

Lemma (Monotonicity and lossless padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Moreover given any finite $P$ there is $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$.

Proof: If $P\subset Q$ then every unit pair of $P$ is a unit pair of $Q$, so $U$ is monotone under inclusion: $U(Q)\ge U(P)$. Hence to get $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$ it suffices to extend an extremal set. Let $P^*$ with $|P^*|=n$ achieve $U_{\max}(n)$. Consider
$$F = P^* \cup \bigcup_{p\in P^*} S(p,1),$$
where $S(p,1)=\{x:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. $F$ is a finite union of points and $1$-dimensional circles, hence has Lebesgue measure zero and in particular $F\ne \mathbf{R}^2$. Choose $q\in \mathbf{R}^2\setminus F$. Then $q\notin P^*$ and $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P^*$. Let $P'=P^*\cup\{q\}$. Then $|P'|=n+1$ and no pair involving $q$ is at distance $1$, while all old pairs persist. Hence $U(P')=U(P^*)=U_{\max}(n)$. Therefore $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')=U_{\max}(n)$. Iterating, $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing. $\square$

Corollary (Reduction to squares). To prove the lower bound it suffices to prove it for cardinalities $m^2$, $m$ integer large, and then pad to general $n$.

Indeed suppose for all large integers $m$ there is a set $G_m$ with $|G_m|=m^2$ and $U(G_m)\ge c_0 m^2\cdot 2^k$ with $2^k\ge m^{c_1/\log\log m}$ as will be constructed later. Then for general $n$, let $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, so $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$. By monotonicity,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)\ge c_0 m^{2+c_1/\log\log m}.$$
Since $m>\sqrt{n}/2$ for large $n$ and $\log\log m = \log\log n+o(1)$, this transfers to $c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for suitable absolute $c,c'>0$ after adjusting constants. Lossless padding above shows we may add $n-m^2<2m+1$ far-away points inductively, each chosen outside the finite union of existing points and unit circles, preserving the count exactly; a fortiori $U_{\max}(n)\ge U(G_m)$. Hence the $m^2$ construction implies the general-$n$ bound. The upper bound $O(n^{4/3})$ will be proved directly for every $n$.

Remark: This explicitly weakens \"what is $U_{\max}(n)$?\" to best-known upper and lower bounds. We do not claim $\Theta(n^{4/3})$, $\Omega(n^{4/3})$, tightness, or matching exponents.

rollouts.solution_body:
Let $P\subset \mathbf{R}^2$ be finite and let $U(P)$ be the number of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subset P$, $p_1\ne p_2$, with $|p_1-p_2|=1$. For $n\ge 1$ put
$$U_{\max}(n)=\max_{|P|=n} U(P).$$
Since $0\le U(P)\le \binom{n}{2}$ is integer-valued, the maximum exists. We prove the best-known, non-tight statement. No exact formula, no $\Theta$-matching, no best-possible exponent is claimed; the gap remains open.

Claim: There exist absolute constants $c>0$, $C>0$, $c'>0$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,
$$c\, n^{1+c'/\log\log n} \le U_{\max}(n) \le C\, n^{4/3}.$$
In particular $\log\log n$ is defined and $>0$ for $n\ge n_0$ (e.g. $n_0\ge 16$). The upper bound holds for all $n$ after adjusting $C$; the lower bound is asymptotic.

Lemma (Monotonicity and lossless padding). $U_{\max}(n)$ is nondecreasing in $n$. Moreover given any finite $P$ there is $q\notin P$ with $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P$, so $U(P\cup\{q\})=U(P)$.

Proof: If $P\subset Q$ then every unit pair of $P$ is a unit pair of $Q$, so $U$ is monotone under inclusion: $U(Q)\ge U(P)$. Hence to get $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U_{\max}(n)$ it suffices to extend an extremal set. Let $P^*$ with $|P^*|=n$ achieve $U_{\max}(n)$. Consider
$$F = P^* \cup \bigcup_{p\in P^*} S(p,1),$$
where $S(p,1)=\{x:|x-p|=1\}$ is the unit circle centred at $p$. $F$ is a finite union of points and $1$-dimensional circles, hence has Lebesgue measure zero and in particular $F\ne \mathbf{R}^2$. Choose $q\in \mathbf{R}^2\setminus F$. Then $q\notin P^*$ and $|q-p|\ne 1$ for all $p\in P^*$. Let $P'=P^*\cup\{q\}$. Then $|P'|=n+1$ and no pair involving $q$ is at distance $1$, while all old pairs persist. Hence $U(P')=U(P^*)=U_{\max}(n)$. Therefore $U_{\max}(n+1)\ge U(P')=U_{\max}(n)$. Iterating, $U_{\max}$ is nondecreasing. $\square$

Corollary (Reduction to squares). To prove the lower bound it suffices to prove it for cardinalities $m^2$, $m$ integer large, and then pad to general $n$.

Indeed suppose for all large integers $m$ there is a set $G_m$ with $|G_m|=m^2$ and $U(G_m)\ge c_0 m^2\cdot 2^k$ with $2^k\ge m^{c_1/\log\log m}$ as will be constructed later. Then for general $n$, let $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$, so $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$. By monotonicity,
$$U_{\max}(n)\ge U_{\max}(m^2)\ge c_0 m^{2+c_1/\log\log m}.$$
Since $m>\sqrt{n}/2$ for large $n$ and $\log\log m = \log\log n+o(1)$, this transfers to $c\,n^{1+c'/\log\log n}$ for suitable absolute $c,c'>0$ after adjusting constants. Lossless padding above shows we may add $n-m^2<2m+1$ far-away points inductively, each chosen outside the finite union of existing points and unit circles, preserving the count exactly; a fortiori $U_{\max}(n)\ge U(G_m)$. Hence the $m^2$ construction implies the general-$n$ bound. The upper bound $O(n^{4/3})$ will be proved directly for every $n$.

Remark: This explicitly weakens \"what is $U_{\max}(n)$?\" to best-known upper and lower bounds. We do not claim $\Theta(n^{4/3})$, $\Omega(n^{4/3})$, tightness, or matching exponents.

node.input_summary: Subproblem 1: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle

output.title: Weakened statement, monotonicity, and padding principle
output.formal_claim: We prove best-known bounds, not exact determination: there exist absolute constants c>0, C>0, c'>0 and N0 such that for all n >= N0, c * n^{1 + c'/loglog n} <= U_max(n) <= C * n^{4/3}. No claim of matching exponent, Theta-tightness, or best-possible exact value is made. U_max is monotone nondecreasing, and it suffices to prove the lower bound for square cardinalities m^2 with padding to general n.
output.proof:
Let P finite in R^2, |P|=n. Let U(P) be number of unordered pairs {p1,p2} subset P, p1!=p2, with |p1-p2|=1. Let U_max(n)=max_{|P|=n} U(P). The max exists since for fixed n the count is integer in [0, C(n,2)] and the condition is closed; U_max(n) <= n(n-1)/2 < infinity.

We do not determine U_max exactly. The exponent gap is open. We prove only the stated upper O(n^{4/3}) and lower Omega(n^{1+c'/loglog n}) for large n. In particular no Theta claim.

Monotonicity: U_max(n+1) >= U_max(n). Indeed let P_n achieve U_max(n). Let S = P_n union (union_{p in P_n} S^1(p,1)), where S^1(p,1) is unit circle centred at p. S is finite union of 1-dimensional circles plus finite set, hence not equal to R^2; its complement is non-empty. Pick q not in S. Then q distinct from P_n and |q-p| != 1 for all p in P_n. Let P_{n+1}=P_n union {q}. Every unit pair of P_n remains a unit pair of P_{n+1}, and any pair involving q contributes >=0. Hence U(P_{n+1}) >= U(P_n)=U_max(n). Taking max over (n+1)-sets, U_max(n+1) >= U(P_{n+1}) >= U_max(n).

Iterating, adding k points successively outside the finite union of unit circles of the current set preserves all old pairs. Thus any construction on m points yields for any n>=m a construction on n points with at least as many unit pairs.

Padding from squares: Let n large, m=floor(sqrt(n)), so m^2 <= n < (m+1)^2 = m^2+2m+1, and n-m^2 <= 2m+1 <= 3 sqrt(n). If we construct Q_m with |Q_m|=m^2 and U(Q_m) >= f(m^2) for some nondecreasing f, then by padding n-m^2 far points as above we obtain P_n with |P_n|=n and U(P_n) >= U(Q_m) >= f(m^2). Hence U_max(n) >= f(m^2). Since m^2 = n - O(sqrt(n)) >= n/2 for large n (e.g. n>=16), and f is of form t^{1+c'/loglog t}, we have f(m^2) >= c_1 n^{1+c_1'/loglog n} after adjusting constants, using loglog(m^2)=loglog n + o(1). Explicit transfer is done in lower-bound section; monotonicity justifies reduction to m^2.

Henceforth assume n >= N0 large enough that loglog n >0 (e.g. n>e) and m>=4, and prove upper bound for all n and lower bound for m^2 then transfer. Adding points far away never destroys existing unit distances.

Step2 Pruned arc graph: for circle with ki incidences discard if ki<=2 losing at most 2n; if ki>=3 order points cyclically and join consecutive by circle arcs giving e_arc>=I-2n, v=n, no arc contains third P-point in interior. Need lattice lower scaled by 1/sqrt(R) and point vs unit-circle incidence upper I=2U. No Theta, no exact value, no best-possible matching claim; gap remains open.
output.primary_route: Step0 Monotonicity and reduction: pad from squares to all n avoiding finitely many unit circles. Let C be n unit circles centered at P, distinct centers give distinct circles, no point on own circle, so I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly. Two points in at most 2 unit circles, two unit circles in at most 2 points, so incidence graph K2,3-free but K2,2 occurs. Step1 Weak bound: by Kovari-Sos-Turan for K2,3-free, I(m,N)=O(m N^{1/2}+N) and symmetrically, in particular I(n,n)=O(n^{3/2}). Prove double-count of V shapes. Step2 Cutting bootstrap: take random sample of circles, build 1/r-cutting of arrangement of unit circles into O(r^2) cells each meeting O(N/r) circles, plus handling of points on cell boundaries by recursion or direct circle bound. Use pseudo-segment property of circles cut at vertical tangencies to get cutting lemma for circles with standard Clarkson-Shor sampling; tangencies give zero crossings, intersections in P handled as boundary points. Derive recurrence I(m,N) <= O(r^2) I(m/r^2, N/r)+O(r N + m). Optimize r to get I(m,N)=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N). Specialize m=N=n to O(n^{4/3}), hence U=O(n^{4/3}). Constants non-optimal. Step3 Lower number theory: R=product of first k distinct primes 1-mod-4, cite r2(R)=4*2^k via sum-of-two-squares divisor formula, R odd non-square so orbits size 8 giving 2^{k-1} unordered directions. Cite quantitative prime theorem kth 1-mod-4 prime O(k log k) so log R=O(k log k) via Chebyshev-type bound, no full PNT needed beyond upper. Step4 Maximal k choice: m=floor(sqrt(n)), choose k maximal with R<=m^2/16 so sqrt(R)<=m/4. Then log R lower bound forces k>=c log m/loglog m and 2^k>=m^{c/loglog m}. Step5 Geometry counting: Gm grid m^2 points, for each vector v with |v|^2=R have |vx|,|vy|<=m/4 so translates inside >=(m-|vx|)(m-|vy|)>=m^2/2 uniformly. Sum over ordered vectors r2(R), divide by 2 for unordered, get Omega(m^2 2^k) pairs at distance sqrt(R). Scale by 1/sqrt(R) to distance 1, pad to n losing constant, transfer exponent to n^{1+c/loglog n}. Naive grid alone insufficient.

active_obligations: O1 Prove I=2U exactly and K2,3-free with at most 2 circles through 2 points. O2 Prove weak KST bound I=O(m N^{1/2}+N). O3 Prove 1/r-cutting for unit circles with O(r^2) cells and correct recurrence to O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N), handling tangencies, P-points on boundaries, and constants. O4 Prove r2=4*2^k, log R=O(k log k), maximal k gives both sqrt(R)<=m/4 and 2^k>=m^{c/loglog m}. O5 Prove uniform translate bound >=m^2/2, divide by 2, scaling and padding to all n with loglog transfer.
output.next_task: Execute cutting recurrence in full and primorial maximal-k calculation with explicit constants.

risky_lemmas: Cutting lemma for circles with O(r^2) cells and recurrence constants; r2 formula application to squarefree product; primorial upper bound log R=O(k log k) without full PNT-AP.

Need (a) scaled integer grid lower with R product of k distinct 1-mod-4 primes giving many representations, (b) upper via I(P,C)=2U(P) for n points vs n unit circles centered at P. No Theta, no exact value, no matching exponent claimed; gap remains open.
output.primary_route: Step0 Monotonicity and unordered vs ordered: pad from squares to all n with points far from all existing unit circles. Step1 Incidence reduction: C = {S(p,1): p in P} are n distinct circles, p not on own circle, each unit pair gives 2 incidences, so I=2U exactly. Two points in at most 2 unit circles, two circles in at most 2 points, so K2,3-free but K2,2 occurs. Step2 Pseudo-segment reduction distinct from cyclic arc-graph: remove O(n) vertical-tangent points, split each circle minus leftmost/rightmost points into open upper and lower x-monotone arcs. Each incidence with non-extreme point lies on exactly one piece, extremes charged separately O(n). Obtain m<=2n pseudo-segments, N=n points, same I up to O(n). Claim any two pieces from distinct circles meet at most twice, and after splitting upper-vs-upper and lower-vs-lower they meet at most once: two unit circles meet at most twice with one meeting in upper-upper only if transverse; prove by monotonicity and circle geometry. Treat upper family and lower family separately. Step3 Crossing lemma for simple graphs from Euler E<=3V-6, random sampling to cr>=e^3/64v^2 for e>=4v, constants non-optimal. Build incidence graph per family by connecting consecutive points along each x-ordered piece, prune pieces with <=2 points losing O(m), multiplicity at most 2 reduced to simple losing factor 2, vertices = N incidence points, edges ~ I. Crossings bounded by pair budget: two pseudo-segments cross at most once if same type, so cr<= number of pairs O(m^2)=O(n^2). Tangencies give 0, P-points are vertices not crossings. Deduce I=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N)=O(n^{4/3}), hence U=O(n^{4/3}). Step4 Lower: R=product of first k 1-mod-4 primes, r2(R)=4*2^k by sum-of-two-squares divisor formula for squarefree case, no zero/diagonal as R odd non-square, orbit size 8 gives 2^{k-1} unordered directions. Cited quantitative prime theorem gives log R=O(k log k). With m=floor(sqrt(n)) choose k maximal with R<=m^2/16 so sqrt(R)<=m/4. Then k>=c log m/loglog m and 2^k>=m^{c/loglog m}. Grid G={0..m-1}^2 has for each vector v with |v|^2=R at least (m-|vx|)(m-|vy|)>=m^2/2 translates. Sum directed then divide by 2 gives Omega(m^2 2^k) pairs at distance sqrt(R). Scale by 1/sqrt(R) to distance 1, pad to n, transfer exponent to n^{1+c/loglog n}.

node.input_summary: Generate candidate research strategy for problem: Given a finite set P of n points in R^2, let U(P) be the num...

analysis.plan: Need distinct route from crossing arc-graph primorial route while preserving correct architecture. Upper must still get O(n^4/3) but via different proof of unit-circle incidence bound: polynomial partitioning / cutting method rather than pruned cycle-arc crossing graph. Lower must still get n^{1+c/loglog n} but via different number-theoretic presentation: divisor construction with averaging / pigeonhole over radii rather than maximal-k primorial with explicit m^2/16 cutoff. Must weaken best possible / Theta to best-known gap. Must keep I=2U exact, K2,3-free not K2,2-free, monotonicity padding.

output.normalized_problem: For finite P in R^2, |P|=n, let U(P) count unordered pairs at distance 1, Umax(n)=max U(P), monotone by far-away padding. Prove best-known bounds: there exist absolute c,C,c1>0 such that for large n, c n^{1+c1/loglog n} <= Umax(n) <= C n^{4/3}. Upper via n points vs n distinct unit circles centered at P with I=2U. Lower via integer grid scaled by 1/sqrt(R) where R has many representations as sum of two squares. No Theta, no exact value, no Omega(n^{4/3}) claim.
output.primary_route: Step0 Monotonicity and reduction: padding lemma, distinct centers imply distinct unit circles, p not on own circle, so I(P,C)=2U(P) exactly, at most 2 unit circles through 2 points. Step1 General incidence via polynomial partitioning: prove I(m,N)=O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) for points vs distinct unit circles by induction using degree-D partitioning polynomial. Use Guth-Katz / Kaplan et al. version: R^2 cut by Z of degree D into O(D^2) cells each with O(m/D^2) points; bound cell incidences by weak KST K2,3-free bound O((m_cell)^{2/3?} actually O(m_cell^{3/2}? ) combined carefully, plus incidences on Z via Bezout: each circle meets Z in O(D) points unless circle component of Z (at most O(D) such circles), control separately. Optimize D ~ m^{1/3}N^{-1/3} to get m^{2/3}N^{2/3}. Specialize m=N=n to get O(n^{4/3}). This avoids pruned arc-graph and crossing lemma entirely. Step2 Weak base needed for cells: prove K2,3-free Kovari-Sos-Turan I=O(m N^{2/3}+N) or O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) weak version via double counting of pairs on same circle. Step3 Lower via averaging over R: consider square grid G_m, count pairs at all distances sqrt(r) for r<=Rmax, sum_{r} N_r = Omega(m^4 / Rmax?) or total pairs in disk, then pigeonhole exists r with many representations. Refine to r product of 1-mod-4 primes to guarantee r_2(r)=2^{k+2}. Use divisor formula for squarefree product and quantitative prime number theorem for arithmetic progression to keep r <= m^2/100 while 2^k >= m^{c/loglog m}. Boundary loss uniform because displacement <= sqrt(r) <= m/10. Scale by 1/sqrt(r) and pad to all n. Gives Omega(n^{1+c/loglog n}). Naive grid alone gives only linear.
backup_routes: Backup1: lifting + cuttings proof of same incidence bound: cut circles into O(N) pseudo-segments via vertical decomposition, apply general cutting lemma to get O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}) without polynomials, kept as alternative verification. Backup2: inversion at a point to reduce unit-circle incidences to line-circle or line incidences with dyadic richness decomposition, remark only. Backup3: elementary lower bound Omega(n log n / loglog n) by divisor averaging without PNT-AP if prime theorem unavailable, explicitly weakened. Rejected as primary: Euler V=O(n^2) planarization, straight-line unit-distance graph, K2,2-free, I-n identity, line Szemeredi-Trotter applied directly to circles, sampling alone upgrading weak to strong circularly.
output.first_hard_obstruction: Upper obstruction distinct from arc-crossing concurrency: making polynomial partition induction close with correct exponents requires controlling incidences on the partition curve Z. Each unit circle not contained in Z meets Z in at most 2D+O(1) points by Bezout, but circles contained in Z must be bounded by O(D) in number via degree argument, and points on Z need inductive hypothesis with careful splitting of m0 vs m_cell. Choice of D must balance cell term vs curve term to yield m^{2/3}N^{2/3}. Lower obstruction: finding R simultaneously small (sqrt(R)<<m) and highly representable (2^k large) needs quantitative distribution of 1-mod-4 primes; averaging alone gives only log factor, need primorial product with log R = O(k log k) and pigeonhole maximality.
active_obligations: O1 Prove I=2U exact with distinctness and K2,3-free, at most 2 circles through 2 points. O2 Prove weak KST incidence as base for partition cells. O3 Prove polynomial partitioning incidence bound: existence of D-partition, cell decomposition O(D^2) cells, Bezout intersection bound, components bound, induction to O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N), optimize D. O4 Prove r2 formula for squarefree product of k distinct 1-mod-4 primes, primorial size estimate via cited quantitative prime theorem, existence of small highly representable radius, uniform translate count, ordered-unordered division, scaling and padding with loglog transfer. O5 Weaken Theta and best-possible-tightness to best-known upper and lower with large-n qualification.
output.next_task: Execute polynomial-partition incidence lemma fully with explicit Bezout and component bounds and induction, then execute averaging-primorial lower bound with full prime estimate and boundary count.
output.concrete_next_task: Write Lemma 1 (I=2U and K2,3-free), Lemma 2 (weak KST), Lemma 3 (polynomial partition incidence O(m^{2/3}N^{2/3}+m+N) with D choice), Theorem upper specialization, Lemma 4 (r2 and primorial size), Lemma 5 (grid translates and scaling), Theorem lower with padding.
output.readiness_assessment: Outline survives, detail needs proof: partition curve handling and prime size estimate are the two hard steps not yet executed; no complete proof yet.
risky_lemmas: Polynomial partitioning existence and cell incidence summation closing to m^{2/3}N^{2/3} without circularity; Bezout bound for circles vs degree-D curve and bound on circles contained in Z; quantitative 1-mod-4 primorial estimate log R=O(k log k) and simultaneous smallness plus large 2^k.

preserved_critiques.claim: Do not claim Theta, exact, best-possible tight, or Omega(n^{4/3}) lower; do not use naive Euler V=O(n^2) giving O(n^2); do not use straight-line graph; do not claim K2,2-free; do not use I-n; do not claim KST alone gives n^{4/3}; do not apply line Szemeredi-Trotter to circles; tangency and concurrency issues in arc-graph route are bypassed here but Bezout and component issues replace them and must be proved.

analysis.plan: Need distinct route from crossing arc-graph primorial route while preserving correct architecture.
