Must weaken best possible / Theta to best-known gap. Must keep I=2U exact, K2,3-free not K2,2-free, monotonicity padding.

falsifier_report.assessment: The normalized target is correct and the overall architecture is plausible: I(P,C)=2U(P) for distinct unit circles centered at P, a point-unit-circle incidence bound O(m^(2/3)N^(2/3)+m+N) specializing to O(n^(4/3)), and a grid scaled by 1/sqrt(r) for r a squarefree product of many 1-mod-4 primes giving n^(1+c/loglog n). However this is not yet a complete proof. The polynomial-partition upper bound is only sketched and contains a misstated or circular weak KST base, an unproved cell-summation, and unresolved incidences for points and circles on the partitioning curve. The lower bound is essentially the primorial construction again, not averaging alone, and still needs the quantitative prime estimate and maximal or explicit choice of k. Best-possible, Theta, exact, and Omega(n^(4/3)) claims must remain withdrawn.
unresolved_to_preserve: Preserve unresolved: the full polynomial-partition incidence lemma with points on Z and contained circles; the correct non-circular weak KST base and how it is used only inside cells or as a fallback; the quantitative primorial estimate log R = O(k log k) for primes 1 mod 4; the explicit choice of k giving simultaneously r <= m^2/100 and 2^k >= m^(c/loglog m); monotonicity padding from square grids to all large n; withdrawal of Theta, exact, and best-possible-tight claims.
minimal_weakenings: Weaken the claim to: the outline reduces the theorem to two citable or provable hard lemmas, namely a Kaplan-Guth-Katz type point-unit-circle incidence bound and a quantitative prime-product estimate. If the partition-on-Z step cannot be completed, fall back to the crossing arc-graph proof or state the incidence bound as a cited theorem with hypotheses checked. If PNT for arithmetic progressions is not allowed, weaken the lower bound to the elementary divisor-averaging bound such as Omega(n log n / loglog n) rather than n^(1+c/loglog n). Keep large-n qualification and exclude small n where loglog n is nonpositive.
dropped_objections: No objection is dropped to the exact identity I=2U, to distinct centers giving distinct circles, to K_{2,3}-freeness rather than K_{2,2}-freeness, to at most two unit circles through two points, to monotonicity by far-away padding, to scaling a grid by 1/sqrt(r), or to the boundary estimate when sqrt(r) <= m/10. The arc-graph tangency and concurrency objections are genuinely bypassed by the partition route, but they are replaced by partition-curve objections rather than eliminated from the proof burden.
weakest_lemmas: Weakest are Lemma 3, the polynomial-partition incidence bound, especially summation over cells and treatment of Z and contained circles; Lemma 2, the weak KST statement, whose exponent is misstated and whose strong form would be circular; and Lemma 4, the simultaneous smallness and high representability of r via primes 1 mod 4. Lemma 5 grid translation is comparatively routine once sqrt(r) <= m/10 and representation counting conventions are fixed.
hidden_assumptions: Assumes a degree-D partitioning polynomial exists with O(D^2) open cells each containing O(m/D^2) points for arbitrary finite point sets and for the needed range of D; assumes each unit circle not contained in Z crosses O(D) cells; assumes real Bezout can be applied through complex projective closure without common components; assumes contained circle components have degree exactly 2 and are counted by D/2; assumes induction can be applied to points on Z despite those points having special algebraic structure; assumes D can be optimized continuously and rounded without regime errors; assumes the kth prime congruent to 1 mod 4 is O(k log k) or an equivalent Chebyshev bound in arithmetic progression; assumes padding points can be added far away while preserving all existing unit pairs and adding none needed for the lower bound; assumes ordered signed representations convert to unordered point pairs by exactly division by 2 after excluding zero and diagonal vectors, which is valid here only because r is odd and not a square in the chosen squarefree 1-mod-4 product case and because no representation has a zero coordinate or |a|=|b| unless proved.
boundary_cases: Need handle n small and loglog n <= 0; m=N and also general m,N regimes for the incidence lemma; D<1 or D larger than sqrt(m); points exactly on Z; circles tangent to Z; circles contained in Z; coincident or repeated circles excluded by distinct centers but must be stated; points on their own center circle impossible for radius 1; k=0 or k=1 in the lower bound; representations with zero coordinate, repeated absolute values, or sign symmetries for general r not of the chosen form; grid boundary when |v_x| or |v_y| is close to m; padding from m^2 to arbitrary n between consecutive squares; tangency giving one intersection rather than two in any auxiliary circle-intersection count.
theorem_misuse: Potential misuse includes citing Kovari-Sos-Turan with exponent N^(2/3) instead of the pair-counting exponent, using the target incidence bound as its own base case, applying Bezout to count point-circle incidences on Z rather than circle-curve intersections, invoking Guth-Katz partitioning as if it directly partitions circles rather than points, applying Szemeredi-Trotter for lines to unit circles without a valid pseudo-segment or polynomial argument, and citing the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions only qualitatively when a quantitative upper bound for the product of the first k such primes is required. The formula r_2(r)=2^(k+2) is valid only under the squarefree distinct 1-mod-4 prime hypothesis and a stated ordered-signed convention.

hmed_records.revised_draft:
Let $G$ be a finite graph drawn in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices as distinct points and edges as continuous curves joining their endpoints, with no edge passing through a third vertex except at endpoints, no three edges concurrent in an interior point, and no tangencies. Define $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ as the minimum number of interior intersection points of pairs of edges over such drawings, counting each transverse crossing once. We allow only drawings where adjacent edges do not cross and no edge crosses itself in an optimal drawing: if two edges sharing an endpoint crossed, a local rerouting near the crossing eliminates it without creating new crossings, and similarly for self-crossings. Hence in an optimal drawing each crossing involves two edges with four distinct endpoints. Monotonicity holds: if $H\subseteq G$ as a (spanning or induced) subgraph, then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\le \mathrm{cr}(G)$, by restricting a drawing of $G$.

Assume known Euler bound: every simple planar graph with $V\ge 3$ vertices satisfies $E\le 3V-6$. We extend to possibly disconnected. Indeed let components have $v_i,e_i$. If $v_i=1$, $e_i=0=3v_i-3$. If $v_i=2$, $e_i\le 1\le 3v_i-3$. If $v_i\ge 3$ and planar, $e_i\le 3v_i-6\le 3v_i-3$. Hence for $c$ components, $e=\sum e_i\le 3v-3c$ unless a single component with $v\ge 3$ gives $e\le 3v-6$. If $c\ge 2$ then $e\le 3v-6$. If $c=1$ and $v\ge 3$ then $e\le 3v-6$. So any simple planar graph with $v\ge 3$ has $e\le 3v-6$, connected or not.

Lemma (linear). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v$ for all $v$, and $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$ if $v\ge 3$.

Proof. Take an optimal drawing with exactly $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ crossings. While a crossing remains, delete an edge participating in some crossing. Deleting that edge removes at least one crossing from the drawing. Hence after at most $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ deletions we obtain a planar (crossing-free) subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e-\mathrm{cr}(G)$ edges. If $v\ge 3$, planarity and simplicity give $e'\le 3v-6$, so $e-\mathrm{cr}(G)\le 3v-6$, i.e. $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e-3v+6$. For $v<3$ a simple graph has $e\le 1$ and $\mathrm{cr}(G)=0$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge 0\ge e-3v$ holds since $e-3v\le 1-3<0$ for $v=1,2$ and $e=0$ for $v=0$. Since $e-3v+6\ge e-3v$, the weaker bound $\mathrm{cr}\ge e-3v$ holds for $v\ge 3$ as well. This covers disconnected graphs and avoids $v<3$ counterexample to the $+6$ form (e.g. $v=2,e=1$). No loops are present; loops would require separate handling. $\square$

Lemma (crossing lemma, simple). Let $G$ be simple with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $e\ge 4v$. Then $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(64v^2)$. Constants are non-optimal.

Proof. Use random induced subgraphs. Choose each vertex independently with probability $p\in(0,1]$ to be kept, and let $G_p$ be the induced subgraph with random $v_p,e_p$ and $\mathrm{cr}_p$ defined as the number of crossings of the optimal drawing of $G$ restricted to surviving vertices and edges. Then $\mathbb{E}[v_p]=pv$. An edge survives iff both endpoints survive, so $\mathbb{E}[e_p]=p^2e$. A crossing survives iff the four distinct endpoints of the two crossing edges all survive, by the no-adjacent-crossing property of the optimal drawing. Hence $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cr}_p]=p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)$. For each realization, the linear lemma in the form $\mathrm{cr}_p\ge e_p-3v_p$ holds (valid for all $v_p$ including small). Taking expectations, $p^4\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge p^2e-3pv$, so $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e/p^2-3v/p^3$.

If $e\ge 4v$, set $p=4v/e\le 1$. Then $e/p^2=e^3/(16v^2)$ and $3v/p^3=3e^3/(64v^2)$, giving $\mathrm{cr}(G)\ge e^3/(16v^2)-3e^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(64v^2)$. If $v\le 2$ the hypothesis $e\ge 4v$ cannot hold for simple $G$ ($e\le 1$), so the implication is vacuous. This proves the claim. $\square$

Corollary (multiplicity at most $2$). Let $H$ be a multigraph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, no loops, and edge-multiplicity at most $2$. Then either $e<8v$ (linear regime) or $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge e^3/(512v^2)$. More precisely, passing to a simple subgraph loses at most a factor $2$.

Proof. For each parallel pair keep one representative edge; delete at most one per pair. Let $H'$ be the resulting simple spanning subgraph with $v$ vertices and $e'\ge e/2$ edges, no loops. By monotonicity, any drawing of $H$ restricts to a drawing of $H'$ with no more crossings, so $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le \mathrm{cr}(H)$. If $e'<4v$ then $e\le 2e'<8v$, the trivial linear bound. If $e'\ge 4v$ (which implies $v\ge 3$ or vacuous small-$v$ as above, and in any case the simple crossing lemma applies), then $\mathrm{cr}(H)\ge \mathrm{cr}(H')\ge (e')^3/(64v^2)\ge (e/2)^3/(64v^2)=e^3/(512v^2)$. In particular, if $e\ge 8v$ then $e'\ge 4v$ and the cubic bound holds. The split $e<4v$ versus $e\ge 4v$ for simple graphs becomes $e<8v$ versus $e\ge 8v$ for multiplicity $\le 2$ up to constants. Disconnectedness is already handled by the planar bound; loops are absent in the arc-graph application since pruned cycle arcs join distinct consecutive points. Constants $64,512$ are non-optimal and allowed. $\square$

Remark. For the unit-distance application with $v=n$ and $\mathrm{cr}(H')\le n^2$, this gives either $e'=O(n)$ or $(e')^3/n^2=O(n^2)$, hence $e'=O(n^{4/3})$ in all cases, and similarly $e=O(n^{4/3})$.
